units.la: Libellus hic, DE MAGISTRATVVM IN SVBDITOS IVRE, ITIDEMQVE SVBDITORVM ERGA MAGISTRATVS SVOS OFFICIO, (admodum Illustris ac Generose Comes ac Domine, Domine clementissime) antehac, anno scilicet à nato Christo, 1576. in Gallia excusus, &c. à viro quodam, literarum fautore summo, ante menses aliquot mihi transmissus est. Hunc dignum iudicaui, qui meis sumptibus in publicum prodiret. Comperi enim, vtrique ordini & lectu vtilem fore & scitu apprime necessarium esse; hoc praesertim tempore turbulentissimo, quo Satanas, acerrimus ille Christi & vere Christiano-rum hostis, infidus ac molitionibus suis & organorum suorum, Anti-Christo Romano, Babylonicae meretrici, adhaerentium (Efauitas volo) omnia sursum deorsum volvere, magistratuum animum paternum a subditis alienum facere, vicissimque obedientiam subditorum, magistratui debitam, labefactare; & hac demum arrepta occasione, ferro flammaque omnes, se suosque non adorantes, perdere, omniaque illorum bona evertere (quod DEVS tamen clementer proprohibet) maximopere nititur. Viro itaque cuidam docto præsentem hunc libellum, ut relegeret & emacularet, indiceque rerum & verborum memorabilium locuplete donaret, tradidi.
units.tr: This little book, ON THE RIGHT OF MAGISTRATES OVER THEIR SUBJECTS, AND ON THE DUTY OF SUBJECTS TOWARDS THEIR MAGISTRATES, (Most Illustrious and Noble Count and Lord, my most gracious Lord), was printed in France some time ago, in the year of Christ 1576, and a certain man, a great lover of literature, sent it to me a few months since. I judged it worth publishing at my own expense. For I found that it would be useful to read for both orders and very necessary to know, especially in this most turbulent time, when Satan, that most bitter enemy of Christ and of true Christians, faithless and with his schemes and his instruments, the adherents of the Roman Antichrist, the Babylonian harlot (I mean the Jesuits), strives with all his might to turn everything upside down: to make the paternal mind of magistrates alien to their subjects, to weaken in turn the obedience of subjects owed to the magistrate, and finally, seizing on this opportunity, to destroy by sword and fire all who do not worship him and his, and to overthrow all their goods (which God, in his mercy, forbid). Therefore I handed this present book to a learned man, so that he might reread and correct it, and furnish it with a full index of notable matters and words.

Farewell, father of your country, with your noble wife and illustrious offspring. Given at Frankfurt on the Kalends of August, in the year 1608.

units.la: DE IVRE MAGISTRATVVM IN SVBDITOS, ET OFFICIO subditorum erga Magistratus.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE RIGHT OF MAGISTRATES OVER THEIR SUBJECTS, AND THE DUTY OF SUBJECTS TOWARD MAGISTRATES.

units.la: QVÆSTIO I.
units.tr: QUESTION I.

units.la: An, ut Deo sine exceptione obediendum, ita & magistratibus.
units.tr: Whether obedience is to be rendered to magistrates without exception, as it is to God.

units.la: OLA vnius Dei Opt. Max. voluntas cum perpetua fit, & immutabilis omnis Iustitiæ Regula, illi soli sine exceptione parendum esse dicimus. Quod vero ad obedientiam Principibus debitam attinet, vtique fi ex Dei ore perpetuo imperarent, tanquam Deo illis quoq; semper, & sine exceptione, obedien-dum esset: At cum plerumque contrarium illis eueniat, addenda est ad illam hæc conditio, dum nihil vel impium, vel iniquum præcipiant. Impia mandata voco, siue irreligiosa, quæ aut ea iubent, quæ Deus in prima Legis suæ tabula vetat, aut ea vetant, quæ in illa & Deus præcipit. Iniqua vero præcepta dico, quiquibus id fieri inhibetur, vel non fieri iubetur, quod quisque pro sua vocatione, aut publica, aut priuata, proximo ex charitate debet.
units.tr: Since the will of the one God, most good and great, is perpetual and unchangeable, and every rule of justice is likewise unchangeable, we say that obedience is to be given to him alone, without exception. As for the obedience due to princes, certainly if they commanded continually from the mouth of God, they would have to be obeyed always and without exception, just as God is. But since the opposite usually happens, this condition must be added to that obedience: provided they command nothing either impious or unjust. I call commands impious or irreligious those which order what God forbids in the first table of his Law, or forbid what God commands in that table. I call commands unjust those which forbid, or order not to be done, what each person owes to his neighbour out of love, whether in a public or a private calling.

units.la: Hoc porro tum rationibus, tum manifestis exemplis probare non erit difficile. Ait Dominus per Esaiam Prophetam, cap. 48. verf. 11. Gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Quamuis autem non ita perspicue Dominus locutus esset, reipsa tamen constat, non posse fine scelere edicta, ex solo hominum arbitrio manantia, iis exaequari, quae Deus ipse mandauit. At par esset, aequalisque Dei & hominum authoritas, si hominibus perinde ac Deo, fine exceptione, parere semper esset necesse. Addo etiam, quoties Dei iussa hominum mandatis postponuntur, toties homines supra Dei thronum euehi. Iam ad exempla veniamus.
units.tr: To prove this both by reasons and by clear examples will not be difficult. The Lord says through the prophet Isaiah, ch. 48, verse 11: My glory I will not give to another. Although the Lord has not spoken so plainly elsewhere, it is in fact clear that edicts arising from the mere will of men cannot be placed on a level with what God himself has commanded without wickedness. Yet there would be an equal authority of God and men if it were always necessary to obey men without exception, just as God. I add also that as often as the commands of God are set after the commands of men, so often men are raised up above the throne of God. Now let us come to examples.

units.la: Pharaonis edictum, Exod. 1. verf. 21. de occidendis omnibus pueris masculis Hebraeorum, iniquum erat, eique merito obstetrices parere recusarunt, quarum domibus seu familiis idcirco Deus benedixit. Nabuchadnezaris autem, de statua aurea adoranda, edictum, Daniel 3. plane impium & irreligiosum fuit: Et ideo Danielis socii, illi obtemperare nolentes, pietatis & constantiae suę Deum approbatores, idq; manifesto miracuraculo, habuerunt. Mandatum autem Icsi-belis,1.Reg.18.verf.13. de occidendis Dei Prophetis,& impium & simul iniquum fuit: pie ergo fecit Abdias qui illos non modo non occidit,sed viuos & occultauit & aluit. Cum porro Antiochus 1. Machab. iuberet, Idolis sacrificia offerri, sacrosanctas ceremonias violari,& diuina scripta Prophetarum legisque igne comburi: sanctè certe illius furori, qui reliqui erant fideles Duce Mathathia, sese opposuerunt. Principes etiam sacerdotum, &summum scribarum cocilium, cum Euangelii prædicationem suis minis prohibere conarentur; tantum abest, vt illis Christus, aut post eū Apostoli, morem gesserint, vt ille quidem sæpe publice in templo, illis inuitis, concionaretur; Iohan. 9.22. Hi vero aperte responderint, se malle Deo obsequi quam hominibus. Actor. 5.22. Quorum exemplum constantissime postea sancti Martyres sunt sequuti. Itaque rursus infero: Magistratuum omnium authoritatem (quantumuis magna potentia & imperio sint præditi) duabus hisce metis, à Deo ipso positis, veluti septis, concludi, PIETATE scilicet & CHARITATE: Quas si transilire ipsis contigerit, meminisse iuuabit Apostolici illius dicti; Præstat Deo quam hominibus obedire: nec vel ex eorum fimus caterua, quibus Dominus
units.tr: Pharaoh's edict, Exod. 1, verse 21, concerning the killing of all the male children of the Hebrews, was unjust, and the midwives rightly refused to obey it; for this reason God blessed their houses or families. The edict of Nebuchadnezzar, Dan. 3, concerning the adoration of the golden statue, was plainly impious and irreligious; and therefore Daniel's companions, refusing to obey it, had God as the approver of their piety and constancy, and this by a manifest miracle. The command of Jezebel, 1 Kings 18, verse 13, concerning the killing of the prophets of God, was both impious and at the same time unjust; so Obadiah acted piously, for he not only did not kill them but hid them alive and fed them. Again, when Antiochus, 1 Macc., ordered that sacrifices be offered to idols, the holy ceremonies be violated, and the divine writings of the prophets and the Law be burnt with fire, those who remained faithful under the leader Mattathias rightly set themselves against his fury. The chief priests and the high council of the scribes, when they tried by their threats to forbid the preaching of the Gospel, were so far from obeying them that Christ, and after him the Apostles, did not comply: Christ often preached publicly in the temple against their will, John 9:22; and they answered openly that they would rather obey God than men, Acts 5:22. The holy martyrs afterwards followed their example most steadfastly. Therefore I infer again: the authority of all magistrates, however great their power and command, is enclosed by two boundaries set by God himself, as by hedges, namely PIETY and CHARITY. If they happen to leap over these, let them remember that saying of the Apostle: It is better to obey God than men. Nor should we be among those of whom the Lord

units.la: minus per Michæam, Mich. 6. 16. maledicit, quod impiis Regis fui mandatis obedient; vel peruersa corum exempla imitemur, qui immanissimos etiam tyrannos, tàquam Deos adorarūt, Dei & titulos & effectaillis tribuentes. Quod de Domitiano præcipue testaturimpurus ille Poeta Martialis, cum scribereaufus est, Editum Domini Deique no- stri. Vtinam vero hoc nostro seculo non in- ueniatur, quiab adulatione eiusmodi haud longe absint.
units.tr: complains through Micah, Mic. 6:16, because they obey the impious commands of their kings; nor should we imitate the perverse examples of those who worshipped even the most savage tyrants as gods, ascribing to them both the titles and the deeds of God. Of Domitian in particular the unclean poet Martial bears witness to this, when he dared to write: The edict of our Lord and God. Would that in our own age such men, who are not far removed from such flattery, were not to be found.

units.la: QVÆSTIO II.
units.tr: QUESTION II.

units.la: Quousque iustum esse, quod mandatur, præsumi possit?
units.tr: How far may what is commanded be presumed to be just?

units.la: Hoc vero iacto fundamento, lubet et- iam in quedâ alia inquirere, quæ ad hoc argumentum pertinere videntur, vt multo- rum cöscientiis satisfiat. Primo autem quæ- ritur, Num Magistratus teneatur, omnium le- gum suarum cuius rationem reddere, vt & quas & pias esse comprobet? Respondeo, Non tenerì: Quinimo æquum esse, vt probi omnes subditi probe de dominis suis senti- ant, nihilque iniusti deillis aut præsumant aut suspicentur: imo nec decere, vt de rebus etiam dubiis nimis curiose priuati homines inquirant, præter suum vel captum, vel co- ditionem. Si quorum tamen hæsitat consci- entia, possunt illi ac debent etiam (modeste
units.tr: Having laid this foundation, I now wish to inquire into certain other matters that seem to belong to this subject, so that the consciences of many may be satisfied. The first question is this: is the magistrate bound to give an account of all his laws, to show that they are both just and pious? I answer that he is not bound. Indeed, it is fitting that all good subjects should think well of their rulers and neither presume nor suspect anything unjust in them. Nor is it proper for private persons to inquire too curiously into even doubtful matters, beyond their own understanding or station.

units.la: tamen & pacifice) scrutari, quid rationis & iustitiæ mandato infit, quo aliquid facere veliubentur vel inhibentur: stat enim fir- mum Apostoli dictum, Rom. 14.23. Quicquid fit fine fide (id est dubitante conscientia, iu- fteneid fiat, an secus) peccatum est. Caeterum, fiaperte irreligiosum autiniquum est, quod præcipitur, tum, quæ supra dicta sunt, locum habeant.
units.tr: If, nevertheless, someone's conscience hesitates, such people can and ought (modestly and peacefully, however) to examine what reason and justice require in the command by which they are bidden or forbidden to do something, for the Apostle's firm saying stands: Rom. 14.23, Whatever is done without faith (that is, with a doubting conscience, as to whether it is done rightly or not) is sin. Moreover, if what is commanded is plainly irreligious or unjust, then what has been said above applies.

units.la: QVÆSTIO III.
units.tr: QUESTION III.

units.la: Quousque obedientia iniquis impiisve manda-tis, aut præstanda aut neganda sit?
units.tr: How far must obedience be rendered to unjust or impious commands, or must it be refused?

units.la: Præterea quæritur, Quousque hæc sententia, de non obseruandis irreligiosis iniquisve Magistratuum edictis, extendenda sit? Hic respondeo: Vnicuique considerandum, quid sua ferat conditio ac vocatio, siue generalis sea sit ac publica, siue privata. Edicitne Magistratus, vt id agas quod Deus prohibet? (quemadmodum Pharao Ægyptiacis obstetricibus, Exod. 1.16. & Herodes suis sattellitibus Matth. 2.17. mandans, vt bimulos omnes trucida-rent) tum recte officio fungeris, si manda-tum eiusmodi non fueris executus. Sicut de Lam. Papin. clarissimo Iurisconsulto Papiniano legi-mus, qui, etsi Christianus non erat, maluit tamen à tyranno Caracalla occidi, quam fratri-
units.tr: Next it is asked how far this principle, that impious or unjust edicts of magistrates are not to be obeyed, must be extended. My answer is this: each person must consider what his condition and calling require, whether it is general and public or private. Does the magistrate order you to do what God forbids? (As Pharaoh commanded the Egyptian midwives, Exod. 1.16, and Herod commanded his soldiers to slaughter all the male children, Matt. 2.17.) Then you discharge your duty rightly if you do not carry out such a command. So we read of the most distinguished jurist Papinian, who, although he was not a Christian, preferred to be put to death by the tyrant Caracalla rather than either approve the fratricide he had committed or defend it by his advocacy.

units.la: Lam. Papin. ... ICC.
units.tr: Lam. Papin. ... ICC.

units.la: fratricidium quod patrarat, vel probare vel suo pitrocinio defendere.
units.tr: Papinian's fratricide, either to approve it or to defend it by his advocacy.

units.la: Sin vero id tyrannus vetat, quod Deus mandat, nequaquam te officio defunctum putes, si simpliciter obedire tyranno recu- saueris, nisi & Dei simul mandato obtempe- res, sicut Abdiam fecisse diximus, 1Reg.18.13. qui non solum Prophetas Dei non intere- mit, sed etiam seruauit & educauit, contra Achabi & Iezabelis mandatum; Quoniam scilicet iubet Dominus, fratribus periculi- tantibus, quantum pro sua cuique vocatio- ne licet, opem ferre. Sic & Apostoli Act.5.(vt supra diximus) non solum non cessarunt ab Euangelii praedicatione, vt sacerdotibus ob- sequerentur; sed contra, constanter praedi- carunt vbiq;: quoniam hoc mandatum ex- presse a Domino acceperant, Ite, praedicate Euangelium omni creaturæ, &c. Matth.28.
units.tr: But if the tyrant forbids what God commands, you should not think yourself free of duty if you simply refuse to obey the tyrant, unless you at the same time obey the command of God. So Obadiah did, as we said above, 1 Kings 18.13, who not only did not kill the prophets of God but also preserved and fed them, against the command of Ahab and Jezebel. For the Lord commands that, when brothers are in danger, each person should give help as far as his calling allows. So also the Apostles, Acts 5 (as we said above), not only did not cease preaching the gospel in order to obey the priests, but on the contrary preached constantly everywhere, because they had received this command expressly from the Lord: "Go, preach the gospel to every creature," etc., Matt. 28.

units.la: Cum ergo hodie videmus plerofq; Magistratus ita fasicinatos ab Antichristo Romano, vt seuerissimis mandatis subditos, execrando Missæ sacrificio adesse, cogant; piorum omnium officium requirit, non so- lum vt id non praestent, verum etiam, vt Ec- liæ ac Elisæi, totius denique veteris puræ & veræ Ecclesiæ exemplo, sese piis coetibus adiungant, ibi verbum Dei audiant, Sacra- mentisque communicent, prout Christus id sse-
units.tr: Therefore, when today we see many magistrates so bewitched by the Roman Antichrist that they compel their subjects by the most severe commands to attend the execrable sacrifice of the Mass, the duty of all the pious requires not only that they do not comply, but also that, following the example of the Church and of Elisha, and indeed of the whole of the old, pure and true Church, they join themselves to pious assemblies, hear the word of God there, and partake of the sacraments, as Christ commanded to be done in the Church.

units.la: id fieri in Ecclesia praecepit, Idem quoq; ob-feruare conuenit in officiis, quae homines hominibus tam iure diuino quam naturae debent, vtpote liberi parentibus, vxor mari- to, pastor gregi, & in summa proximus pro- ximo. Ab iis enim non decet nos vllis vel e- dictis, vel minis, vel etiam iniustissimis poe- nis, ab flerreri aut abducit modo, ne quicquam obedientiae (quam imprimis Deo debemus, qui his omnibus maior est) ex huiusmodi praestitis officiis, decedat.
units.tr: The same principle should also be observed in those duties which men owe to men by divine right as much as by natural law: children to parents, wife to husband, minister to flock, and in short neighbour to neighbour. For we ought not to be turned aside or led away from these duties by any edicts, threats, or even the most unjust punishments, so that nothing of obedience (which we owe first of all to God, who is greater than all of these) is lost from the duties thus performed.

units.la: QVAESTIO IV.
units.tr: QUESTION IV.

units.la: Quomodo a Magistratu iniuriam passus, sese aduersus illum tueri possit?
units.tr: How may one who has suffered injury from a magistrate defend himself against him?

units.la: HInc etiam quaeri solet, Quid bona conscientia virpius tum agere debeat, aut possit, cum Magistratus ipsum quidem ministrum sua iniqui- tatis non facit, sed in illum ipsum iniuriae est? Haec quaestio, quia pluribus constat membris, di- stinctione opus habet. Si ergo Magistratus qui subdito iniuriam intulit, alteri superio- ri Magistratui subesset, licebit, per leges, iniu- riam passo ad supremum Magistratum re- currere: sicut Paulum fecisse legimus, cum ad Festo Iudeae praefecto ad Caesarem prouoca- uit, Act. 25. 10. ut illius iniustitiam declinaret, Verum, qui priuatae sunt conditionis, duo hic potissimum ob-ruent: Primum, ne quid.
units.tr: Here it is also commonly asked: What ought a good conscience to do, or what can it do, when the magistrate does not make the person a minister of his iniquity but himself inflicts the injury? Since this question has several parts, it needs distinction. If, then, the magistrate who has done the injury to a subject were subordinate to another higher magistrate, the one injured may, by law, appeal to the supreme magistrate, as we read Paul did when he appealed to Caesar against Festus, the governor of Judea, Acts 25.10, in order to avoid his injustice. But for those of private condition, two points chiefly must be observed here. First, that they attempt nothing except by legal means.

units.la: Subditum ne quid nisi iuridice experiantur: Deinde videant, non solum quid liceat, sed maxime quid expediat. Is ipse enim Paulus, cum Phi- lippis, contra ius ciuium Romanorum, vir- gis ignominiose, indicta causa, per Magi- stratus imprudentiam caesus fuiflet, Actor.16. iudicans fe sua patientia Dei gloriam ma- gis promoturum; ius suum vlterius pro- secutus non est, sed fatis illi tum fuit, Magi- stratum iniustitiæ, contra leges commissæ, admonere.
units.tr: Second, they should consider not only what is lawful but above all what is expedient. For Paul himself, when at Philippi he had been beaten with rods, shamefully and without a hearing, by the carelessness of the magistrates, contrary to the right of Roman citizens, Acts 16, judged that by his patience he would promote the glory of God more; he did not pursue his right any further, but it was enough for him then to warn the magistrates of the injustice committed against the laws.

units.la: At vero fi contingat (quod nimis frequenter nostro tempore vluuenit) inferiorem Magistratum in alterum Magistratum infe- riorem violenter aliquid moliri contra su- perioris expressam voluntatem: Tum certe dixerim, licere lefo magistratui, tentatis pri- mis omnibus legitimis & pacificis mediis, fe- legibus armare, & iustam defensionem in- iustæ violentiæ opponere, quemadmodum à Nehemia, Nehem.4. aduerlus Sanabalatum & ipsius locios, factitatum est.
units.tr: But if it should happen (as too often occurs in our time) that an inferior magistrate violently attempts something against another inferior magistrate, contrary to the express will of the superior, then I would say that the injured magistrate may, after first trying all lawful and peaceable means, arm himself with the laws and oppose just defence to unjust violence, as was done by Nehemiah against Sanballat and his associates, Neh. 4.

units.la: Quid fi autem supremus Magistratus iis est, à quo iniuria proficiscitur? Dominus Iesus, & post eum omnes Martyres, suo exemplo fatis docuerunt, Iniurias patienter fe- rendas: Et, hæc summa est Christianorum gloria, iniuriam ab omnibus pati, nemini autem inferre. Quid igitur (dixerit quispiam)
units.tr: But what if the supreme magistrate is himself the source of the injury? The Lord Jesus, and after him all the martyrs, by their example have sufficiently taught that injuries are to be borne patiently; and this is the highest glory of Christians: to suffer injury from all, but to inflict it on no one. What then, someone may say?

units.la: {a} Inferior Magistratus, ab alero infe- riore, contra superioris voluntate probe cogni tam, impe- ditus, armata fe illi potest opponere.
units.tr: {a} An inferior magistrate, hindered by another inferior magistrate acting against the clearly known will of the superior, may arm himself and oppose him.

units.la: nihilne remedii ergo fupereft aduerfus fummum Obiectio. Magiftratum,fua authoritate potentia abuten- tem,contra omnia iura tum diuina tum humana? Supereft fane, etiam à rebus humanis peti- tum. Hoc vero cum dico, nemo putet, me vel fanaticis Anabaptiftis, velaliis feditiofis subditoris, ac turbulétis hominibus, fauere velle;quos contra fue ego potius digniffimos cenfeam omnium premii mala- teliquorum hominum odio, & feueriffimis sistratum etiam fuppliciis. Verumenimuero dicendu mihi, quod reseft in hocargumento: Nec exiftimandum eft, eos,qui docent, quibus viis (falua confcientia) manifeftae tyrannidi obfifti poffit, bonos & legitimos magiftra- tus vel ea fpoliare authoritate, quaà Deo donati funt, vel feditionibus viam fternere. Quinimo certum eft, neque Magiftratuum authoritatem ftabiliri, neque publicam trā- quillitate poffe conferuari (qui tamen præ- cipuus finis eft omnium bene conftituta- rum politiarum) nifi & ftudiofe caueatur, neirrepattyrannis,&fi iam irrepfit,diligen. ter aut aboleatur,aut propulsetur.
units.tr: Is there then no remedy left against the supreme magistrate, who abuses his authority and power against all laws, both divine and human? Objection. There is indeed a remedy, and it must be sought even from human means. But when I say this, let no one think that I wish to favour the fanatical Anabaptists, or other seditious and turbulent subjects, whom I would judge most worthy of punishment, more than all other men, by the hatred of everyone and by the most severe penalties. But I must say what remains on this argument: it should not be thought that those who teach by what means (with conscience intact) manifest tyranny may be resisted are overthrowing good and lawful magistrates, either by stripping them of the authority God has given them or by paving the way for sedition. Indeed it is certain that the authority of magistrates cannot be made firm, nor public tranquillity preserved (which is nevertheless the chief aim of all well-founded commonwealths), unless care is taken with diligence that tyranny does not creep in, and, if it has already crept in, that it is either abolished or driven off.

units.la: QVÆSTIO V. An manifefta tyrannis armis reprimi ture poffit?
units.tr: QUESTION V. Whether a manifest tyranny can lawfully be repressed by arms?

units.la: Veritur ergo, An fubditi iufte aliquo modo, fine Dei offenfa, manifefta tyrannidem fum- mi Magiftratus reprimere, vel etiam armis, fi opus eft,
units.tr: The question is therefore raised: whether subjects may justly, in some way and without offence to God, restrain the manifest tyranny of the supreme magistrate, or even, if need be, repel it by arms,

units.la: B est, propulsare possint? Hanc quæstionē vt dilucidius soluam, quædam mihi prius ponenda sunt, tanquam totius quæstionis bases: Nempe, Populos non à Magistratibus primum dimanasse, sed quicunque vel ab vno Principe, vel ab electis à se Primatibus, regi voluerunt, eos antiquiores suos Magistratibus fuisse. Unde concluditur, non populos propter Magistratum, sed contra Magistratus propter populum fuisse creatos: sicut tutor pupillo, non pupillus tutori constituitur: & pastor ob gregem, non grex propter pastorem. Id cum per se satis manifestum sit, tum ex omnium fere nationum historiis confirmari poterit; adeo, vt Deus ipse, etsi Saulem precibus populi elegisset, quem Samuelis substituere, 1. Sam. 10. 11. voluerit tamen eum populi suffragiis in Regem & creari & suscipi. Sic Dauid, etsi Rex à Deo ipso primum electus esset, noluit tamen Regni administrationem suscipere, nisi prius & suffragiis & libero tribuum Israeliticarum consensu confirmatus, 2. Sam. 2. & 5. Similiter factum est vt postea etiam, quamuis regnum ex Dei constitutione familiæ Dauidis effet additum, is demum tamen ex Dauidis posteris regnaret, quem populus approbasset, & non alius (nisi forte aliquid extra ordinem accideret, quod impedimentum afferret; vt cum modo Ægyptii, modo Syrii
units.tr: ...are able to repel? To make this question clearer, I must first set down certain things, as the foundations of the whole question. Namely, that peoples did not originate from magistrates; rather, whoever wished to be ruled either by one prince or by chiefs chosen by themselves were older than their magistrates. From this it follows that peoples were not created on account of magistrates, but magistrates were created on account of peoples: just as a guardian is appointed for a ward, not a ward for a guardian, and a shepherd for the flock, not the flock for the shepherd. This is sufficiently clear in itself, and it can also be confirmed from the histories of almost all nations; so much so that God himself, although he had chosen Saul by the prayers of the people, whom he wished to set in place of Samuel (1 Sam. 10.), nevertheless wished him to be both created and received as king by the votes of the people. Likewise David, although he had first been chosen king by God himself, nevertheless was unwilling to take up the administration of the kingdom unless he had first been confirmed both by the votes and by the free consent of the tribes of Israel (2 Sam. 2. and 5.). In a similar way it came about later that, although the kingdom had been added to the family of David by the constitution of God, yet he alone of David's posterity would reign whom the people had approved, and no other (unless perhaps something outside the ordinary course happened to hinder this; as when at one time the Egyptians, at another the Syrians...

units.la: De Magistratuum origine.
units.tr: On the origin of magistrates.

units.la: ET OFFICIO SVBDITORVM
units.tr: And the Duty of Subjects

units.la: Syrii Reges in populum Dei tyrannidem exercebant) adeo, vt hoc quidem regnum hereditarium effet, si familiam spectes, sed fi «personā electiuum, id est, ab electione popu- « lipendens. Quod videre est ex historiis vitæ Salomonis, 1. Para.29.22. Roboami, 1. Reg.12. Ioæ, 2. Reg.11.12. Oziæ, 2. Par. 26.1. & Ioachaz, 2. Par.36.1. Vnde & Abfolon occasionem paternı regni vsurpandi captauit. 2. Sam.15.4. Sic enim ei, 2. Sam.16.18. respondit Chufaia- micus Dauidis, Nequaquam, sed quem elegerit Deus & populus iste, nempe vniuersus Israel, illius ero, & cum illo manebo. In summa, fi libet veteres historias, a profanis etiam scriptori- bus lite├ris mandatas, scrutari, constabit (id quod natura etiam ipsa alta voce acclamare. videtur) Magistratus, quorum authoritate inferiores regerentur, ideo creatos, quod necesse eflet, vel totum humanum genus perire, vel medium aliquem ordinem confitui, quo vnus pluresve reliquis imperant, qui bonos tuerentur, improbos autem poenis coercerent. Atque hoc est quod non solum Plato, Ariftoteles & reliqui naturales philosophi (sola rationis humanæ luce instructi) & docuerunt & probarunt: Verum etiam Deus ipse, ore Pauli ad Romanos, tu quis fere mundi dominos, scribentis, Rom. 13. verbis claris confirmauit. En, quæ sit omnium, tum rerum publi-carum,tum potestatum,origo,àDeo omnis boni auctore optima ratione repetita. Quod & Homerus agnouit & libere {a}testatus est; Reges Iouis alumnos & populi pastores, appel-lans. Quid igitur obstabit,quin deMagistra-tuum maxime supremorum, potestate ser-monem instituentes, ad primam illam ori-ginem ex qua fluxerunt, transcendamus, & ad quem finem constituti fuerint, confide-remus? cum certissimum sit, omnem de re-bus iustis vel iniustis disputationem, à fine & ordiendam & finiëdam: Tum enim recte & ordine aliquid factum censendum est, cum ad eum finem pertigit, ad quem desti-natum fuerat.
units.tr: The Syrian kings exercised tyranny over the people of God. So it was hereditary if you look at the family, but if you look at the person it was elective, that is, dependent on the choice of the people. This can be seen from the histories of Solomon (1 Chron. 29:22), Rehoboam (1 Kings 12), Joash (2 Kings 11:12), Uzziah (2 Chron. 26:1) and Jehoahaz (2 Chron. 36:1). Hence also Absalom sought occasion to usurp his father's kingdom (2 Sam. 15:4). For Hushai, David's friend, answered him in these words: "By no means, but whom God and this people, namely all Israel, choose, his will I be, and with him I will remain" (2 Sam. 16:18). In sum, if one examines the ancient histories, even those committed to writing by profane authors, it will be clear (as nature herself seems to cry out with a loud voice) that magistrates were created, by whose authority inferiors are governed, because otherwise either the whole human race would perish, or some middle order had to be established, by which one or more rule over the rest, to protect the good and restrain the wicked by punishments. This is what not only Plato, Aristotle and the other natural philosophers, instructed by the light of human reason alone, both taught and proved; but God himself, through the mouth of Paul writing to the Romans, confirmed in clear words about those who are almost the lords of the world (Rom. 13). Behold, the origin of all commonwealths and all powers alike, rightly traced back to God, the author of all good. Homer also recognised this and freely bore witness to it, calling kings nurtured by Zeus and shepherds of the people. What then will stand in the way of our discussing the power of the highest magistrates, going back to that first origin from which it flowed, and considering to what end they were appointed? For it is most certain that every discussion of whether things are just or unjust must both begin and end with the end in view. Then indeed a thing is judged to have been done rightly and in order when it has reached the end for which it was destined.

units.la: Cum igitur de Magistratuũ officio quæ-ritur, fatebuntur omnes, fas quidem esse,il-los &officii admonere,& libere quoq; quo-ties ab eo deslectunt, reprehendere. At ve-ro, vbi agitur de manifestissimis tyrannis, vel cohibendis, vel pro ipsorum merito ple-ctendis; tum plerique adeo patientiam, & preces ad Deum, commendant, vt pro sedi-tiofis & pseudochristianis habeant, & da-mnent, quotquot ceruices suas ad carnifici-nam non submittant.
units.tr: When, therefore, the office of magistrates is under discussion, everyone will admit that it is right to remind them of their duty and also, whenever they stray from it, to rebuke them freely. But when the matter concerns the most manifest tyrants, whether they are to be restrained or punished according to their deserts, many people so commend patience and prayers to God that they regard as seditious and false Christians, and condemn, all who do not submit their necks to the executioner.

units.la: Locus hic sane lubricus est, ideo rursus, lectores obsecro, meminerint eorum quæ proxiproxime à me dicta sunt, ne ex iis quæ deinceps dicenda erunt, malas nectant consecutiones. Probatur quidē mihi maxime Christiana patientia, vt præ cæteris omnibus virtutibus laudabilis & nunquam satis cōmendata; ad quam fateor studiose homines esse adhortandos, quia plurimum ad consequendam æternam beatitudinem habeat momenti: Seditiones, & omnem confusionem, ceu immania monstra, detestor: In afflictionibus præsertim, ab vno Deo pendendum esse censeo: Preces cum seria respiscentia coniunctas, agnosco necessaria & vera esse remedia ad profligandam tyrannidem; quādoquidem malum hoc inter flagella, à Deo immissa ad populum castigandum, merito connumeratur. Sed nego hæc omnia obstare, quo minus liceat populis, manifesta tyrannide oppressis, simul cum precibus & pœnitentia, aliis iustis aduersus illam remediis sese tueri: Idque firmissimis hisce rationibus nixus, confirmo.
units.tr: This place is certainly slippery, so once more I beg my readers to keep in mind what I have said just before, lest they tie false conclusions to what is to be said afterwards. I truly approve of Christian patience, as praiseworthy above all other virtues and never sufficiently commended; I confess that men ought to be earnestly exhorted to it, because it contributes greatly to obtaining eternal blessedness. I detest seditions and every confusion, as monstrous evils. Especially in afflictions, I hold that one must depend on God alone. I acknowledge that prayers joined with earnest repentance are necessary and true remedies for overthrowing tyranny, since this evil is rightly reckoned among the scourges sent by God to chastise the people. But I deny that all these things stand in the way of peoples oppressed by manifest tyranny being permitted, at the same time as prayers and repentance, to defend themselves against it by other lawful remedies. Relying on these very firm reasons, I affirm this.

units.la: His positis, quæ supra de origine Regum & aliorum Magistratuum probata sunt; sequitur; non esse Reges legitimos eos, qui vi vel fraude eam potestatem vsurpant, quæ nullo iure ad ipsos pertineat. Duo sunt vero eiusmodi Tyrannorum genera: Alii enim in concives suos dominationem vsurpant, contra leges subiectos, posi-
units.tr: With these points laid down, which have been proved above concerning the origin of kings and other magistrates, it follows that those are not lawful kings who seize by force or fraud that power which does not belong to them by any right. Now there are two kinds of such tyrants. Some usurp dominion over their own fellow citizens, subjecting them against laws that have been laid down and accepted,

units.la: positas & receptas, sicut Iulius Cæsar, fubfiͤto Diͤatoris perpetui titulo, Romanam Rempub. inuasit: & multi alii tyranni, in Græcia præsertim, patrię suæ libertatem op-presserunt. Alii autem, non contenti ea qua iurein suos potiuntur dominatione suas di-tiones, cum dispendio libertatis vicinorum suorum, dilatant & limitibus ampliant; qua ratione Monarchiæ, iam à mundi initio, in tantam peruenerunt amplitudinem: cuius rei nobis sacræ literæ exemplum in Nim-broto exhibent, Genef.10. verf.18. Sicut etiam hac via videmus Israelitas plerunque à vi-cinis populis oppressos fuisse. Itaque, cum tyranni illi nihil iuris habuerent in Dei po-pulum, Israelitis dico licuisse, non solum e-di&tis irreligiosis harum nationum non pa-rere, sed etiam iustam defensionem illorum iniquæ violentiæ opponere: Ideoque præ-sectos tribuum grauiter peccaffe, quoties coniunctis animis & viribus peregrino ho-fti, pro patria libertate, non occurrerunt, siquidem obsistendi facultas illis daretur: constat enim, etiam priuatos homines, iure tam diuino quam humano, teneri, laboran-ti & oppressæ patriæ suæ totis viribus fuc-currere; præsertim vero, cum & de Religio-ne, & simul de libertate, periclitatur. Verum est enim, quod pirata ille, captiuus ad Ale-xandrum kandrü ductus, dicere ausus est, Nihil differre je ab illo, nisi quod ille magna nauium copia mun-dum depradaretur, ipse autem vnica nauicula. His non aduersatur, quod quidam solent obii-ere: A Deo, scilicet, transferri & permutariτe- gna, ac imperia sideoq, sape tyrannos potiri victoria Deo annuente, Absit enim, vt propterea vel Lucani sententiæ subscribam, qui hoc mo- do, ius celeri datum fuisse, canere ausus est: vel Demosthenis caulam vt iniquam damnem, quod, patriæ suæ libertatem aduersus Phi- lippi Macedonis violentiam defendens, vi- &tus succubuerit, Philippus autem victor euaserit. Quibus exemplis ideo vtor, non vt iis, tanquam regulis, piorum conscientiæ ni- tantur; sed quia & celebria sunt & plerisque fam oppref- notissima: atque etiam, quod etsi hæc inter forum iusta / profanas gentes acciderint, non tamen vsq; adeo ab æquitatis norma distent, vt merito dici non possit, ab altera parte ius stetisse, ab altera iniustitiam. Nec enim à solo euen- tu prospero aut infelici (vt etiam Demo-fthenes Æschini aduersario suo, infelicem ipsi successum Chæronensis præclii expro-branti, respondit) iudicandum censuerim, num iuste quid an iniuste susceptum fit. Nā (vt magis Christiane loquamur) solet ple-runque Deus vel hominum peccata ita vl-cisci, vel suos eousque experiri, vt ipsorum conficonsiliis (quamuis per fe bonis,& iustis)lô-gealium exitum tribuat, quam ipsi cogita-rint: vt videre est potissimum in eo bello, quod reliquæ tribus Ifraeliticæ in Beniami-tas gesserunt,Iudic.20.At Deus interim non minus iustus manet quocunque inftrumen-to fuaiudicia exequatur; nec populi minus legitimam causam aduersus hostes tyran-nos habuisse sunt existimandi, quia iusto a-liquoDei iudicio prostrati corruerint. Quâ-obrem probari mihi nunquam potuit eorû opinio, qui, finedifcrimineaut exceptione vlla, omnes simul Tyrannicidas vno calcu-lo damnant; quibus olim Græci tam egre-gia præmia decernebant. Nec magis placet eorum sententia, quibus pleræque libera-tiones, in libro Iudicum notatæ, ita exoti-cæ videntur atq; extraordinariæ, vt eas nul-lo modo in exemplum trahi posse putent: Nam vtut verum fit, illos populi Ifraelitici Iudices, diuino quodam ac extraordinario instinctu, ad ea præclara facinora patranda commotos & excitatos fuisse; nō tamen statim consequitur, ipsos Israelitas (vel magistratum gerentes, vel etiam priuatos) non potuisse iure ordinario propulsare tyrannidem exterorum, qui à populo neq; electi, neque probati effent. Quod vero liberationes illæ per eos duntaxat acciderint, quos Deus
units.tr: as Julius Caesar did, under the title of perpetual dictator, when he invaded the Roman commonwealth; and many other tyrants, especially in Greece, oppressed the liberty of their native land. Others, not content with the dominion they hold by right over their own people, extend their realms and enlarge their borders at the expense of the liberty of their neighbours; by this method monarchies had from the beginning of the world reached such great size. Sacred Scripture gives us an example of this in Nimrod (Gen. 10. 18.). In the same way we see that the Israelites were often oppressed by neighbouring peoples. Therefore, since those tyrants had no right over the people of God, I say it was lawful for the Israelites not only to refuse obedience to the irreligious edicts of these nations, but also to oppose a just defence against their unjust violence. And so the leaders of the tribes sinned gravely whenever, with united minds and forces, they did not come to meet the foreign enemy for the liberty of their country, if the power to resist had been given to them. For it is established that even private persons are bound, by divine as well as human right, to come with all their strength to the aid of their labouring and oppressed country, especially when both religion and liberty are in danger together. What that pirate said is true, when he was brought captive to Alexander the Great and dared to say that he differed from Alexander in nothing except that Alexander plundered the world with a great fleet, while he himself did so with a single little ship. Not opposed to this is what some are accustomed to object: that kingdoms and empires are transferred and exchanged by God, and therefore tyrants often gain victory with God's consent. Far be it from me, therefore, to subscribe to the opinion of Lucan, who dared to sing that in this way the right was given to the swift; or to condemn the cause of Demosthenes as unjust, because he defended the liberty of his country against the violence of Philip of Macedon, was conquered by force, and Philip emerged the victor. I use these examples not as rules on which the consciences of the pious should rest, but because they are both famous and very well known to most people; and also because, even if these things happened among profane nations, they nevertheless do not depart so far from the standard of equity that it could rightly be said that justice stood on one side and injustice on the other. For I would not judge whether something has been undertaken justly or unjustly from the outcome alone, whether prosperous or unfortunate (as Demosthenes also answered his adversary Aeschines, who reproached him with the unhappy result of the battle of Chaeronea). For (to speak more in a Christian manner) God usually either punishes the sins of men in this way, or tests his own people to such an extent that he gives the outcome of affairs to counsels that are good and just in themselves, different from what they had thought. This is especially seen in that war which the other Israelite tribes waged against the Benjamites (Judg. 20.). But meanwhile God remains no less just, by whatever instrument he carries out his judgments; nor should it be thought that the peoples had any less lawful cause against their tyrant enemies because they were thrown down and fell by some just judgment of God. For this reason I could never approve the opinion of those who, without any distinction or exception, condemn all tyrannicides together by one vote, for whom the Greeks of old decreed such excellent rewards. Nor does the view of those please me who think that most of the deliverances recorded in the book of Judges are so exotic and extraordinary that they cannot in any way be drawn into example. For although it is true that those judges of the Israelite people were moved and roused by a certain divine and extraordinary impulse to accomplish those glorious deeds, it does not immediately follow that the Israelites themselves (whether holding magistracy or even as private persons) could not, by ordinary right, repel the tyranny of foreigners who had been neither chosen nor approved by the people. As for the fact that those deliverances came only through those whom God raised up outside the ordinary course, this does not contradict the argument, but rather rebukes the stupor and the spirit of the Israelites, broken by God's just judgment on account of their sins. Therefore, so that it may be lawful to imitate those examples rightly and by right, I think these true means are to be held: namely, if anyone against others unjust domination or

units.la: extra ordinem excitauit, mec fententiz non refragatur, sed potius stuporem, & fraetum iusto Deiiudicio Israelitarum animum, ob sua scelera, coarguit. Vtigitur ea exempla recte aciure imitari liceat, vera hæc media tenenda existimo, nempe: Si quis inalios iniustam dominatio- nem vel captet, veliam vfurparit (fiuealie- nigena is fit, fiue tanquam Vipera ex patriæ visceribus prorumpat, vt eam nascendo in- serimat) cum priuati homines ante omnia Magistratus suos legitimos adeant, vt, fi fie- riporeft, publicus hostis publica authorita- te, & communi omnium consensu, depella- tur. Sin autem magistratus vel conniueat, velalioqui officium præstare recuset, tunc priuatus quisque legitimum patriæ suæ(cui, post Deum, totum fe debet) statum tueri pro viribus satagat, aduersus eum qui legiti- mus magistratus censeri non potest, cum eam dignitatem, contra leges publicas, vel iam vfurparit, vel vsurpare tentet.
units.tr: Nor does this opinion (the judgement) stand against that; rather, it exposes the stupor of the Israelites and their minds broken by the just judgement of God because of their sins. Therefore, if it is right and lawful to imitate those examples, I think these true means are to be held: if anyone seeks or seizes unjust dominion over others (whether he is a foreigner or bursts forth like a viper from the bowels of his own country, so that he is born into it and planted there), then private men must first approach their lawful magistrates, so that, if it can be done, the public enemy may be driven out by public authority and by the common consent of all. But if the magistrate either connives at the evil or otherwise refuses to perform his duty, then each private man, who owes himself wholly after God to the lawful state of his country, should strive with all his strength to defend it against the one who cannot be regarded as a lawful magistrate, since he has either already usurped that dignity against the public laws or is trying to usurp it.

units.la: Hic porro animaduertendum est, vitium quod ab initio vsurpationi ineiat, posse po- ftea emendari: adeo, vt qui ab intitio Tyran- nus fuit, possit legitimus & inuiolabilis Ma- gistratus effici; fi videlicet postea liber & le- gitimus accesserit eorum consensus, qui ve- rum & legitimum Magistratum creare & pote. B.
units.tr: Here, moreover, it must be noted that a fault which attaches to usurpation from the beginning can afterwards be remedied, so that one who was a tyrant from the start may become a lawful and inviolable magistrate; namely, if afterwards the free and lawful consent of those who are able to create and constitute a true and lawful magistrate comes in.

units.la: constituere possunt. Exempli gratia: Iustum erat bellum, duce Pompeio aduersus Cæsarem susceptum, quamuis in eo Cæsar victor extiterit: Sed fi verum fuit, Populi Romani postea libero & voluntario aflenfu Cæsarem dominium illud summum, prætextu perpetuæ Dictaturæ, consecutum fuisse, iam quærendum amplius non effet, an coniuratio in eum facta iusta ac legitima fuerit, nisi statim probetur, eum Dictatura ipsa manifeste abusum. Audeo id quoque certissime affirmare, optimates illos ciues Romanos potuisse, ac etiam debuisse, Rempublicam aduersus Triumuiratum defendere: sed non ausim dicere, Cinnam, & fociosiure potuisse in necem Augusti coniurare, post Regiam legem (quam vocant) promulgatam & receptam. Verum hic quoque distinctione opus est. Nam dabitur hoc mihi, opinor; Consensum, fiue à toto fiue à maiore populi parte, vel vltro praftitum, vel vi aut metu extorsum, potius rescindendum esse, quam obferuan-dum, fi certo constet, illum cum aequitate & bona flate manifeste pugnare. Quis enim sibi persuadeat, populum aliquem sponte ac sciens-ter, nulla vi adactum, sese Principi alicui subiicere voluisse hoc cofilio, vt postea abipfo iuguletur & penitus exscindatur? Atenim duo hic rursus sunt obseruanda, quoties ea vel
units.tr: For example: the war which was waged under Pompey against Caesar was just, although Caesar emerged victor in it. But if it was true that, afterwards, by the free and voluntary assent of the Roman people, Caesar obtained that supreme dominion under the pretext of perpetual dictatorship, then it would no longer need to be asked whether the conspiracy made against him was just and lawful, unless it were at once proved that he manifestly abused the dictatorship itself. I dare also affirm most certainly that those optimate citizens of Rome could, and indeed ought, to have defended the commonwealth against the triumvirate; but I would not venture to say that Cinna and his associates could lawfully conspire for the death of Augustus after the so-called Royal law had been promulgated and received. Yet here too a distinction is needed. For I suppose this will be granted me: consent, whether given by the whole people or by the greater part of it, whether freely offered or wrung out by force or fear, ought rather to be annulled than observed, if it is clearly established that it manifestly conflicts with equity and sound condition. For who could persuade himself that some people, of its own accord and knowingly, without any force compelling it, wished to submit itself to some prince with this design, that afterwards it might be throttled by him and utterly destroyed? But here two things again must be observed, whenever such consent...

units.la: vel rescindenda vel corrigenda sunt, quibus in- considerate consensus est præstitus. Primum, ne quid temere, deinde, ne quid per seditionem ten- tetur, aut siat; sed insto ordine, ac modeste, quan- tum eius sieri poterit. Præsens Reipublicæ Christianæ status duo nobis huius rei ex- empla suppeditat, utrumque sane maximi momenti. Primum est, iniuste illius ac irre- ligiose subiectionis, qua sese Reges & populi Antichristo Romano iureiurando obstrin- gerunt: Quo iureiurando ipsos non magis ligatio; nul teneri, assero, quam finominatim & aper- te Satanæiurassent, sese omnia iura, tum diuina, tum humana, euersuros. Alterum, est, temporariæ illius, ut vocant, iurisdictionis, quam Prælati Ecclesiastici sibi vendicarunt: Quia enim ex diametro pugnat tum cum sastiorū, Christi mandato, tum cum ipsius & Apo- stolorum omnium apertissimis exemplis (vt præ cæteris D. Bernhardus manifeste o- sendit) consequitur profecto, quod in se- ipsa nulla sit: quandoquidem nec Principes ea se exuere aut spoliare, nec Ecclesiastici eam vel à Regibus vel à populis suscipere potuerunt, vel pretio aquirere; nedum, vt vi ac dolosis artibus eam vsurpare debue- rint, quemadmodum eos secisse constatin potissima mundi parte. Hæc vero dicta sint in Tyrannos, qui dominium, vel in conciconciues suos, vel in exteros populos, sibi iniuste vendicarunt.
units.tr: Such covenants, whether they were made rashly or extorted, must be annulled or corrected. The rule has two parts. First, nothing should be attempted or done rashly, and second, nothing should be attempted or done through sedition; rather, the remedy should proceed in due order and with moderation, as far as that can be managed. The present state of the Christian commonwealth gives us two examples of this, both of the greatest importance. The first is that unjust and impious submission by which Kings and peoples have bound themselves by oath to the Roman Antichrist. I maintain that they are no more bound by that oath than if they had sworn openly and by name to Satan that they would overthrow all rights, both divine and human. The second is that so-called temporal jurisdiction, which the ecclesiastical prelates have claimed for themselves. For it flatly contradicts both the command of Christ and the most manifest examples of Christ himself and of all the Apostles (as Saint Bernard in particular clearly shows). It follows that this jurisdiction has no validity in itself. Princes could not strip themselves of it or surrender it, and the churchmen could not receive it from Kings or peoples, nor acquire it for a price, much less seize it by force and crafty arts, as we know they have done in the greater part of the world. These things are said against tyrants who have unjustly claimed lordship over their own fellow citizens or over foreign peoples.

units.la: QVÆSTIO VI.
units.tr: QUESTION VI.

units.la: Quod fit officium subditorum erga superiores, qui in tyrannidem sunt prolapsi.
units.tr: What is the duty of subjects towards superiors who have fallen into tyranny?

units.la: SVpereft, vt iam alteram quæstionem tra-ctemus, quæ non immerito his nostris temporibus à plerisque est agitata, Quid, scilicet, liceat bona conscientia subditis, quoties summi ipsorum Magistratus, alioqui legitimi, in Tyrannos degenerant manifestos: An tum supremorum Magistratuum, in Tyrannos apertos conuenerforum, authoritas tam sacra & intemerata esse debeat, vt eam ferre subditi omnino teneantur, adeo, vt nullo modo illi resistere possint: vel, si resistere quidem aliquo modo licet, an fas sit illis, ad arma usque progredi? Respondeo, Tria omnino esse subditorum genera, seu subditos in triplici differentia. Alii enim priuati sunt homines, nulla publica administratione fungentes: Alii magistratum quidem gerunt, sed his summis Magistratibus subiiciuntur, (vt quos subalternos & inferiores Magistratus appellamus:) Tertii, etsi summum quidem Imperium non habeant, nec supremaac ordinaria potestate fungantur, constituti tamen sunt in eo ordine, vt sint quasi frena & habenæ.
units.tr: It remains now to take up the second question, which is not without reason much debated in our own times: what, namely, may subjects in good conscience do whenever their supreme magistrates, otherwise lawful, degenerate into manifest tyrants? Is the authority of supreme magistrates who have turned into open tyrants to be so sacred and inviolable that subjects are wholly bound to bear it, so that they can in no way resist them? Or, if resistance is in some way permitted, is it lawful for them to go as far as arms? I answer that there are altogether three kinds of subjects, or subjects in three different positions. For some are private persons, holding no public office. Others do hold a magistracy, but are subject to these supreme magistrates, being what we call subordinate and inferior magistrates. The third kind, though they do not hold the supreme power and do not exercise the supreme and ordinary authority, are nevertheless placed in such a rank that they serve as it were as the bridles and reins for keeping the supreme magistrate in duty. But as these kinds are different, so the answer must be given differently for each.

units.tr: For keeping the supreme magistrate in duty. But as these kinds are different, so the answer must be given differently for each.

units.tr: If, therefore, those who are of private condition have willingly and openly submitted to the domination of an unjust usurper (as the Roman people, willingly, submitted itself to Augustus and his successors), or if their lawful magistrate has become a manifest tyrant (such as Abimelech among the Israelites, the thirty at Athens, and the decemvirs at Rome, and others elsewhere), I say that it is not lawful for any private person (apart from an extraordinary calling by God himself, which I do not touch on here) to oppose force with force against the tyrant on his own private authority. Rather, he must either depart from the tyrant's rule and change his dwelling, or flee to God by prayer and patiently bear the yoke of the tyrant, provided only (as we said at the beginning) that the tyranny is not compelling him to serve it against someone, or to omit any of those things that are owed either to God or to his neighbour. But it might be objected against this my answer that what we have already laid down about the double kind of tyrants, against whom we said private persons too can and must resist with all their strength, seems at first sight to fall back into the same thing.

units.la: quis priuatus dominium vsurpet, siue quis, sua dominatione legitima non contentus, tyrannidem exercet: Vnde consequens videri possit, eandem etiam vtroque casu decisionem habere. Sed si penitius in resipsas intueamur, conspicuum est, quam maxime haec duo genera differre, licet prorsus similia videantur. Is enim qui alienos inuadit, nullo modo sibi subditos, etsi cupiatiuste, & ex bono & æquo, dominari (sicut de Pififtrato & Demetrio Phalereo apud Atheniēnses legitimus) potest tamen iure impediri, etiam armata manu; & à quibusuis, vel infi- ma sortis, quibus vim inferre voluerit, nulla iure illi obstringātur. Qui autem à populo suo semel probatus & susceptus fuit, etsi suo iure abutitur, retinet tamen authoritatis suæ fundamentum in proprios & priuatos subditos, quoniam mutuo consensu, ac publice, contracta obligatio, nullius priuati voluntate solui dirimiue potest. Quod si secus fieret, infinitæ rerum perturbationes, ipsa etiam tyrannide peiores, sequeren-tur: & in locum vnius tyranni, quem profligare mens esset, mille succederent. Praeterea vnica ratio, ex authoritate verbi Dei petita, maioris hic esse debet momenti, quam quicquid in contrarium adduci posset. Pausus, Rom. 13. vers. 5. priuatis officium prascriptum est, sed subditis suis, sicut ipse paulus scripsit.
units.tr: Why private persons should not resist a lawful magistrate who exercises tyranny in the same way as they would resist an unjust usurper. Scripture not only forbids resisting magistrates (both supreme and subordinate), but also commands obedience to them for the sake of conscience. The apostle Peter too, in 1 Pet. 2 v. 17, bids us honour the king, perhaps mindful (as is likely) of the rebuke he had heard from his Master when, as a private man, he had drawn the sword against the public power (though he was abusing his own authority against the Lord). But no one doubts what kind of Caesars Tiberius and Nero were then, and the other governors of the provinces. The holy martyrs followed this example of the martyrs, when the most savage tyrants put them to death most cruelly, not only under emperors who violated the laws of the Romans, which had often been promulgated in favour of the Christians, as happened under Julian the Apostate. To sum up (so that I may at last finish this part of the question): I say that it is not lawful for any private person to oppose a tyrant by open force, to whose domination the people has previously given its willing consent. For if in private contracts, agreements and promises we are bound to keep to them, so that we would rather suffer loss than break faith, how much more must private persons take care not to withdraw in any way from an obligation solemnly contracted by public consent?

units.la: Cur priuati, legitimo magistratui, tyranni dem exercenti, non perinde ac iniusto vsurpatori resistere debeant. bens, non modo magistratibus (tam summis quam subalternis) resistere prohibet, sedillis etiam propter conscientiam obedire præcipit. D.Pe- trus quoque 1. Petr. 2. verf. 17. iubet, Regem honore afficere, memor (vt verisimile est) eius reprehensionis, quàm à magistro audierat, cum gladium priuatus aduersus publicam potestatem (sua tamen authoritate in Domi- num abutétem) strinxisset: At nemo nescit, quales tum Cæsares effent Tyberius & Ne- ro, reliquique prouinciarum præfecti. Hoc ss. Martyr- um exemplum sancti Martyres fuit fe- rum exem- cuti, dum eos immanissimi tyranni crude- lissime interfecerunt, non solum sub Impe- ratoribus, qui in Christianos, ex Romano- rum legibus, sæpe in gratiam Christia- norum prometulgata, violabat, vt accidit sub Iuliano Cæsare Apostata. In summa (vt hanc quæstionis partem tandem absoluam) Non licere, dico, cuiquam priuato, vi aperta sefeiy- ranno opponere, cuius dominationi prius populus volens consensum præbuerit. Si enim in priuatis contractibus, pactis conuentis & promissis eo ipso stando est, vt potius damnum pa- tiamur, quam fidem fallamus: quanto magis priuati cauere debent, ne ab obligatione so- lenni, ac publico consensu contracta, vllo modo resiliant?
units.tr: I come now to the inferior magistrates, who are as it were intermediate, and (as the common people say) subordinate, between the supreme magistrate and the people. By this designation I understand not the domestic officers of the king himself (who, that is, perform some office in the royal court and serve the person of the prince rather than the kingdom), but rather those who hold public offices (that is, offices pertaining to the state of the kingdom, whether in matters of justice or of war), who for this reason are called ministers not of the king but of the Crown or Kingdom (between which there is the greatest difference) in the monarchies themselves. Of this kind at Rome were the consuls, praetors, the prefect of the city, and the governors of the provinces (which offices were assigned to the people itself, and to the Senate, even in the time of the emperors), and similar officials of the Commonwealth or Empire, who for that reason were called magistrates of the Roman people even under the last emperors. Such also among the Israelites were the leaders of the individual tribes, the commanders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens, and the elders of the people. These political offices, first ordained by Moses, were by no means afterwards abolished, when that aristocratic state was changed into a monarchy; indeed, under Solomon they were carefully set up and observed.

units.la: Venio nunc ad inferiores Magistratus, qui sunt velut intermedii, & (vt vulgus lo- quitur) fubalterni, inter summum magi- stratum, & populum. Quorum appellatione intelligo, non domesticos Regis ipsius officiarios (qui scilicet munus aliquod in Basilica Re- gia exercent, & ipsius personæ, potius quam Regno, inseruiunt) sed eos potius, qui publi- cis muneribus(id est, ad Regni statum, vel iu- diciorum causa vel rerum bellicarum, perti- nentibus) funguntur, qui ideo in ipsis Mo- narchiis, non Regis, sed Coronæ siue Regni (in- ter quæ summum est discrimen) administri nuncupantur; cuiusmodi Romæ quidem e- rant Consules, Prætores, Præfectus vrbi, Præsides prouinciarum (quæ tum ipsi po- pulo, tum Senatui, etiam tempore Impera- torum, tribuebätur;) & similes Reipublicæ vel Imperii officiales, qui propterea populi Romani Magistratus, sub nouissimis etiàlmpe- ratoribus, di&i sunt. Tales quoque eranta- pud Israelitas Duces singularum tribuum, Millenarii, Centuriones, Quinquagenarii, Decuriones, & seniores populi: Quæ politi- ca munera, à Mose primum ordinata, ne- quaquam postea sunt abrogata, cum status ille Aristocraticus, in Monarchicum muta- retur; quinimo sub Salomone exacte con- stituta & obseruata. Eius generis varii magi-
units.tr: Various orders of magistrates of this kind still exist today in most Christian kingdoms, among whom rightly belong those who are called dukes, marquises, counts, viscounts, barons and castellans, as those who formerly held public offices and duties, appointed to them in a fixed order and by lawful means. Although these offices afterwards passed into hereditary dignities, they by no means lost their former right and authority. Moreover, to this order are to be reckoned those who are chosen in cities to various duties, such as those commonly called mayors, viguiers (or vicars), consuls, captains, syndics, scabins and the like.

units.la: stratuum ordines sunt etiam hodie in plerisq; Christianorum Regnis, inter quos iure censendi sunt, qui Duces, Marchiones, Comites, Vicecomites, Barones, Castellani vocantur, vt qui olim officia & munia publica exercerent, ad ea certo ordine legitimeque allecti: Quae etsi postea in dignitates hæreditarias transierunt, nequaquam tamen pristinum ius & authoritatem amiserunt. In hunc ordinem præterea connumerandi sunt, qui in ciuitatibus ad varia munera eligutur, quales sunt quos vulgo Maiores, Viguerios, (seu Vicarios) Consules, Capitaneos, Scindicos, Scabinos & eiusmodi, nuncupant.
units.tr: Orders of magistrates still exist today in most Christian kingdoms, and among them are rightly counted those who are called dukes, marquises, counts, viscounts, barons and castellans, since they formerly exercised public offices and duties, being appointed to them in a set order and lawfully. Although these offices later passed into hereditary dignities, they by no means lost their former right and authority. To this order are also to be reckoned those who are chosen in cities for various duties, such as those commonly called mayors (maiores), viguiers (viguerios, or vicars), consuls, captains, syndics, scabins and the like.

units.la: Hi porro omnes, etsi supremo Magistratus subsunt, ab eoque mandata accipiunt, ab eo denique inaugurantur, & approbantur, non tamen ab eo proprie pendent, sed ab ipsa suprema pendent, sed ab ipsa supremitate; id est a summa Imperii seu regni & authoritate: ideoq; defuncto eo qui summum Magistratum gessit, manent in suo quisque gradu, vt prius: quemadmodum & ipsa suprema potestas eadem manet. Quod enim is, qui in demortui locum succedit, eiusmodi inferiores Magistratus, vt & ciuitatum privilegia, confirmat (quam consuetudinem in Romano Imperio primum inuexisse Tybe-
units.tr: All these, however, although they are subject to the supreme magistrate and receive their commissions from him, and are finally installed and approved by him, do not properly depend on him. Rather, they depend on the supreme power itself, that is, on the highest authority of the empire or kingdom. Therefore, when he who held the supreme magistracy dies, each of them remains in his own rank as before, just as the supreme power itself remains the same. For the successor of the deceased confirms such inferior magistrates, and the privileges of cities as well; a custom which Suetonius, in his life of Vespasian, reports was first introduced in the Roman Empire by Tiberius Caesar (and which was not in use in Gaul in earlier centuries, except perhaps when the kingdom passed not from parents to children but to outsiders).

units.la: riim rium Cæsarem, tradit Suetonius in Vespasiano: quæque nec prioribus seculis in vsu erat in Gallia, nisi forte, cum regnum à parentibus non ad filios transibat, sed ad exteros.) Id vero, inquam, non efficit, vt fummus Magistratus, eorum ἀρχικὸς, id est, primarius auctor, fit habendus, à quo principium habeant: cum & supremus ipse, antequam in pofleffionem summæ suæ administrationis vere mittatur, iusiurandum vicissim ipsi supremæ potestati præstet, iuxta conditiones in iuriurandi formula expressas: sicut postmodum ipse à singulis quoque officiariis iuramentum suscipit: Adeo, vt eiusmodi cõfirmatio nullum ius nouum conferat (quemadmodum necinueftitura nouiVafalli, aut à nouo domino facta) sed noua est duntaxat veteris iuris agnitio, propter mutationem personæ. Hinc apparet, mutuam esse obligationem inter Regem & Regni officiarios: neque totam Regni administrationē Regi foli esse commissam, sed supremum duntaxat eius gradum: & singulos officiarios inferiores eius partem obtinere, pro suo quemque gradu, idque certis vtrinque conditionibus. Quæ conditiones si ab inferioribus Magistratibus non seruentur, supremi est Magistratus, illos vel officio abdicare, vel coercere, causa tamen cognita, & non nisi eo ordine,
units.tr: ...to Tiberius Caesar, as Suetonius reports in Vespasian. And this practice was not in use in Gaul in earlier centuries, unless perhaps when a kingdom passed not from parents to sons but to outsiders. Yet this, I say, does not make the highest magistrate to be regarded as the primary author [ἀρχικὸς] from whom the lower magistrates derive their beginning. For even the supreme ruler himself, before he is truly put into possession of the supreme administration, swears an oath in turn to the supreme power itself, under the conditions expressed in the form of the oath. Afterwards he likewise receives an oath from each of the officials. So this confirmation confers no new right, just as a new vassal's investiture, or one made by a new lord, confers none. It is merely a new acknowledgement of the old right, made necessary by the change of person. From this it is clear that the obligation between the king and the officials of the kingdom is mutual. The whole administration of the kingdom has not been committed to the king alone; only the highest rank of it has. Each of the lower officials holds a part of it, according to his own rank, and this on certain conditions binding on both sides. If the lower magistrates do not observe these conditions, it is the duty of the supreme magistrate either to dismiss them from office or to restrain them, but only after the case has been heard, and only in the proper order.

units.la: {*} Mutua esse supremorum ad inferiores, & inferiorum ad supremos Magistratus obligationem, vt in officio contineant. ne, quem Regni leges præscribunt, nisi & iu- s speciaiureiurando, quo se ex legibus regna- turũ promisit, discedere velit. Ediuerso ve- ro, si is, qui regiam dignitatem vel electione vel iure hæreditario adeptus est, manifeste ab iis conditionibus deflectat, sub quib.no- minatim rex est & agnitus, & approbatus: quis dubitet, inferiores Regni Magistratus, ipsaque adeo prouincias ac ciuitates, qua- rum administratio illis commissa est, à suo iureiurando hactenus saltem esse ipso iure li- beratos, vt ipsis liceat sese manifeste eius Re- gni oppressioni opponere, cuius tutelam & protectione, pro suo quisq; munere, cũ iu- reiurando susceperunt? Quid igitur? dicet quispiã, an qui modo profummo Magistratu habe- batur (cuius autoritas esse debet inuiolabi- lis) mox, pro eiusq; inferioris nutu, tanquã pri- mus homo reputabitur, vt liceat in eũ, tanquam in publicum hostem, irruere? Minime vero, in- quam: Hoc enim est fenestram, vt aiunt, ad quasuis impias seditiones & coniuratio- nes aperire: At enim nos de publica & ma- nifesta tyrannide, deque eiusmodi tyrannis sermonem habemus, qui nullas omnino commonefactiones admittere aut ferre possunt. Deinde non agimus hic de tyran- no prorsus é suo solio deturbando, & abiici- endo: sed quærimus, an ne quisquã ipsius mani-
units.tr: {*} The obligation of supreme magistrates to inferior ones, and of inferior ones to supreme magistrates, is mutual, so that each keeps to his duty. Unless the king who is prescribed by the laws of the kingdom also wishes to depart from the oath by which he promised to reign according to the laws, who could doubt that the lower magistrates of the kingdom, and indeed the provinces and cities whose administration has been entrusted to them, are at least so far freed by law from their oath that they may openly oppose themselves to the oppression of that kingdom, whose protection and defence they undertook by oath, each in his own office? What then? Someone will say: will he who a little while ago was held to be the supreme magistrate, whose authority ought to be inviolable, now be regarded as a private man at the nod of his inferior, so that it is lawful to attack him as a public enemy? Certainly not, I reply. For this would open a window, as they say, to all kinds of impious seditions and conspiracies. But we are speaking here of open and manifest tyranny, and of such tyrants as can admit or bear no warnings at all. Furthermore, we are not dealing here with the complete overthrow and removal of a tyrant from his throne, but we ask whether anyone may, and ought to, oppose himself to his manifest violence, according to his rank.

units.la: festa violentia, pro suo gradu, sese opponere possit, ac debeat? cum iam prius ostensum sit, ⁊ quum non esse, quempiam pro suo arbitrio publice contractam obligationem soluere, quisquis tandem is fuerit, & quantumuis etiam iustam de tyranno conquerendi causam habeat. Verum, cum vicilsim isti inferiores regni administri, à potestate ipsa suprema hoc munus accepe-rint, vt de obseruatione & custodia legum inter eos caueant, qui ipsorum curæ sunt commissi: seseque ipsi ad id omni fide præstandum iureiurando obstrinxerint, quo nulla illius culpa absolui possunt, qui ex Rege Tyrannus factus, apertissime eas conditiones transgreditur, sub quibus Rex designatus fuerat, quarumque obseruatio-nem ipse iurauerat. Annon æquum omni iure tam diuino quam humano fuerit, aliquid istis inferioribus Magistratibus am-plius concedi, ratione præstiti ab ipsius iu-ramenti de procuranda legum obseruatio-ne, quam illis qui priuatę sunt omnino conditionis, & absque vllo publico munere? Dico igitur, si eo necessitatis fuerint adacti, teneri ipsos omnino aduersus manifestam tyrannidem salutem eorum procurare (etiam armata manu si possunt) qui ipsorum fidei & curæ sunt traditi: tantisper, dum ex communi statuum vel Νομοφυλάκων (id est, eorum
units.tr: ...that anyone, whoever he may be and however just his complaint against the tyrant, may dissolve by his own choice a publicly contracted obligation. Yet since, in turn, those inferior officers of the kingdom received this duty from the supreme power itself, to take care for the observance and keeping of the laws among those entrusted to their care, and since they have bound themselves by oath to perform this faithfully, they cannot be released from that oath by anyone who, from a king, has become a tyrant and openly transgresses the conditions under which he was designated king and whose observance he himself swore to. Would it not be right, by every law both divine and human, to grant these inferior magistrates more than those who are wholly private persons and hold no public office? This is because they have sworn to procure the observance of the laws. I say, therefore, that if they are driven by such necessity, they are bound altogether to procure the safety, even by armed force if they can, of those who have been handed over to their trust and care, against manifest tyranny. They must do this until, by the common counsel of the estates or of the Nomophylakes [νομοφύλακες], that is, of those in whom lies all authority over the laws of that kingdom or empire under discussion, it is better provided for the commonwealth, and properly arranged.

units.la: Inferiores magistratus, vbi tyrannis manifesta in regnum recurrere debent, ac interim sui fidei commissos tueri & protegere. eorum, penes quos est omnis legum Regni illius, aut Imperii, de quo agitur, authoritas) consilio, melius rebus publicis confultum fit, & vt decet prouisum. Hoc porro non est, seditio- sum, aut in supremum suum Magistratum perfidum esse, sed potius fidelissimum iura- menti sui obseruatorem, erga eos quorum gubernationem quisque susceperit, aduer- sus periurum, & Regni illius oppressorem, cuius protectorem esse debuerat. Isto iure me- rito vsi sunt Romæ Brutus & Lucretius, aduer- sus Tarquinium superbum, tyrannidem aperte ex- ercentem, (etsi priuatim quoque ad illos hæc causa pertineret) cum hic quidem Præfectus vrbi, ille vero Tribunus Celerum, populum Romanum conuocassent, cuius authorita- te tyrannus Regno pelleretur, bonaque eius publicarentur. Nec dubium est, si prehen- dere eum potuissent, quin & iuxta leges, quas violarat (cum earum defensor esse de- buisset) eum fuissent damnaturi: Falsissima enim, & execrandi potius adulatoris, quam fidi subditi in principem, vox est, supremu Magistratum nullis legibus subiici: cum contra Magistra- nevnica quidem lex fit, secundum quam tus legibus gubernationem suam instituere non debe- patriis te- at, qui, omnium legum se defensorem ac est. vindicem fore, est iuramento pollicitus. Ita- Exempla. quetenenda est potius praeclara illa Marci Aure-
units.tr: Inferior magistrates, where there is manifest tyranny over the kingdom, must have recourse to the kingdom and meanwhile defend and protect those entrusted to their faith. Moreover, this is not seditious, nor is it treachery against one's supreme magistrate. Rather, it is to be the most faithful keeper of one's oath, towards those whose government each has undertaken, against a perjurer and oppressor of that kingdom, whose protector he ought to have been. Brutus and Lucretius at Rome rightly used this right against Tarquinius Superbus, who openly exercised tyranny. (Even privately, this cause would have concerned them.) The one was prefect of the city, the other tribune of the Celeres. They summoned the Roman people, by whose authority the tyrant was driven from the kingdom and his goods were confiscated. There is no doubt that, had they been able to seize him, they would have condemned him according to the laws he had violated, when he ought to have been their defender. For it is a most false and detestable saying, rather of a flatterer than of a faithful subject towards a prince, that the supreme magistrate is subject to no laws. On the contrary, there is a single law, the ancestral law, according to which a magistrate ought not to establish his government except under the laws, and who has sworn to become defender and avenger of all the laws.

units.la: Supremos ... Exempla. 1. Aurelii Imperatoris sententia: Digna vox est, Principem, se legibus subditum esse, profiteri. Quod etiā facto coprobauit potentissimus ille, nec vnquam satis laudatus Imperator Traianus, qui cum Surae (quem Tribunum militum creabat) pro more paratonium nudū porrigeret, Talem, inquit, ensem accipe, quem pro me ita demum strinxeris, si iuste imperauero: quod si per- peram quicquam per me fieri cognoueris, eo in per- niciem meam vtaris velim. Sed nunc ad sacram historiam conuertamur, quae vera & irrefragabilia multa exempla nobis suppeditabit, quibus obfirmentur piorum conscientiae. Cum Dauid ad necem quaereretur a Saule, crudelissimo & perfidissimo tyranno, neminē habuit ex ducibus Tribuum, Millenariis, Centurionibus, aut senioribus populi, qui causam suam tutaretur, aduersus tam impotentem tyrannidem, non solum inimicum ipsius Dauidis, sed etiā in totius Regni (maxime post summorum sacerdotum horrendam cędem) perniciem vergentem. Itaq; vt tyranni furorem deuitet, nō solum huc atque illuc profugus vagatur, sed cum priuatus amplius nō esset (quinimo vnus e regni ministris, dux Icil. exercituum Israelis) & praeterea ius successionis regiae a Deo illi promissum fuisset (quod nec Saulem latebat) armis sese & militib. communit, tētatis prius omni-
units.tr: Supreme magistrates... Examples. 1. Let us therefore hold fast rather to the famous saying of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius: It is a worthy saying that a prince professes himself subject to the laws. That most powerful emperor, never sufficiently praised, Trajan, also confirmed this by his deed. When he offered the bare sword, according to custom, to Sura, whom he was appointing tribune of the soldiers, he said: Take such a sword, which you should draw for me only if I command justly. But if you find that anything is done wrongly by me, I would have you use it against me to my destruction. But now let us turn to sacred history, which will supply us with many true and irrefutable examples, by which the consciences of the pious are confirmed. When David was sought for death by Saul, the most cruel and treacherous tyrant, David had among the leaders of the tribes, the commanders of thousands, the centurions, or the elders of the people, no one to defend his cause against so overbearing a tyranny, which was tending to the destruction not only of David himself, his enemy, but of the whole kingdom, especially after the horrible slaughter of the chief priests. And so, to avoid the tyrant's rage, he did not only wander as a fugitive here and there. But since he was no longer a private man (indeed he was one of the ministers of the kingdom, the commander Icil of the armies of Israel), and since the right of royal succession had moreover been promised to him by God, which Saul also knew, he protected himself with arms and soldiers.
