units.la: omnibus aliis mediis,1. Sam. 24. v. 21. 1. Sam. 22. v. 2. Interim tamen suis limitib. se continens, tantum abest, ut vel in regis persona quicquam moliatur, cum etiam deprehensum, viuú sal-uumq; ēmanibus suis dimiserit, 1. Sam. 24. v. 7. vel, regnum ipsum invadat, vt etiam Saule rege mortuo, cui se successurum certo sciebat, ne pedem quidem extulerit ad regiam sedé occupandam, nisi quantū Deus ipse eum promouet, & totius populi cōsensu aduocatur, 2. Sam. 2. v. 1. Attamen satis constat, propositū illi fuisse, armis sese tueri ob prædictas causas, 1. Sam. 23. v. 9. Quorsum enim alioqui illæ militum copiæ, quibus comitabatur? Quod vero tam aníxie Deū consulit, num cines Keila eum, & milites suos, in manus Saulis sint traditu-ri? aperte ostēdit, statuisse illū omnino, moenia oppidi illius Sauli obsidenti opponere, si in tuto se illic fore cognouisset. Quod facū damnari non potest, nisi & Dauid seditionis ac perduellionis insimuletur (cp tamen ne suspicari quidē licet) & prudens Abigail mē-dacii arguatur, 1. Sam. 25. v. 28. qua Dauidem iusta defensione aduersus iniustū persecutorē vtentē, bella Domini gerere, aperte professa est. Habemus & aliud exemplū euidentissimū, 2. Chro. 21. v. 10. de oppido Lobna, quod domici-lium erat Sacerdotum. Illud enim defecit ab Ioram, sexto Dauidis successore, ne amplius illi
units.tr: ...with all other means having first been tried. Yet he kept himself within his limits, so far was he from attempting anything against the king's person. Even when he found Saul in his power, he let him go alive and unharmed from his men, 1. Sam. 24. v. 21. 1. Sam. 22. v. 2. 1. Sam. 24. v. 7. Nor did he attack the kingdom itself. Even after Saul was dead, whom he knew for certain he would succeed, he did not set foot to occupy the royal seat, except as far as God himself advanced him and he was called by the consent of the whole people, 2. Sam. 2. v. 1. Nevertheless, it is quite certain that he intended to defend himself with arms for the reasons stated, 1. Sam. 23. v. 9. For what else were those troops of soldiers for, with which he went about? That he consulted God so anxiously, whether the men of Keilah would deliver him and his soldiers into Saul's hands, clearly shows that he had fully resolved to oppose the walls of the town to Saul besieging it, if he found he would be safe there. This act cannot be condemned, unless David is also accused of sedition and treason (which one may not even suspect), and the prudent Abigail is convicted of lying, 1. Sam. 25. v. 28. She openly professed that David, using just defence against an unjust persecutor, was waging the wars of the Lord. We have another most evident example, 2. Chr. 21. v. 10. concerning the town of Libnah, which was the residence of the priests. It revolted from Jehoram, the sixth successor of David, so that it would no longer be subject to him.

units.la: {4} Lobnenses illi subesset; eiusque defectionis causa in i- pso historiæ contextu exprimitur, nempe, quod Rex Ioram Dominum Deum patrum suorum dereliquisset. At cum ad sacerdotes oppidum ipsum pertineret, clare liquet, longe diuer- sum esse hoc Lobnensium factum ab Edu- meorum defectione, quæ sub eodem Rege & eodem tempore accidit. Neque enim ve- ro simile est, Edumeos ab Israelitarum sub- iectione sese subtraxisse, vt vero Deo adhæ- rerent, cui nunquam ex animo seruierant, sed odio duntaxat Israelitarum & recupe- randæ libertatis cupiditate. At sacerdotes, vel illi saltem (si hos prius lecessisse arbitra- bimur) qui post Deum Lobnæ dominium obtinebant, pietatis suæ egregium specimen ediderunt, cum simul & Deo & tyranno pa- rere non valentes, huius iugum excusse- runt, vt in Dei cultu & obsequio permane- rent. Hæc duo ex SS. scriptura petita exempla, præter supra citatas rationes, ita sunt cer- ta & authentica, vt sola (meo iudicio) suffi- cere possint, ad obfirmandas inferiorum Ma- gistratuum conscientias; quoties eos neces- sitas cogit, post tentata omnia alia remedia, ad arma confugere, vt suos aduersus tyran- nidem manifestam tueantur ac conseruent; non concitandæ, sed potius vitandæ seditio- nis gratia: sicut maiorum nostrorum ætate tyrantyrannis eorum, qui in Heluetios domina- bantur, occasionem Magistratibus Muni- cipalibus dedit, vendicandi sese in eam li- bertatem, qua hodie fruuntur.
units.tr: {4} ...that Lobnah should no longer be subject to him; and the cause of that defection is stated in the context of the history itself, namely, that King Jehoram had forsaken the Lord God of his fathers. But since the town belonged to the priests, it is clear that the defection of the Lobnites was very different from the defection of the Edomites, which happened under the same king and at the same time. For it is not likely that the Edomites withdrew from subjection to the Israelites in order to cling to the true God, whom they had never truly served, but only out of hatred for the Israelites and a desire to recover their liberty. The priests, or at least those (if we suppose that these left before them) who held lordship over Lobnah after God, gave an outstanding example of piety, since they could serve neither God and the tyrant together, and so they shook off the tyrant's yoke that they might remain in the worship and obedience of God. These two examples taken from Holy Scripture, apart from the reasons cited above, are so certain and authentic that they alone (in my judgement) are sufficient to confirm the consciences of the lesser magistrates, whenever necessity compels them, after all other remedies have been tried, to take up arms, so that they may defend and preserve their own people against manifest tyranny; not in order to stir up sedition, but rather to avoid it. Thus in the time of our ancestors the tyranny of those who ruled over the Helvetians gave the municipal magistrates occasion to claim for themselves that liberty which they enjoy today.

units.la: Repetitio VI. Quaestionis.
units.tr: Repetition of the Sixth Question.

units.la: Ordines sive statuS, ad frenandos supremos magistratus constituti, possunt ac de- bent omnibus modis illis refi- ere, cum in tyrannos de- generant.
units.tr: The orders or estates, appointed to restrain the supreme magistrates, can and ought, by all means, to resist them when they degenerate into tyrants.

units.la: Vpereft, vt de tertio subditorum gene- re loquamur; qui, etsi reuera ac certo quodam respectu supremorum Magistra- tuum obedientiae subsint, alio tamen refpe- ctu, maxime rebus angustis extremisque, cöftituti sunt defensores ac protectores iu- rium ipsius suprema potestatis, vt summos Magistratus in officio retineant, eofq;, fi o- puserit, & coerceant & multent. Hic vero meminisse oportet eorum, quae supra dicta sunt, nempe populum extitisse priusquam magi- stratus vllus effet, & propter populum Magi- stratus creatos, non contra populum propter Magi- stratum. Quantumuis enim quidam popu- lia suis regibus originem traxisse videantur (vt a Romulo populus Romanus creatus fuit- sedicitur, quia prius originalis populus non fuerit, sed multitudo quaedam ex variis gentibus & populis collecta) id tamen ad alios trahi haud quaquam poterit, vt inde Regula generalis constituatur. Praeterea, ne Romulus quidem in has gentes collectitias, nisi ex ipsarum consensu, dominatus est. Indefequitur, Magistratuum omnium, quantumuis supremorum ac potentium, authoritatem, a publica eorum authoritate pendere, qui ipsos ad hunc dignitatis gradum euexerunt, non contra.
units.tr: It remains to speak of the third kind of subjects; who, although in truth and in a certain respect they are subject to the obedience owed to the supreme magistrates, yet in another respect, especially in narrow and extreme circumstances, are appointed as defenders and protectors of the rights of the supreme power itself, so that they may keep the highest magistrates in their duty and, if they have offended, both restrain and punish them. Here, however, we must remember what was said above: namely, that the people existed before any magistrate did, and that magistrates were created on account of the people, not the people on account of the magistrate. For although some peoples seem to have derived their origin from their kings (as it is said that the Roman people was created by Romulus, because the original people did not exist before him, but was a certain multitude gathered from various nations and peoples), this cannot by any means be extended to others, so that a general rule may be established from it. Moreover, not even Romulus ruled over these gathered nations except with their own consent. It follows that the authority of all magistrates, however supreme and powerful, depends on the public authority of those who raised them to this rank of dignity, not the reverse.

units.la: Ac, ne quis obiiciat, hanc quidem primam fuisse Magistratuum originem, sed postea populos sese prorsus eorum potentia, & arbitrio subiecisse, quos pro summis Magistratibus recepissent, & omnem suam libertatem, sine exceptione, illis omnino resignasse: Nego primum, certo de hac omnimoda abdicatione constare: Quin contra affirmo, nullam gentem (quandiu ius & aequitas viguerunt) Reges suos aut creasse, aut probasse, nisi certis appositis conditionibus: Quas si illi manifeste violant, efficitur, vt qui hanc in illos authoritatem conferre potuerunt, non minus potestatis in ea illis rursus admenda retinuerint. Quod vt clarius appareat, dispiciamus, an non per omnes aetates, interfamosissimas quasque Nationes, & magis notas perpetuo visu, hoc comprobari possit.
units.tr: And lest anyone object that this was indeed the first origin of magistrates, but afterwards the peoples wholly submitted themselves to the power and will of those whom they had received as supreme magistrates, and entirely surrendered all their liberty to them without exception: I deny, first, that there is certain evidence of this total abdication; indeed I affirm the contrary, that no nation (as long as right and equity flourished) either created or approved its kings except on certain attached conditions. If these kings clearly violate those conditions, it follows that those who were able to confer this authority upon them have likewise retained the power to take it back again. So that this may appear more clearly, let us examine whether this can be shown to hold true in all ages and among the most famous nations, and those best known through constant record.

units.la: Ducamus autem exordium a Romanorum Re-
units.tr: Let us begin with the kingdom of the Romans,

units.la: rum Regno, ac deinde Imperio, licet hi ve- tustiores non fuerint. Titus Liuius, initia Romani Regni describens, refert; cum cen- tum illi, Interreges nominati, qui post Romu- li (primi huius populi progenitoris) mor- tem populo per vices praerant, plebi non placerent, communi consensu statutum, vt deinceps Reges suffragiis populi crearentur, & Senatus authoritate firmarentur. Idem, de Tarquinio Superbo, vltimo Rom. Regelo- quens; Neq; enim (inquit) ad ius Regni quic quā praeter vim habebat, vt qui nec populi iussu, neque autoribus patribus regnaret. Ac mox multa tecen set, quae ab illo contra Maiorum instī- tuta fierent: Hic enim, inquit, Regum primus, vt traditur à prioribus, morem de omnibus Se- natum consulendi soluit. Rempublicam domi- ficis consiliis administrauit, bellum, pacem, fo- dera, societatemque per seipse, cum quibus voluit, iniussu populi ac Senatus, fecit diremitque. Ex quibus verbis satis constat, Romanorum Reges non, nisi certis conditionibus, fnif- fe admissos; quas si non praestarent, popu- lus, iuxta ciuium distinctos ordines conuo- catus, non minus ad illos exauctorandos, quam adeos constituendos, potestatis ha- beret: quod erga illum ipsum Tyrannum facto ipso satis demonstrarunt. Caeterum prae- ter id, quod Seneca ex libris Ciceronis de Repu- blica lica annotauit, nempe, prouocationem fuisse ad Regem ad populum (quod in caula capitali Horatii sororicidæ factitatum est, qui a delegatis per Tullium Hostilium Regem Iudicibus damnatus, a populo postea est absolutus) præter id, inquam, testatur etiā Dionysius; Romulum dum cum suis de statu Romano constituendo consilium cepisset, pronuntiasse, Regem quidem custodem esse legum; at interim penes populum reliquam potestatem fuisse creandorum Magistratuum, Legum constituendarum, & indicendi belli. Quod primis Gallicæ Monarchiæ architectis pro archetypo fuisse, verisimile est, vt infra docebimus. Adhæc ex Collatini, qui primus cum Bruto Consul fuit, historia patet, populum (cuius appellatione non tantum status ille plebeius, quem hodie tertium appellamus, intelligendus est, sed tres illi simul ordines, qui Romæ erant, nempe, Patricius, Equestris & Plebeius) eandem authoritatem in Consules quoque habuisse: quamuis illi suprema in Republica potestate potirentur, vbi Dictatore carerent. Id enim testatur etiam Liuius, his verbis: Timens Consul, ne postmodum priuato sibi, eadem illa, cum bonorum amissione, additaque insuper alia ignominia, acciderent, consulatu se abdicauit. At Collatinus nullius criminis incusabatur, sed suspectum erat duntaxat populo
units.tr: and then the empire, although these are more ancient. Titus Livy, describing the beginnings of the Roman kingdom, reports that when the hundred men called interkings, who after the death of Romulus (the first progenitor of this people) presided over the people in turn, did not please the commons, it was agreed by common consent that from then on kings should be created by the votes of the people and confirmed by the authority of the Senate. The same Livy, speaking of Tarquin the Proud, the last Roman king, says: "For he (said he) had no right to the kingdom, except force; since he reigned neither by the command of the people nor with the approval of the fathers." And soon afterwards he adds many things that were done by him contrary to the institutions of the ancestors: "For he, said he, was the first of the kings, as is handed down by those before him, to break the custom of consulting the whole Senate. He administered the commonwealth by private counsels; war, peace, treaties and alliances he made and broke by himself, with whom he wished, without the command of the people or the Senate." From these words it is quite clear that the Roman kings were admitted only on certain conditions; and if they did not fulfil these, the people, called together according to the distinct orders of citizens, had no less power to depose them than to appoint them. This they showed in fact against that very tyrant. Moreover, besides what Seneca noted from the books of Cicero's On the Commonwealth, namely that there was an appeal from the king to the people (which was done in the capital case of Horatius the sister-slayer, who, condemned by judges appointed by King Tullus Hostilius, was afterwards acquitted by the people), Dionysius also bears witness, besides this, that Romulus, when he had taken counsel with his men about establishing the Roman state, declared that the king was indeed the guardian of the laws; but that meanwhile the remaining power, of creating magistrates, of making laws and of declaring war, lay with the people. It is probable that this was the model for the first architects of the French monarchy, as we shall show below. Furthermore, it is evident from the history of Collatinus, who was the first consul with Brutus, that the people (by which name is to be understood not only that plebeian estate which we today call the third estate, but those three orders which were at Rome together, namely the patricians, the equestrians and the plebeians) had the same authority over the consuls as well, although they held supreme power in the commonwealth where there was no dictator. For Livy also bears witness to this, in these words: "The consul, fearing that afterwards the same things would happen to him as a private man, with the loss of his goods and with further disgrace added, resigned from the consulship." Yet Collatinus was accused of no crime, but was merely suspected by the people.

Inde ergo facile est col- ligere, multo magis hoc iure populum vsu- rum fuisse, fi quis Consùl alicuius criminis reus effet peractus: quamuis ex Legum prae- scripto exspectandum effet, vt (quia tempo- rarium Magistratum gerebant) tempus ita- tutum implerent, priusquam causam dicere cogerentur. Fateor quidem, Decemuiros po- ftea creatos, à quibus ad alium Magistratum non erat prouocatio; verum, cū alternatim impe- rent, licebat ab vnius sententia ad alterum appellare: tatum abest, vt cuiufquam immé- fa, & nullis limitibus conclusa potestas, po- pulo Romano vtquam placuerit; quin tan- dem etiam Decemuiros ipsos, officio sese abdicare, coegit. Quod vero ad Dictatoris po- teftatem attinet, verum est quidem, abillo non licuisse ad alium prouocare: sed hac dignitas nō, nisi extrema aliqua necessitate laboran- te, & pene oppressa Republica, in vsu erat, & id quidem ad breuissimum tempus, fème- fre fcil. Sed (quod etiam maius est) fi quan- do ab huius suprema potestate ad populum à Dictatorem prouocatum est, confentitille vltro: vtex re ad popu- lis quae Romae, Anno ab V.C.CCCXX. Inter L. Papirium Dictatorem & Qu. Fabium contigerunt, videre est. Quid fi vlterius progredi libet, & ad Ca- fares
units.tr: The name of the Tarquins, of whose family Consul Collatinus was, is mentioned here. From this it is easy to infer that the people would have used this right all the more, if any consul had been convicted of some crime, although by the prescription of the laws they would have had to wait until the consuls, who held a temporary magistracy, had completed their appointed term before being compelled to plead their case. I grant that the decemvirs were created afterwards, and that there was no appeal from them to another magistrate. But since they ruled in turn, it was permitted to appeal from the sentence of one to the other. So far was it from ever pleasing the Roman people to have any power that was immense and bounded by no limits, that at last they even forced the decemvirs themselves to lay down their office. As for the power of the dictator, it is true that one could not appeal from him to another. But this office was in use only when the state was in some extreme necessity and almost crushed, and even then only for a very short time, namely six months. But (what is even more significant) if at any time an appeal was made from the supreme power of the dictator to the people, he himself consented willingly. This can be seen from the affair that took place at Rome in the year 320 from the founding of the city, between Lucius Papirius the dictator and Quintus Fabius. What if we wish to go further, and come to the Caesars

units.tr: 3 On the Right of Magistrates.

units.la: fares vsq; pertingere? Etsi Iulius Cæsar Rem-pub. vi potius, quà voluntario populi affen-su, occupasset; videri tamen voluit, à popu-lo, iuxta antiquas consuetudines, dignitates omnes, & munera quæ obtinebat, confecu-tus; & ob id duntaxat reprehensus existima-tur à multis (ac etiam tandem iure occisus) quod nimis multas dignitates cumulasset. Augustus, eius successor, adoptatus quidem ab illo fuit, sed non hæres Imperii reliƈtus: ideo persuadere conatus est, se iure, & à pulo obtinuisse, quod vi occuparat. Nec Tyberius alia ratione ei successit. Et post eū Caligula, summo tum Senatus tum populi consensu, Cæsar est appellatus. Claudius vero prius quidem imperium militari & coempto fauore, obtinuit, at non, nisi consentiente populo, illud rexit, qui tum volēs sese in miseram seruitutem præceps dedidit. Nero aūt illi succedens, cum veneno illum sustulisset, Imperium aperta violentia occupauit. Sed eius exitus exemplum nobis singulare suppeditat eius auth oritatis, quàm Senatus ad-huc tū retin-bat. Nā is iure suo vtens (quod diu quasi sopitum delituerat) dicitur nomi-natim, Neronem, populi Romani hostem prius iu-dicatum, capite damnasse. Vnde apparet, ipsos etiam Cæsares, Tyrannos factos, iuridice & coerceri & damnari potuisse: ipsorumque Impe-
units.tr: ...reach? Although Julius Caesar had seized the commonwealth by force, with the people's assent only in appearance, he nevertheless wished it to seem that he had obtained all his dignities and offices from the people, according to ancient custom. For this alone he is thought by many to have been blamed, and even at last rightly killed, because he had heaped up too many dignities. Augustus, his successor, was indeed adopted by him but was not left as heir to the empire, so he tried to persuade people that he had obtained by right and from the people what he had seized by force. Nor did Tiberius succeed in any other way. After him Caligula was named Caesar with the full consent of both the Senate and the people. Claudius indeed first obtained power by the army and by bought favour, but he did not rule except with the consent of the people, who then, wishing to be slaves, rushed headlong into wretched servitude. Nero, succeeding him, after poisoning him, seized the empire by open violence. But his end offers us a singular example of the authority which the Senate still then retained. For, using its right (which had long lain dormant as if asleep), it is said to have condemned Nero to death by name, having first judged him an enemy of the Roman people. From this it appears that the Caesars themselves, when they had become tyrants, could be restrained and condemned by legal process.

units.la: Imperiū, etsi latissime ex lege Regia (propter Lex Regia, Augustum lata, & propter Vespasianum confirmata) pateret, certis tamen limitibus definitum, nec fine exceptione probatum fuisse, quamdiu iuri & æquitati locus fuit. Ecquid enim aliud est Tyrannis, quam pote- stas aduersus leges sese exerens? de cuius amplitudine & expansione nobis dicere non est propositum (quæ enim effrena cupiditatis & malitiæ Tyrannorum meta esse potest?) sed de lege gitima tantum Regum, aliorumque Principum potestate legibus finita. Atqui hæc qui- dem de Romanis.
units.tr: The empire of the Caesars, although it extended very widely under the Royal Law (the Lex Regia, enacted for Augustus and confirmed for Vespasian), was nevertheless defined by fixed limits and was never approved without exception, as long as there was room for right and equity. For what else is tyranny than a power exercised against the laws? I do not propose to speak of its extent and expansion (for what limit can there be to the unbridled desire and malice of tyrants?), but only of the lawful power of kings and other princes, which is bounded by laws. But so much for the Romans.

units.la: Athenienses porro, cum abrogatam Democratiam in Ariftocratiam commutassent, ex Athenis, Triginta primum viros, postea Decem en sum Regi tantum, publicæ gubernationi præfecerunt, publica. Vt ipsorum historiæ perhibent: Quos cum authoritate sua abuterentur, deinceps & ab officio remouerunt, & dignis suppliciis ex- iam affecerunt, eodem scilicet iure in eos ventes, quo illos primum creauerant.
units.tr: Again, the Athenians, when they had abolished democracy and changed it into an aristocracy, first placed thirty men over public government, and afterwards ten, as their histories report. When these abused their authority, the Athenians in turn removed them from office and punished them with deserved penalties, proceeding against them by the very same right by which they had first created them.

units.la: Notum est etiam Lacedæmonios, Reges IIII. suos pro arbitrio ex Heraclidarum familia eli- gere solitos. Quod mutarely candrum volu- isse, tradit Plutarchus, sed fruitra. Regeauté certis conditionib. electo, Epboros constitue- runt, qui Reges in officio retinerent, ac vel- uti habenis frænarent. Hi porro alios modo expu-
units.tr: It is well known that the Lacedaemonians were accustomed to choose their two kings at their own pleasure from the family of the Heraclidae. Plutarch relates that Cleomenes wished to change this, but in vain. Once the kings had been chosen under certain conditions, they appointed the Ephors, whose task was to keep the kings in their duty and, as it were, to restrain them with reins. These in turn sometimes expelled the kings and sometimes put them to death.

units.la: Exempla Lacedæmo- nus petita. expulerunt, modo capitis supplicio affece-runt, donec tandem proditione Cleomenis tyranni, omnes occiderentur: quo facto Lacedæmon, simul cum dominatione, libertatem amisit. Venit autem hic mihi in mentem pulcherrimus ille Xenophontis locus, quo, de Lacedæmoniorum Republica verba faciens, tradit, Regem & Ephoros singulis inter sibi se mutuo iureiurando obligare consue-uisse; hos quidem omnium ciuium, illum proprio suo nomine: ac Regem quidem hoc iuramento policeri; se ex praescripto constitutarum legum re-spaturum: Ephoros autem, se ciuitatem illi con-seruaturos, si iusiurandum seruasset.
units.tr: ...and at last, through the treachery of the tyrant Cleomenes, all of them were killed; and when this happened Lacedaemon lost its liberty together with its dominion. Here there comes to my mind that most beautiful passage of Xenophon, where, speaking of the commonwealth of the Lacedaemonians, he relates that the king and the Ephors were accustomed to bind each other by oath, the Ephors on behalf of all the citizens and the king in his own name: the king promised by this oath that he would rule in accordance with the prescribed laws, and the Ephors that they would preserve the kingdom for him, if he kept his oath.

units.la: IV. Exempla ex Israel. tarü mo-narchia. Israelitica Monarchia omnium felicissima cur extitit.
units.tr: IV. Examples from the Israelite monarchy. Why the Israelite monarchy was the most felicitous of all.

units.la: Veniamus nunc ad Israeliticam πολιτείαν, omnium, quæ vnquam fuerunt, perfectissimam, si ea Israelitæ contenti fuissent. Hoc vero primum eam veluti supra sidera euehit, quod, ab initio, Deus ipse æternus eius vnicus Monarcha fuerit, non eo tantum nomine, quod ipse rerum omnium supremum do-minium obtineat, sed singulari quodam modo; nempe, quod leges per Moysen visibiliter Israelitis constituerit, quod populum suum per Iehosuam in terram promissam, ex-erto veluti brachio, introduxerit, Ios. 2. vers. 16. quod denique illis præfuerit eosque regerit, in eorum scilicet persona, quos ipse immediate ad illius gubernacula prefecifset, qui Iudices vocabantur. Eo igitur tempore πολιτεία Israelis vere Monarchica fuit, (quā-uis Deus quorundam ministerio, pro beneplacito suo, vteretur.) Quod si regna omnia hunc Monarcham haberent, vel saltem omnes Monarchiae ab hoc summo mundi totius Domino se regi semper paterentur, non minus superflua esset haec, de qua agitur, quaestio, quam ea nunc pernecessaria esse agnoscitur. At enim felix ille huius Reipubl. status, (qui nulli unquam, praeter huic populo, obtigit) stupendo & insolenti modo mutatus est. Nam reliquarum gentium Monarchiae in ty-ranidem, ipsorum Monarcha-rum culpa, deflexerunt: At Israelitae, cum tam bonum non agnoscerent, optimum illum suum Monarcham, qui tyrannus fieri nunquam poterat, veluti inuitum adegerunt, vt ipsis Regem ex hominibus constitueret, sicut & reliquis populis. Dominus ergo tandem illorum votis annuit, sed in ira & indignatione sua: non quasi statum Monarchicū per se eo facto damnare voluerit, sed quia haec mutatio a populo cerebricoso & refractario esset profecta. Interea hoc difficile mutari nec poterat, nec debet: Regem nullum a condito mundo (etiamsi optimum quemque felicem) extitisse, qui sua auctoritate non fuerit aliquatenus abusus, adeo vt omnino faten-dum sit, dum fit, (id quod Philosophi etiam sola ratione naturali instruction agnouerunt) Monarchicam dominationem, perniciem ac interitum potius populo afferre, quam praesidium & salutem, nisi habenis quibusdam coarctetur, quibus fiat, ut maximum illud bonum, quod ex eapote st emanare, colligi; & ingens malum, quod alioqui omnino ex illa consequi necesse est, vitari & impediri possit. Vtor hac praefatione, de Israelitici Regni primordiis sermonem ingressus, quoniam horum omnium clara illicexempla extant: ad quę, vt tam Reges quam populi folicite animaduerterent, esset operae pretium, ne alios ab aliis opprimi tam saepe contingeret; sed potius vtrisque Dei (a quo solo omnis manat tranquillitas) gloria ita curae esset, vt, & qui imperant, & qui parent, simul pacifice sese tueri satagerent. Verum vt eo redeam, unde sum digressus; Dominus merito in populum suum ira percitus, vt quid illis ex temerario illo, quo agitabantur, affectu expectandum esset, clare ostenderet. Praedicit illis per Samuelem, mirisomnino verbis, quod fit ius illud futurum, quod historia ius Regis vocat: Nempe in summa; Regem pro libidine, & personas, & bona subditorum, vsurpaturum, & ad suos vsus conversurum: quod certe Tyrannicum est potius, quam Regium. Quis enim merito dubitare bitare ausit, Dei solius esse, meram suam voluntatem loco rationis obtrudere? cum nihil iustum dici possit, nisi quod prius Deus voluerit: Dei enim solius voluntas vera est, ac certa omnis iustitiæ Regula, vt ab initio dictum est. Contra vero hominibus accidit, quorum etiam ratio iustis ac sanctis legibus subiici, & moderari debet; in iis præcipue, qui aliis præsunt adeo, vt toto cœlo errent, qui Samuelis verba ita accipiunt, quasi is author Regibus esse voluerit, quidlibet audendi: aut, quacunque illi caca voluntate egerint, approbarit: iuxta execrandum impuræ illius incestuosæ dictum: Si libet, licet: quod, proh dolor! plusquam satis nostro hoc sæculo iactatur, & præstatur. Quinimo ita accipienda sunt Samuelis verba, quasi Israelem increpans diceret, Non sufficit vobis Deum ipsum pro Monarcha vestro habere, vt fuit hactenus, peculiari quodam fauore: sed alium ac talem expetitis, qualem habent reliqui populi: ContingEt ergo vobis talis: At audite rursus, quid iuris ille in vos fit vsurpaturus, & qua æquitate ac iustitia vobis dominaturus. Hunc esse sensum verborum Samuelis, experientia ipsa postea ostendit: Dico igitur, Quamuis Deus nominatim Dauidem elegisset, oportuisse tamen eum etiam à populo eligi: qui in eo eligendo recte, prout debuit, Dei voluntatem D luntatem fit secutus, 2. Sam. 5. verf. 1. Idem acci- dit quoque in Salomone, qui à Deo primum electus, à populo secundario Rex creatus fuit, 1. Par. 29. verf. 22. Et in genere, quamuis diadema regium, ex Dei mandato, hæreditario iure ad familiam Dauidis pertineret, populus tamen, vt supra à nobis ostensum est, ex demortui Regis liberis eum eligebat, quem regnare mallet. Idque duplici obligatione interueniente, vt patet ex historia Ioas, 2. Reg. 11. verf. 4. & 17. Nam tam Rex, quam populus, solenni iureiurando Deo primum polli-cebantur, se leges ipsius tam Ecclesiasticas, quam Politicas obseruaturos. Adhibebatur postea & aliud iuramentum mutuum inter Regem ipsum, & populum. At vero, dixerit quispiam, eratne propterea ius populo (id est, ordinibus populi) in eum, quem elegerat, cum officium non præstaret, animaduertere? Erat profecto, quod quatuor exemplis potestatem probari poterit. Si enim licuit Dauidi aduersus Saulis tyrannidem sese tueri, vt paulo ante visum est, & Lobnei fibus ab obedientia lorum debere (qui tamen inferiores tantum Magistratus erant) nonne inde merito colligam, Regis ordinibus multo etiam plura ipso iure hi u sse? Huc quoque pertinet id, quod prudenti Ioiadæ sacerdotis consilio, ab ipsis ordinibus aduersus Athaliam (quæ Regi-
units.tr: Let us now come to the Israelite commonwealth, the most perfect of all that have ever existed, had the Israelites been content with it. This first of all raises it, as it were, above the stars: that from the beginning the eternal God himself was its only Monarch, not only because he holds supreme dominion over all things, but in a singular manner; namely, because he established laws for the Israelites visibly through Moses, because through Joshua he led his people into the promised land with an outstretched arm (Ios. 2. vers. 16.), and because finally he ruled over them, through those whom he himself had immediately placed at the helm, who were called Judges. At that time, therefore, the commonwealth of Israel was truly monarchical, although God used the ministry of certain men as he pleased. But if all kingdoms had this Monarch, or at least if all monarchies always allowed themselves to be ruled by this supreme Lord of the whole world, this question which we are discussing would be no less superfluous than it is now acknowledged to be most necessary. But that happy state of this commonwealth (which fell to no people except this one) was changed in a strange and extraordinary way. For the monarchies of other nations have turned into tyranny through the fault of their own monarchs. The Israelites, however, not recognising so great a good, forced their best Monarch, who could never become a tyrant, as it were against his will, to give them a king from among men, as the other peoples had. So the Lord at last yielded to their wishes, but in his anger and indignation: not as if he wished to condemn the monarchical state in itself by this act, but because this change came from a stubborn and refractory people. Meanwhile, this matter could neither be nor ought to be changed easily: since the creation of the world there has been no king (even if each was a good and happy one) who has not in some measure abused his authority, so that it must be fully admitted, as long as it is so (as the philosophers too recognised from natural reason alone), that monarchical domination brings ruin and destruction on a people rather than protection and safety, unless it is restrained by certain reins, so that the greatest good which can flow from it may be gathered, and the great evil which must otherwise follow from it may be avoided and prevented. I make this preface as I enter upon discussion of the beginnings of the Israelite kingdom, because clear examples of all these things exist there; and it would be worth while for both kings and peoples to take careful note of them, so that one people would not so often oppress another, but rather that both would be so concerned for the glory of God (from whom alone all tranquillity flows) that both those who rule and those who obey would strive to preserve peace together. But to return to where I digressed: the Lord, justly stirred to anger against his people, wished to show clearly what was to be expected from the rash passion by which they were driven. He foretold to them through Samuel, in remarkably strong words, what kind of right that would be which the history calls the right of the king: namely, in short, that the king would seize at his own pleasure both the persons and the goods of his subjects and turn them to his own uses, which is certainly more tyrannical than royal. For who would dare to doubt that it belongs to God alone to thrust his bare will in place of reason? since nothing can be called just except what God has first willed: for the will of God alone is true, and the sure rule of all justice, as was said at the beginning. But it is otherwise with men, whose reason too must be subjected to and governed by just and holy laws, especially those who rule over others. Those therefore are wholly mistaken who take Samuel's words as if he wished to be the author for kings to dare anything, or as if he approved whatever they did from blind will, following that accursed and impure saying of that incestuous man: If it pleases, it is allowed, which, alas, is bandied about and practised more than enough in our own age. Indeed Samuel's words should be understood as if, rebuking Israel, he were saying: "It is not enough for you to have God himself as your Monarch, as he has been until now by a peculiar favour; you seek another and such a king as other peoples have. Such a king you shall have. But hear again what right he will seize over you, and with what equity and justice he will rule over you." That this is the meaning of Samuel's words experience itself showed afterwards. I say therefore that although God had named David beforehand, it was still necessary that he be chosen also by the people, who in choosing him followed God's will rightly, as was proper (2. Sam. 5. vers. 1.). The same happened also with Solomon, who, though first chosen by God, was made king secondarily by the people (1. Par. 29. vers. 22.). And in general, although the royal diadem, by God's command, belonged by hereditary right to the family of David, the people nevertheless, as we have shown above, chose as king whichever of the sons of the dead king they preferred to reign. And this was done with a double obligation intervening, as is clear from the history of Joash (2. Reg. 11. vers. 4. and 17.). For both the king and the people first promised solemnly before God that they would observe his laws, both ecclesiastical and political. Afterwards another mutual oath was taken between the king himself and the people. But someone may say: was it therefore lawful for the people (that is, the estates of the people) to call to account the one they had chosen, when he did not perform his duty? Certainly it was, and this power can be proved by four examples. For if it was lawful for David to defend himself against the tyranny of Saul, as was shown a little earlier, and if the Lobnei were bound to disobey the commands of their superiors (although they were only inferior magistrates), do I not rightly conclude from this that the estates of the king had much more such right by law? To this also belongs what was done against Athaliah, who had been made queen (and had ruled the kingdom for six full years), by the estates themselves, on the prudent counsel of the priest Jehoiada. Finally, the example of Amaziah (2. Reg. 14. vers. 19.) is still much plainer; the Jerusalemites were hostile to him even to the point of killing him. But if someone thinks this was done by sedition and not lawfully, I ask him to consider carefully...

units.la: Regina constituta, sex integris annis Regnū administrarat) patratum fuit. Denique Amasiæ exemplum, 2.Reg. 14.19. multo est adhuc apertius, quem Hierosolymitani ad necem vsque fuⁿt infestati. Quod si id per seditionem factum quispiam arbitretur, & non legitime, is quaso diligenter ad sequentes rationes attendat. Nusquam dicitur Amasias aseruis domesticis occisus(sicut id patri suo Ioas contigisse, & Ammoni Manassis filio, legi-mus) sed potius communi quodam Hierosolymitanorum consessu: neq; id occulte, & quasi per insidias(qui fuit quam plurium tyrannorum exitus) sed vi aperta, & velut publica autho-ritate: nec subito aliquo tumultu, sed postquam ille fuga sese in vrbem Lachis receperisset, vnde & ipsius cadauer reportatum, & in patrum suo-rum sepulchrum conditum, scribitur. Nihil denique hic neque ante, neque post Amasiæ mortem conspicitur, quod seditionis suspicio-nem habeat: sed omnes circumstantiæ euin-cunt cunctas potius consilio, & meditata deli-beratione Hierosolymitanorum (simul taci-to fœdere, tanquam præcipua ordinum pars, coniunctorum) tentata & patrata fuisse, etsi id extra ordinem, & quasi perfunctorie, ac-ciderit: nullo certe priuato odio, sed propter ipsius impietatem, qua præcipuam iuramen-ti sui partem violarat. Ideoque nuspiam le-gimus, gimus, post eius mortem vel querimoniam vllam, vel inquisitionem, vel denique poenam aliquam aduersus cadis authores procuratam, aut irrogatam, vel a populo, vel ab ipsius liberis fuisse: quemadmodum post mortem Ammonis & Ioas contigit, 2.Reg.12.10.&14.5.&21.24. in quorum coniuratos occisores, etsi domesticos iustis poenis fuit animaduersum, quamuis vterque illorum improbus fuisset. At contra, mortuum huius cadauer equis in Ierusalem reuectum fuisse legimus, ob reuerentiam tum Regiae dignitatis, tum familiae: & Azariam ipsius filium a populo Iuda vniuerso, Regem illi suffectum. Quod rursus plane ostedit id, quod a potiore Ordinum parte (nempe a Hierosolymitanis) factum fuerat, communi postea consensu confirmatum fuisse: vt iusta de causa, & per eos, executioni mandatum, quibus id liceret. Hinc igitur concludo, ordines seu status populi Israelitici ius habuisse, & ex familia Dauidis sibi Regem quem vellent eligere, & electum postea vel eiuscere vel supplicio etiam, prout res ferebat, affecere.
units.tr: The queen having been installed, she had governed the kingdom for six full years. Finally, the example of Amaziah (2 Kings 14:19) is much clearer still. The people of Jerusalem were enraged against him to the point of killing him. If someone thinks this was done by sedition and not lawfully, I ask him to consider carefully the following reasons. Nowhere is it said that Amaziah was killed by his household servants, as we read happened to his father Joash and to Amon, son of Manasseh. It was rather by a common assembly of the people of Jerusalem. Nor was it done secretly and by stealth, as was the fate of many tyrants, but openly and with what looks like public authority. Nor was it done in a sudden tumult. After he had fled and withdrawn to the city of Lachish, from there, as is written, his body was brought back and buried in the tomb of his fathers. Finally, nothing is seen here, either before or after Amaziah's death, that carries any suspicion of sedition. Rather, all the circumstances prove that the deed was attempted and carried out by the deliberate counsel and considered decision of the people of Jerusalem, acting together under a tacit covenant as the principal part of the estates, even though it happened outside the ordinary course and, as it were, carelessly. Certainly it was not from any private hatred, but on account of his impiety, by which he had violated the chief part of his oath. Therefore we nowhere read that after his death any complaint, inquiry, or finally any punishment was sought or inflicted against his killers, either by the people or by his children. This is in contrast to what happened after the deaths of Amon and Joash (2 Kings 12:10; 14:5; 21:24), where the domestic conspirators who killed them were punished with just penalties, although each of those kings had been wicked. On the contrary, we read that the body of this king was carried back to Jerusalem on horses, out of reverence for both the royal dignity and the family, and that his son Azariah was made king in his place by the whole people of Judah. This again plainly shows that what had been done by the greater part of the estates (namely the people of Jerusalem) was afterwards confirmed by the common consent, so that it was carried out for a just cause, and by those to whom it was lawful. Hence I conclude that the estates, or orders, of the people of Israel had the right to choose for themselves a king from the family of David, whomever they wished, and, once chosen, to depose him or even to punish him with death, as circumstances required.

units.la: Sic nostra memoria Dani Christiernum, crudelissimum tyrannum, non solum Regia dignitate priuarunt, sed carcere conclusum ad mortem vsque detinuerunt, translato Regno ad sapientissimum iustissimumque Reque Regem, illius auunculum, eiusque qui nunc regnat auum.
units.tr: So in our own memory the Danes deprived Christian, that most cruel tyrant, not only of his royal dignity, but shut him in prison and kept him there until his death, transferring the kingdom to the most wise and most just king, his uncle, and to the grandfather of the one who now reigns.

units.la: Quod ad Suecos quoque attinet, fatis norunt omnes, quomodo nostra ætate Gustauus se suosque à Danorum subiectione liberarit: & etiamnum hodie Sueci Regem suum captiuum asseruant, ob non satis prudenter administratum Regnum, quod ad fratrem ipsius translatum est: Cui Dominus benedicat.
units.tr: As for the Swedes too, everyone knows well how in our own age Gustavus freed himself and his people from Danish subjection. And even today the Swedes maintain that their king is a captive, because he administered the kingdom not wisely enough, and the kingdom was transferred to his brother. May the Lord bless him.

units.la: Nota A. Huc referri potest modo dicti Regni status hodiernus; Sueci enim abdicato Sigismundo III. Erici Regis filio, designato Rege Poloniæ, (vt-pote Pontificiorum religioni addicto) Carolo, Du-ci Sudermanlandiæ, &c. Sigismundi prædicti patruo, Principi Christianissimo, & iam designato Regi parere malunt.
units.tr: Note A. The present condition of the said kingdom may be referred to here. The Swedes, having deposed Sigismund III, son of King Eric, who had been designated king of Poland, because he was attached to the religion of the Papists, preferred to obey Charles, Duke of Södermanland, and so on, uncle of the aforesaid Sigismund, a most Christian prince who has already been designated king.

units.la: Scoti etiam superioribus annis Reginam suam abdicarunt, & perpetuo carcere damnauerunt, quod quam plurimorum tur-pium adulteriorum, atque etiam crudelissimæ cædis mariti sui accusaretur: quæ accusatio si legitime probata est, audeo dicere, rectius eos facturos fuisse, si in eam promeritas poenas exercuissent.
units.tr: In former years the Scots also deposed their queen and condemned her to perpetual imprisonment, because she was accused of very many shameful adulteries and of the most cruel murder of her husband. If that accusation was lawfully proved, I dare say they would have acted more rightly had they inflicted the punishment she deserved.

units.la: Caeterum quod ad Angliæ Regnum (omnium quotquot hodie in vniuerso orbe visuntur felicissimum, atque vtinam in ea feli-citate diu perduret) spectat, etiamsi ad eum, qui Regio sanguine proximior est, iure successionis illud denoluatur: apparet nihilominus, tum ex multis historiis memoratu dignissimis, tum ex Polydori testimonio, in vita Henrici, huius nominis primi, Anglorum Regis, omnem fere regnandi authoritatem à consensu Parlamenti (vt vocant) pendere. Et sane si conferre libet beatam illam tranquillitatem (quam iam multis annis fruuntur, sub benignissimo & pacatissimo Serenissimae Reginae Elizabethae dominio) cum miserrimo & infelici statu, tot aliarum regionum: ipsa experientia docebimur, quam sit ea moderatio Regiae potestatis utilis, & beata, si modo ea recta exerceatur, & Reges ipsi Deum timentes, populique sui amantes, sufficiant se ab illa, non regi tanquam pupillos (vt aulici adulatores, qui pane lachrymis miserae plebis pisto sagi- nantur, loqui solent) sed dirigi & moneri, eatamen reuerentia & obedientia quae Maiestati ipsorum conuenit, ac debetur.
units.tr: Furthermore, as for the kingdom of England (the happiest of all those seen today in the whole world, and would that it may long continue in such happiness), even if the right of succession passes to the one who is nearer by royal blood, it nevertheless appears, both from many very memorable histories and from the testimony of Polydore in the life of Henry, the first of that name, king of the English, that almost all the authority of ruling depends on the consent of Parliament, as they call it. And indeed, if it pleases us to compare that blessed tranquillity (which they have enjoyed for many years under the most gentle and peaceful rule of the most serene Queen Elizabeth) with the most wretched and unhappy condition of so many other regions, experience itself will teach us how useful and blessed that moderation of royal power is, if only it is exercised rightly, and the kings themselves, fearing God and loving their people, consider themselves to be not ruled as wards (as the court flatterers, who fatten themselves on the bread and tears of the wretched common people, are accustomed to say), but directed and advised, yet with that reverence and obedience which is fitting and due to their majesty.

units.la: IX. De Polonis porro si quis hactenus dubitauit, Num in eligendo certis conditionibus Regem, ipsi hocius retinuerint, vt à iuramento ipsis discedere liceat, si ille promissis non steterit: poterit id clare intelligere ex vltima illa electione qua sibi Henricum Regis Gallorum fratrem in Regem cooptarunt. Atque in eo mihi plane conuenit cum Episcopo Valentino (huius electionis pro Rege suo, procurato-re)qui in oratione ad Polonos habita, & vul-go excusa eos hoc nomine maxime laudat, quod regum suorum potestatem sapientissimis suis legibus coarctarint, & quasi finibus circumscri-pserint.
units.tr: IX. Concerning the Poles, moreover, if anyone has hitherto doubted whether, in choosing a king under certain conditions, they themselves retained the right to withdraw from their oath if he did not keep his promises, he can clearly understand this from that last election, in which they chose for themselves Henry, brother of the King of the French, as king. And in this I plainly agree with the Bishop of Valence (procurator of this election on behalf of his king), who, in his oration to the Poles, delivered and commonly published, praises them above all on this ground, that they restricted the power of their kings by their wisest laws, and, as it were, marked it off within limits.

units.la: Simili ratione Veneti (quorum Respublica, si ex euentis iudicandum est, omnium felicissi-me, & sapientissime, secundum hominum prudentiam, constituta, & moderata existimatur) Du-cem supremum sibi creant, non tanquam I-dolum aliquod, aut specrum (vt quidam in rebus politicis parum exercitati scribere audent) sed tanquam Principem ac Monarcham, a quo citra vllum tyrannidis periculum omnes Monarchiæ commoditates percipiant. Iam vero sicut Consilium illud, quod vocant generale, Ducis eligendi omnem authoritatem habet (seruatis tamen ritibus ad hoc apud ipsos institutis, & vsita-tis) ita illud ipsum Consilium sibi ius istud retinuit: (sine quo facile reliqua omnia in nihilum abirent) Nempe, illius ipsius Ducis deponendi, & puniendi, si quid tyrannicum vel mo-liatur vel patrauerit: quemadmodum id ex-emplis & facto sæpe comprobatum est. Vi-deant igitur hic reliqui Italiæ populi, qui tā subtiliter de humanis rebus differere, & ra-tiocinari sunt soliti (editis etiam plerisq; de ciuili
units.tr: By a similar reasoning the Venetians (whose commonwealth, if judged by its results, is thought to be the most fortunate and wisest constituted and moderated, according to human prudence) create for themselves a supreme Duke, not as some idol or phantom (as certain men little trained in political affairs dare to write), but as a Prince and Monarch, from whom all the advantages of monarchy are received without any danger of tyranny. Now, just as that council which they call the General Council has all authority in choosing the Duke (the customary rites instituted and used among them being observed), so that same council has retained for itself this right, without which all the rest would easily come to nothing: namely, the right of deposing and punishing that same Duke if he plans or commits anything tyrannical. This has often been confirmed by examples and by fact. Let the remaining peoples of Italy, who are accustomed to discuss and reason so subtly about human affairs (and have also published many books on civil government), see here whether all have acted as prudently in this matter as the Venetians have.

units.la: X. Exempla à Venetorum Respublica.
units.tr: X. Examples from the Venetian Commonwealth.

units.la: Dux Venetus non est Idolum. ciuili gubernatione libellis: ) An in hac re aeque prudenter sese omnes, vt Veneti, gef- ferint.
units.tr: The Venetian Duke is not an idol. Civil government in books. Whether in this matter all have acted as prudently as the Venetians.

units.la: Quid vero de Hispanis dicemus? Status certe huius Regni diu fuit perturbatissi- mus & valde inquietus, quod pleraeque barbarae nationes, tum ex Septentrionibus, tum ex Africa illuc veluti diluuio quodam exundarint, sicut id tum certissimae historiae, tum ipsorum idioma testantur. At fatendum est omnino Gentem hanc prae caeteris semper fuisse sagacem, & prouidam. Et quamuis verū sit illud Aristotelicum, natura Barbaros, mancipia potius esse, quam subditos. Hispani tamen hactenus (quaecunque tandem barbaries regionem eorum inuaserit) in Politiae constituendae ratione, plerisque populis erubescendi occasionem praebent, eosque merito pudefaciunt. Id vero vt probem, citabo duo testimonia prae caeteris insignia, & quae literis aureis insculpi publicis tabulis mererentur: vt & Reges iuste exiis imperare, & populi vicissim recte obedire, docerentur.
units.tr: But what shall we say of the Spaniards? The state of this kingdom was for a long time very troubled and greatly disturbed, because many barbarian nations, both from the north and from Africa, poured into it as if by some flood, as both the most certain histories and their own language attest. But it must be admitted that this people has always been more keen-witted and far-sighted than the rest. And although it is true what Aristotle said, that by nature barbarians are slaves rather than subjects, the Spaniards, whatever barbarism has invaded their region, have hitherto given most peoples occasion for shame in the way they organised their polity, and rightly put them to shame. To prove this, I will cite two testimonies, outstanding above the rest, which deserve to be engraved in golden letters on public tablets, so that both kings are taught to rule justly and peoples in turn to obey rightly.

units.la: Prius testimonium sumptum est ex quarti Concilii Toletani capit. 74. quod habitum est Anno Domini D. C.XLIV. iuxta Sigiberti supputationem. Verba autem Synodi, tum ex viris Ecclesiasticis, tum ex reli-quis quis Regni ordinibus coactæ, sic habent: Nullus apud nos subpræsumptione Regnum arri-piat, nullus excitet mutuas seditiones ciuium, ne-mo meditetur interitus Regum, sed defuncto in pace Principe, primates totius Gentis, cum sacer-dotibus, succeßorem Regni Consilio communi constituant: vt dum vnitatis concordia à nobis retinetur, nullum patria gentisque disidium per vim, atque ambitum moliatur. Quod si hæc admonitio mentes nostras non corrigit, & ad salutem communem cor nostrum nequaquam perducit, audi sententiam nostram. Quicunque ergo ex nobis, vel totius Hispaniæ populis, qualibet coniuratione vel studio, sacramentum sidei suæ (quod pro patria gentisque Gothorum statu, vel conseruatione Regiæ salutis, pollicitus est) temerauerit: aut Regem nece attrectauerit, aut potestate Regni exuerit, aut præsumptione Tyrannica Regni fastigium vsurpauerit, anathema sit in conspectu Dei patris & Angelorum: atque ab Ecclesia Catholica, quam periurio profanauerit, efficiatur extraneus, & ab omni cœtu Christianorum alienus, cum omnibus impietatis suæ sociis, quia oportet vt vna pœna teneat obnoxios, quos similis error inuenerit implicatos. Quod iterum secundo replicamus dicentes, Quicunque à modo, & cætera. Ex deo, si placet omnibus qui adestis, hanc tertio iteratam sententiam, vestra voçis consensu sir-mate. mate. Ab vniuerso clero, vel populo dictum est: Qui cōtra hanc nostram definitionem præsumpserint, anathema; Maran-atha id est, perditio in aduentu domini, sint: & cū Iuda Iscariot partem habeant ipsi, & socii eorum: Amen.
units.tr: The first testimony is taken from the 74th chapter of the Fourth Council of Toledo, which was held in the year of the Lord 633 according to Sigebert's reckoning. The words of the synod, gathered from both churchmen and the rest of the orders of the kingdom, are as follows: Let no one among us presume to seize the kingdom by usurpation; let no one stir up mutual seditions among the citizens; let no one plot the destruction of kings; but, when a prince has died in peace, let the chief men of the whole nation, together with the priests, appoint a successor to the kingdom by common counsel, so that, while the concord of unity is kept among us, no one may attempt the division of the country and nation by force and ambition. But if this admonition does not correct our minds, and does not bring our heart to the common salvation, hear our sentence. Therefore, whoever among us, or among the peoples of all Spain, by any conspiracy or endeavour, has violated the oath of his faith which he pledged for the country and the state of the Gothic people, or for the preservation of the king's safety, or who has killed the king, or deprived him of the power of the kingdom, or by tyrannical presumption has usurped the summit of the kingdom, let him be anathema in the sight of God the Father and of the angels; and let him be made a stranger to the Catholic Church, which he has profaned by perjury, and alien to every assembly of Christians, together with all the associates of his impiety, since it is fitting that one punishment should bind those whom a similar error has entangled. Which we repeat a second time, saying, Whoever from the manner, and so on. Therefore, if it pleases all of you who are present, confirm this sentence, now repeated a third time, by the consent of your voices. It was said by the whole clergy and the people: Whoever presume against this our definition, let them be anathema; Maranatha, that is, perdition at the coming of the Lord; and let them have a part with Judas Iscariot, they and their associates. Amen.

units.la: Quapropter nos ipsi, & sacerdotes omnes sanctam Ecclesiam Christi ac populum admonemus, vt haec tremenda & toties reiterata sententia, nullum ex nobis præsenti atque æterno condemnet iudicio: sed fidem promissam erga gloriosissimum Dominum nostrum Sisenandum Regem custodientes, ac sincera illi deuotione famulantes, non solum diuina pietatis in nobis clementiam prouocemus, sed etiam gratiam antefati Principis percipere mereamur. Te quoque præsentem Regem, ac futuros atatum sequentium Principes, humilitate debita deposcimus, vt moderati & mites erga subiectos existentes, cum iustitia & pietate populos à Deo vobis creditos regatis, bonamque vicissitudinem, qua vos nobis constituit, largitori Christo reddatis, regnantes in humilitate cordis, cum studio bona actionis. Nec quisquam vestrum solus in causa, captiuum, aut reum, sententia feriat, sed consensu publico cum rectoribus ex iudicio manifesto, delinquentium culpa patescat: seruata à vobis in offensis mansuetudine, vt non seueritate magis in illa, quam indulgentia polleatis, vt dum omnia hæc (authore Deo) pio à vobis moderamine conseruantur, & Reges in populis, & populi in Re-gibus. gibus, & Deus in vtrisque latetur. Sane de futu-risRegibus hanc sei-tentiam promulgamus, vt fi quis ex eis contra reuerentiam legum, super-ba dominatione, & fastu regio in flagitiis, & faci-nore, sive cupiditate, crudelissimam potestatem in populo exercuerit, Anathematis sententia à Christo Domino condemnetur, & habeat à Deo sepa-rationem, atque iudicium, propter quod praesum-ferit prava agere, & in perniciem regnum dedu-cere. De Simithilane vero, qui propria scelera metuens, seipsum regno priuauit, & potestatis fascibus exuit, id cum Gentis consultu decreui-mus, vt neque eum, vel vxorem eius, propter mala quae commiserunt, neque filios eorum vnitatis nostra vnquam consociemus, nec eos ad honores, a quibus ob iniquitatem deiecti sunt, aliquando promoueamus.
units.tr: Therefore we ourselves and all the priests admonish the holy Church of Christ and the people that this dreadful sentence, so often repeated, condemn none of us to present and eternal judgement. Rather, keeping faith with our most glorious lord King Sisenand and serving him with sincere devotion, we should not only provoke the divine mercy towards us but also deserve to receive the favour of the aforesaid Prince. We also beseech you, the present King, and the princes of the ages to come, with due humility: be moderate and gentle towards your subjects, rule the peoples entrusted to you by God with justice and piety, and render back to Christ, the bountiful giver, the good return by which he set you over us, reigning in humility of heart and with zeal for good action. Let none of you alone pass sentence on a captive or a defendant in a case; let the guilt of offenders be made plain by the public consent of the leaders, from a manifest judgement. Preserve in your dealings with offences such mildness that you excel not so much in severity as in indulgence, so that while all these things are kept by your pious moderation (God being the author), kings may rejoice in their peoples, and peoples in their kings, and God rejoices in both. Indeed, concerning future kings we promulgate this sentence: that if any of them, against reverence for the laws, by proud domination and royal arrogance, out of wickedness, crime or greed, shall exercise most cruel power over the people, let him be condemned by Christ the Lord with the sentence of anathema, and let him have separation and judgement from God, because he has presumed to act wickedly and to lead the kingdom to ruin. But concerning Simithilane, who, fearing his own crimes, deprived himself of the kingdom and laid aside the fasces of power, we have decreed with the counsel of the nation that neither he nor his wife, on account of the evils they committed, nor their sons shall ever be joined to our fellowship, nor shall we ever promote them to the honours from which they were cast down for their iniquity.

units.la: Est hoc sane singulare exemplum: cui de-cretum aliud, sextae Synodi Toletanae, ad-iciam, in quo, postquam de exigendis Iudaeis e regno statutum effet, adduntur se-quentia: Incassum bonum agitur, si non eius pro-videtur perseuerantia: Ergo postquam ordine pra-misso ad gubernacula accesserit Regni, si ipse te-merator huius extiterit promissi, si anathema Maranatha inconsiderate fuerit pernicie Dei, & pa-bulum efficiatur ignis aeterni, similique cum eo damnatione periculi sint, quicunque facerdo-tum, vel quilibet Christianorum, eius implicati fuerint errori. Ex his facile iudicari poterit, quæ sit Ordinum Hispaniæ, in suos Reges, authoritas, si quid cōtra iusiurandum comi-miserint: cum exiure Feudorum (quæ etiam Regna & Imperia completuntur) Vasallus excommunicato Domino seruitium non debeat, i-mo sacramento fidelitatis sit absolutus; vt habetur libr.2. Feud.tit.28 §.1.
units.tr: This is indeed a singular example. I will add another decree, that of the Sixth Council of Toledo, in which, after it had been enacted that the Jews should be driven out of the kingdom, the following is added: It is in vain that good is done, if its continuance is not provided for. Therefore, once someone has come to the helm of the kingdom in the order laid down, if he himself proves a rash breaker of this promise, if he is inconsiderately made an anathema Maranatha to the destruction of God, and becomes fuel for eternal fire, let those who have been involved in his error, whether priests or any Christians at all, share the same condemnation and danger. From these things it can easily be judged what authority the Orders of Spain have over their kings if they have committed anything against their oath; for by the law of Feuds (which also embrace kingdoms and empires), a vassal owes no service to a lord who is excommunicated; indeed he is absolved from the oath of fidelity, as is found in book 2 of the Feuds, title 28, §1.

units.la: Alterum testimonium, quod proferre sum pollicitus; Formula illa est insignis; quam Arragonii hodie etiam (nisi forte non i-tapridem mutata est) non solum in Regum suorum inauguratione vsurpant, sed etiam in conuentibus illis triennalibus iterant: in quibus Rex sese apud suos Ordines sistere solet, tum vt suis ius dicat, tum vt abiis ius suum recipiat. Ibi enim, post multas pera-ctas cæremonias, inter eum, quem Iustitiam Aragonensem vocant (qui suprema potestatis personam refert, cuique Reges iureiurando se obstringere coguntur) & Regem ipsum, vel creandum, vel iam creatum, Formula hæc totidem verbis pronuntiatur: Nos qui valemos tanto comme vos, y podemos mas que vos, vos elegimos rey: con estas y estas condiciones, intra vos y nos, vn que mada mas que vos. id est; Nos qui tanti sumus quanti vos, & plusquam vos possumus, Regem vos eligimus, his atque his conditionibus: Inter vos, & nos, vnus maior est imperio, quam vos. En, quousque Hispani suos Regesin honore habuerint, prout debue- runt.
units.tr: The second testimony, which I promised to bring forward, is a notable formula, which the Aragonese even today (unless perhaps it has been changed not long ago) use not only at the inauguration of their kings but also repeat at those triennial assemblies in which the King usually presents himself before his Orders, both to declare justice to his own people and to receive his own right from them. For there, after many ceremonies have been performed, between him whom they call the Justice of Aragon (who represents the person of supreme power, and to whom the kings are compelled to bind themselves by oath) and the King himself, whether he is to be created or has already been created, this formula is pronounced in just these words: We, who are worth as much as you and can do more than you, choose you as king, on these and these conditions: between you and us there is one who is greater than the realm. Behold, this is how far the Spanish have honoured their kings, as they ought to.

units.la: Quid plura? Norunt omnes, qua fit au- thoritate coetus ille Principum toto orbe illustrissimus, septem videlicet Electorum Imperii, tam in eligendo Imperatore, quam in eo, quoties opus est, abdicando: sicut, Adolpho, Anno M. CC. XCVI. & Wenceslao, Anno M. CCCC. Imperatoribus accidit.
units.tr: What more? Everyone knows with what authority that most illustrious assembly of princes throughout the world, namely the seven Electors of the Empire, both elects the Emperor and, whenever necessary, deposes him, as happened to the Emperors Adolf in 1296 and Wenceslaus in 1400.

units.la: Erat autem talé iusiurandum, quo fe tunc Reges seu Cæsares Germaniæ obstringebát, quale describitur in Tractatu, cui titulus est, Speculum Saxonicum, lib. 3. §. 54. Cum enim Rex eligitur, cogitur publico iuramento fidelitatem, & hominium (seu, vt vulgus vocat, homagium) Imperio præstare: ac polliceri, fe totis viribus promoturum iuris administrationem; atque adeo omnes iniurias propulsaturum, & denique, omni studio & conatu, iura Imperii conseruaturum.
units.tr: Now the oath by which the kings or Caesars of Germany then bound themselves was such as is described in the treatise entitled the Saxon Mirror, book 3, §54. For when a King is elected, he is compelled by public oath to render fidelity and homage (or, as the common people call it, homage) to the Empire; and to promise that he will promote the administration of justice with all his strength, that he will repel all injuries, and finally that with all zeal and effort he will preserve the rights of the Empire.

units.la: Accedo iam ad Francos: Apud quos, prius-usquam in Galliam venissent, Reges Ori- dinibus populi fui submissos fuisse, testis est Iulius Cæsar, libro 5. capit. 8. de bello Gallico, dum Ambiorigis Eburonum (fiue, vt hodie vocantur, Leodienfium) Reguli, in quadam oratione verba recensens, ait; sua esse ciuf modi Imperii, vt non minus haberet in fe iuris multitudo (legitime scilicet coacta) quam i-
units.tr: I come now to the Franks. Among them, before they came into Gaul, kings were subject to the orders of their people; the witness is Julius Caesar, book 5, chapter 8 of the Gallic War, where, reciting the words of Ambiorix, king of the Eburones (or, as they are called today, the Liègeois), in a certain speech, he says that his own authority was of such a kind that the multitude (lawfully assembled, of course) had no less right over him than he had over the multitude.

units.la: XIII. Exempla Regum Galorum et antea. Francis conuntis fuere. psein multitudinem. Idem etiam probatur ex verbis Veteringentorgis, Regis Aruernorum, causam suam in coetu publico tuentis, vt ea ab eodem Casare recitantur,lib.7.cap.4. Po-stea vero Galli & Franci, sub vno Francogal-lorum nomine, coierunt in vnum: Quorum regnum, cum, singulari Dei beneficio, diu-tissime prorogatum & conseruatum fuerit, nunc quidem ita nutare videtur (quacunque tandem ex parte culpa bareat) vt certissimum eius excidium proxime timendum sit; quod tamen vix accidere potest, nisi cum ingenti reliquarum orbis partium mutatione. Cæterum, quæ mihi nunc de eo dicenda sunt, satis suspicor, quibusdam grata & accepta, quibusdam vero ingratissima & inauspicata futura: At nihil dicenti, nisi id quod res est, spero equidem Deum mihi aduersus omnes calumnias fore propitium. Quanquam igi-tur Francogalli Reges suos, primum ex Merouei familia, deinde ex Caroli Magni posteris, ac tandem ex Hugonis Capeti successoribus eligerent; ita tamen ab initio Monarchiam suam constituisse dico, vt Reges ipsorum non solo iure successionis regnarent, sed si simul, consensu Ordinum Regni, electi forent. Sic Pharamundus electus, solio Regio sublimatus fuit, Anno Domini CCCCXIX. Sic Pipinus, Anno DCCLI. ipsiusque liberi, Carolus, & Ca-
units.tr: XIII. Examples of the kings of the Gauls, even earlier. The same is proved from the words of Vercingetorix, king of the Arverni, defending his cause in a public assembly, as they are recited by the same Caesar, book 7, chapter 4. Afterwards, however, the Gauls and Franks came together into one under the single name of Franco-Gauls. Their kingdom, though preserved and prolonged for a very long time by a singular benefit of God, now indeed seems to totter (for whatever fault, on whatever side), so that its utter ruin is to be feared in the near future; yet this can hardly happen except with a great change in the rest of the world. Still, what I now have to say about it, I suspect, will be pleasing and welcome to some, but most unwelcome and ill-omened to others. Yet, saying nothing but what is the case, I hope God will be favourable to me against all calumnies. Although, therefore, the Franco-Gallic kings chose their kings, first from the family of Merovech, then from the posterity of Charles the Great, and at last from the successors of Hugh Capet, I say that from the beginning they so established their monarchy that their kings reigned not only by right of succession but also if they were at the same time elected with the consent of the Orders of the realm. Thus Pharamond was elected and raised to the royal throne in the year of the Lord 419. Thus Pepin, in 751, and his children, Charles and Carloman, in 768.

units.la: Tres familiae Regum Galliae.
units.tr: Three families of the kings of France.

units.la: & Carolomanus, Anno DCCLXVIII. Ac tandem, Anno DCCLXXI. Carolus in fra- tris partem, ex Ordinum authoritate; fuc- ceffit. Quam authoritatem fecutus ipfe po- ftea, nempe, Anno DCCCXII. Ludouicum fi- lium fuum Imperii haeredem inftituit: ca- ueris nominatim teftamento fuo (ficut Nau- clerus, qui fcriptis illud prodidit, teftatur) vt po- pulus (ideft, Ordines ipfi) quem mallet ex fi- liorum fuorum liberis; in Regni fucceffo- rem eligeret; praecipiens etiam patruis, qui tum fuperuixiffent, vt eiusmodi electionis affen- tirentur: quod factum equidem notatu eft digniffimum; & ad totius huius quaestionis ftatum decidendum accommodatiffimum.
units.tr: And finally, in 771, Charles succeeded to his brother's share by the authority of the Orders. Following this authority, he himself later, namely in 812, appointed Louis his son heir to the empire. He had expressly ordered in his will (as Naucler, who published it in writing, attests) that the people (that is, the Orders themselves) should elect as successor to the kingdom whichever of his sons' children they preferred, also instructing the uncles, who were still alive then, to assent to such an election. This was indeed most worthy of note, and most suited to settling the whole state of this question.

units.la: Atque tale tum fuit Francogallicorum Re- gum iuramentum, tefte Aymoino, qui Ca- rolum, Caluum dictum, fic loquentem indu. cit: Quia, ficut ifti venerabiles Epifcopi, v- nius ex ipfis voce, dixerunt, & certis indiciis ex noftra vnanimitate monftrauerunt, vos acclamaftis, me Dei electione ad veftiam faluatio- nem, & profeftum, atque regimen & gubernatio- nem huc aduehiffe, fciatis, me honorem & cultum Dei, atque fanctarum Ecclesiarum, Domino conferuare adiuuante, & vnumquemque veftrum, fecundum fui ordinis dignitatem & perfonam, iuxta meum fcire & poffe, honorare & faluare, & honorabiliter faluatum tenere velle: Et vnicui-
units.tr: Such, then, was the oath of the Franco-Gallic kings, as witnessed by Aymoin, who introduces Charles, called the Bald, speaking thus: "Since, as these venerable bishops have said with one voice, and have shown by certain signs from our unanimity, you have acclaimed me, by the election of God, as brought hither for your salvation, and for the leadership, rule and government of the realm, know that with the Lord helping me I wish to preserve the honour and worship of God and of the holy Churches, and to honour and keep safe each one of you, according to the dignity of his rank and person, as far as I know and am able, and to hold him honourably preserved; and to preserve to each one of you, in his own order, according to what belongs to him, both ecclesiastical and secular law and justice; so that the royal honour and power, and due obedience and aid, may be rendered to me by each of you, for the holding and defending of the kingdom given to me by God."

units.la: E que in suo ordine, secundum sibi competentes tam Ecclesiasticas quam mundanas legem & iustitiam conseruare: In hoc vt honor Regius & potestas, ac debita obedientia atque adiutorium, ad regnum mihi à Deo datum continendum ac defendendum, ab vnoquoque vestrum, secundum suum Ordinem ac dignitatem atque possibilitatem, mihi exhibeatur, sicut antecessores vestri iure, fideliter & rationabiliter, meis antecessoribus exhibuerunt. Hæc ille totidem verbis.
units.tr: And to preserve, in their own order and according to what is fitting to each, both ecclesiastical and secular law and justice; so that from each of you, according to his own order, rank and ability, there may be rendered to me the royal honour and authority, the due obedience and support, for upholding and defending the kingdom given to me by God, just as your predecessors rightly, faithfully and reasonably rendered them to my predecessors. Thus he speaks, in so many words.

units.la: Eos ipsos vero Ordines potestate Regum, quos elegissent, abdicandorum habuisse, si quid peccassent, infinitis exemplis constat: Childericus, propter flagitia & libidines, publico Consilio, Regno motus & expulsus est, Anno CCCLXI. eique Gilo substitutus, qui ex Merouei familia non erat. Et Chilpericus, Anno DLXXVIII. & Theodoricus, Anno DCLXVII. Quinimo, Anno DCCCX C. Ordines, neglecto Carolo, Lu-douici Balbi filio, Euden, siue Odonem, in Regem elegerunt. Legimus etiam, Hugonem Capetum regno priuasse Carolum, Lotharii fratrem, cum ille negligentius & veluti cunctando, rem ageret, & ad concilium deferret; sperans scilicet fore, vt Regni Ordines illorum controuersiam, pro assueto more, dirimerent. Ac in summa, si regnum Franciae electione non conferebatur, dicendum est
units.tr: That the Estates themselves, by the power of the kings whom they had chosen, could depose them if they had done wrong, is established by countless examples. Childeric, on account of his crimes and lusts, was removed and expelled from the kingdom by public council in the year 361, and Gilo was put in his place, who was not of the family of Merovech. So too Chilperic in the year 578, and Theodoric in the year 667. Moreover, in the year 890 the Estates, disregarding Charles, son of Louis the Stammerer, chose Eudes, or Odo, as king. We also read that Hugh Capet deprived Charles, brother of Lothair, of the kingdom, since the latter acted rather carelessly and, as it were, hesitatingly in the matter and referred it to the council, hoping, of course, that the Estates of the kingdom would settle their dispute, as was their customary practice. And in sum, if the kingdom of France was not conferred by election, it must be said

units.la: ET OFFICIO SVBDITORVM. 15.
units.tr: AND THE OFFICE OF SUBJECTS. 15.

units.la: dum effet, neque Pipinum, neque Capetum ꝛ quicquam iurisin eo habuisse: cum neq; ex ꝛ Merouei masculis hæredibus successores ꝛ decessent Pipino, regnum vsurpante: neq; ex ꝛ Caroli Magni filiis, cum Capetus regium ꝛ diadema sibi vendicaret.
units.tr: while it was still open, neither Pepin nor Capet had any right to it. For the male heirs of Merovech had not failed in succession to Pepin, who usurped the kingdom, nor had the sons of Charlemagne failed when Capet claimed the royal diadem for himself.

units.la: Porro, quod attinet ad eorundem Ordi- num authoritatem, qua vel Regni præci- puas dignitates & officia conferebant, adi- mebantque: vel saltem sollicite animaduer- tebant, quo modo se Reges, tamin iis con- ferendis adimendisve, quàm in tributis exi- gendis, autin aliis Regni præcipuis nego- tiis, tum belli tum pacis tempore, gererent: Ea, inquam, authoritas vetustissimis & val- de authenticis historiis fatis superq; testa- ta est: quæ plane eorum assentatorum impu- dentiam satis arguunt, qui hodie, ex ruinis tanti, tamq; sapienter cõstituti Regni, suam potentiam per sas nefasq; augere non defi- nunt. Et sane, quod nostris téporibus s, qui sanguine est proximior, non conuocatis Ordinibus, in Gallia Regnum succedit, nouamq; rerum faciem inducit, pro eorum libidine, qui eiusmodi successoris fauotem ac gratia captauerint: Quodq; comitia pu- blica statuto tempore amplius nó indicun- tur, sed tum duntaxat, cum id commodum quibusdà videtur, qui inde proprias cõmoditates & securitates aucupantur : Quod praeterea, quoties ordines coguntur, id fit, non tam vt de publicis rebus ferio decerna- tur, quam dicis causa, vt scilicet longis asse- &tatifque orationibus, Rhetorum (imo So- phiftarum potius) more, tempus & actio omnis eludatur: Quodque illicii iudices fe- deant, in quos praecipue omnes accusatio- nes & querimoniae intenduntur : Deniq;, quod tum bella,tum pax,aut inducie decer- nuntur: tributa & exactiones imponuntur: leges de rebus tam publicis, quam priuatis figuntur, & refiguntur: dignitates & praefe- cturae, omnia item munia publica electis vel conferuntur, vel adimuntur, pro quorun- dam tantum(fiue virorum, fiue mulierum, nobilium fiue ignobilium, proborum fiue improborum)arbitrio, qui apud rerum Do- minos maiore pollent authoritate & gratia (vtpote per quorum aures & oculos dunta- xatifti & audiant & videant.) Haec, inquam, omnia a maiorum sanctis moribus, & agen- di ratione quam longissime diffident, & cu primariis legibus quibus Gallicae Monar- chiae fundamenta nituntur, plane ex diame- tro pugnant. Iam vero Iurisconsultis omni- bus, qui cum scientia iuris bonam confcien- tiam coniunctam habent, di/putandum re- linquo, num vlla quantumuis longi temporis prae- scriptio
units.tr: Further, as to the authority of these same Orders, by which they both conferred and removed the chief dignities and offices of the kingdom, or at least watched carefully how the kings conducted themselves, both in conferring and removing these, and in levying taxes, and in other chief affairs of the kingdom in time of war and of peace: this authority, I say, is attested sufficiently and more than sufficiently by the most ancient and thoroughly reliable histories. These things plainly refute the impudence of those flatterers who today, out of the ruins of so great and so wisely established a kingdom, do not cease to increase their own power by right and wrong. Indeed, in our own times, the nearest kinsman succeeds to the kingdom of France without the Orders being summoned, and introduces a new order of affairs at the pleasure of those who have sought the favour and grace of such a successor. Likewise, public assemblies are no longer called at the appointed time, but only when it seems convenient to certain men who thereby seek their own advantages and securities.
