Besides, whenever the Orders are convened, this is done not so much to decide public business in earnest as for show: so that, with long and empty speeches in the manner of rhetoricians (or rather, of sophists), all the time and business is wasted. And also, unjust judges sit, against whom all accusations and complaints are chiefly directed. Finally, although wars, peace or truces are decided, taxes and levies imposed, laws concerning public and private affairs are made and unmade, and dignities and prefectures, indeed all public offices, are conferred on or taken from the chosen, this is done at the will of certain persons, whether men or women, noble or ignoble, upright or wicked, who have greater power and favour with the lords of affairs, inasmuch as they alone hear and see through their ears and eyes. All these things, I say, are wholly remote from the holy customs and practice of our ancestors, and are in direct conflict with the primary laws on which the foundations of the French monarchy rest. Now I leave it to all jurists who combine sound conscience with knowledge of law to dispute whether any prescription, however long, can have or ought to have any place here, by any right, divine or human.

units.la: Taxat Card. Loth. & Guifiof. fcriptio iure aliquo vel diuino, vel humano locum hic habere possit, vel debeat. Atenim quod ho-die adhuc Reges, cum folenni ritu vngun-tur,iuramentum prastant (cuius formula vti-nam publice excuderetur, vt omnibus innote sce-ret)& quod praeterea singulis ciuitatibus sua priuilegia, item publica munera Regni ossi-ciariis confirmare,postquam Regnum sunt adepti, consueuerunt (etsi hic multa fiunt per abusum quæ minime sunt probanda:) Quod denique fi Reges minores sunt state, status ordinesque Regni communi confi-lio statuunt, ad quem illius administratio pertineat:Hæc,inquam, omnia reliquiæ sunt adhuc pristinæ illius authoritatis,qua Ordi-nes pollebant, & quæ nunc paulatim abit in nihilum. Nōdum tamen ducenti anni præ-terierunt, cum ab ipsis Ordinibus Caroli Quinti (qui Sapiens cognominatus est) te-stamentum rescissum fuit, nempe Anno M. C-C C. L X X X.Quid amplius?Anno M.C C-C C.L X VII. cum Ludouicus huius nominis X I.(qui quantū potuit, Monarchiam Gal-licam in tyrannidem transformare conatus est, quod Regii Parasiti Regem emancipare seu seruitio eximere, appellant) merito accu-saretur, quod pessime Regnum administra-ret, dati sunt illi ab Ordinibus, apud Turo-nes conuocatis, XXX.viri, tanquam curatores, à quibus se regi & gubernari patere- tur. Verum est quidem, ipsum postea facile ab illis sese expediuisse, vtpote cui (Claronen- sis Idoli prætextu, quod summa superstitione co- lebat) iuramenta omnia & promissa, non- nisi ludus & iocus essent: Sed tanto cumi- pśius præludicio, & infelici successu, vt præ- ter infamiam qua etiamnum hodie nota- tur, quandiu vixit, nulla vnquam quiete aut pace frui potuerit: & in ipsa adeo morte ex- pertus sit, quid valeat, à subditis potius timeri quam amari. Et quandoquidem de iura- menti violatione mentio incidit, addere libet aliud exemplum valde memorabile. Carolus huius nominis VII. dum adhuc Del- phinus esset, nefario consilio Iohannem vlti- mum Burgundiæ Ducem, è Gallicorum Re- gum prolapia ortum, coram se misere tru- cidari iussit, contra fidem, pacem, atque a- micitiam paulo ante propeMelodunum iu- ratam. Hoc periurium deinde (quamuis tanto Dei iudicio Dux ille esset dignissimus) multis animarum millibus fuit in Gallia ex- piatum, cum totius pene Regni subuersio- ne. Et Carolus ipse Rex eo adaætus mise- riarum, vt à patre suo primum exhæredatus, capitalem suum hostem postea Re- gno inaugurari Lutetiæ conspexerit, ac pro- inde Biturigum ipse, potius quam Galliæ, Rex dicere-
units.tr: The Cardinal of Lorraine and Guise criticise this. But as to the fact that even today the kings, when they are anointed with the solemn rite, take an oath (I wish its formula were published openly, so that it might be known to all), and that after obtaining the kingdom they have been accustomed to confirm to each city its privileges, and likewise to the officials the public offices of the kingdom (although many things are done here by abuse, which by no means ought to be approved); and finally that, if the kings are minors, the estates and orders of the kingdom decide by common counsel to whom its administration belongs: all these things, I say, are remnants of that former authority which the Orders once possessed, and which now gradually passes into nothing. Yet not two hundred years have passed since the will of Charles V (called the Wise) was rescinded by the Orders themselves, namely in the year 1380. What more? In 1317, when Louis X (who, as far as he could, tried to turn the French monarchy into a tyranny, which the royal parasites call emancipating the king or freeing him from servitude) was rightly accused of governing the kingdom very badly, thirty men were given to him as guardians by the Orders convened at Tours, by whom he would allow himself to be ruled and governed. It is true that he later easily freed himself from them, since for him (under the pretext of the Clermont idol, which he worshipped with the greatest superstition) all oaths and promises were nothing but play and jest. But with such great prejudice to himself and so unhappy an outcome that, besides the infamy which still attaches to him today, he could enjoy no quiet or peace for as long as he lived; and even at his death he learned what it is worth to be feared rather than loved by subjects. And since mention of the violation of an oath has arisen, it is pleasing to add another very memorable example. Charles VII, while still Dauphin, by wicked counsel had John, the last Duke of Burgundy, descended from the line of the French kings, cruelly slaughtered before his eyes, against the faith, peace and friendship sworn shortly before at Melun. This perjury was afterwards expiated in France (although that Duke was most deservedly so punished by the judgment of God) with many thousands of lives and with the overthrow of almost the whole kingdom. And King Charles himself was driven into such misery that, first disinherited by his father, he later saw his capital enemy inaugurated as king of the realm at Paris; and therefore he himself was called king of Bourges rather than king of France.

units.la: Hattonis, Archiepiscopi Mogunt. tini, qui cō- tra datam fidem, Alberum Co- mitem Bamber- gensem, diceretur. Tădem vero pacem multo fuode- decore redimere coactus est, vt extractatu apud Atrebates concepto, apparet: In quo (ersi ipse Rex cum Duce Philippo, Ioan- nis interempti, filio, tanquam subdito suo transigeret) hæc clausula nominatim ex- pressa habetur, Cui (inquit) Rex ipse affentie- tur, & diplomate suo comprobabit. Quod si vero hanc transactionem ab ipso violari contigerit, si- ptius clientes, feudatarii, & subditi, profentes & futuri, illi deinceps neque obedire neque inserui- re tenebuntur, sed Ducì potius Burgundiæ, ipsi- usque successoribus, aduersus ipsum omnem obe- dientiam præstabunt: Cunctì denique illi ipsi cli- entes, beneficiarii, subditique, ab omni fide, iure- iurando, obsequio, promissionibus, & obligationi- bus, ac quibuscunque officiis, quibus Carolo Re- gi deuincti prius effent, liberati, immunes, ac prorusus soluti hoc casu habebuntur: ne deinceps illis quicquam horum fraudi, aut oneri im- putari, aut ab illis culpa vlla exigi, possit. Quin- imo hoc ipsum iam iam facere Carolus Rex il- lis præcipiat, & liberos absolutosque ab omni- bus iuramentis, & obligationibus pronuntiet, si quid tale euenerit. Hic scilicet fuit exitus violatæ fidei Regiæ improbo consilio. Hæc autem pacta conuenta, quia bona fide inposterum obseruata fuerunt, maxima Regno quies & pax obtigit. Porro si æ-
units.tr: Of Hatto, Archbishop of Mainz, who, against his given faith, (seized?) Albert, Count of Bamberg, it is said. At last, however, he was compelled to buy peace at great cost to his dignity, as appears from the treaty drawn up at Arras. In it (although the king himself was dealing with Duke Philip, son of the slain John, as with his own subject) this clause is expressly stated: "To which," it says, "the king himself shall assent, and confirm it by his own charter. But if it should happen that this agreement is violated by him, then his clients, feudatories and subjects, present and future, shall not thereafter be bound either to obey or to serve him, but shall rather render all obedience to the Duke of Burgundy and his successors against him. Finally, all those same clients, beneficiaries and subjects shall in this case be considered freed, immune and wholly released from every faith, oath, obedience, promise and obligation, and from whatever duties by which they were previously bound to King Charles; so that nothing of these may thereafter be imputed to them as fraud or burden, nor any fault be exacted from them." Indeed, King Charles himself should now command them to do this very thing, and declare them free and absolved from all oaths and obligations, should any such event occur. Such was the outcome of the violated royal faith, brought about by a wicked counsel. But these agreed pacts, because they were afterwards observed in good faith, brought the greatest quiet and peace to the kingdom. Moreover, if

units.la: E quum tunc visum est,hanc clausulam inseri ac-cidentaria huic promissioni, quae ad Regni administrationem proprie non pertinebat, an minus aequa legitimaque illa promissio, aut conditio censenda erit, quam populus a Rege suo, dum vel crearetur vel inauguraretur, fuerit stipulatus: cum & aequitate maxima & naturali ratione nitatur: videlicet ut Rex ex Legum praescriptis (quarum ipse summus est, esse debet, custos & protector) omnem suam administrationem moderetur?
units.tr: then it seemed right to insert this clause as an addition to that promise, which did not properly pertain to the administration of the kingdom, shall that promise or condition be judged less fair and less lawful, which the people stipulated from their king while he was being created or inaugurated? It rests on the greatest equity and on natural reason: namely, that the king should regulate all his administration according to the prescriptions of the laws, of which he himself is the highest guardian and protector.

units.la: Huc ergo omnium supradictorum summa redit: Summum Imperium ita demum esse penes Reges aut alios supremos Magistratus, vt, si-quidem illi optimas leges iuratasque conditiones transgredientes, in apertos tyrannos degenerent, nec sanis consilis audiant, liberum licitumque sit inferioribus Magistratibus, tum sibi, tum iis quorum curam gerunt providere, & publico tyranno obsistere. Ordines vero vel status Regionis quibus haec authoritas a legibus est collata, eatenus sese tyranno opponere atque adeo ipsi iustas, & promeritas poenas, si opus erit, irrogare & possunt & debent, donec res in pristinum statum restituta sint. Quod si praestiterint, tantum abest, vt seditiosi, aut perduelles habendi sint, vt contra officio suo & iuramento (quo & Deo & patriae sunt obstricti) probe defuncti tum demum censeri debeant. Ac quamuis iam supra eui-dentissi-
units.tr: The sum of all the above therefore comes to this: that supreme power rests with kings or other supreme magistrates on the condition that, if they transgress the best laws and sworn conditions, and degenerate into open tyrants, and do not listen to sound counsel, it is free and lawful for inferior magistrates to provide both for themselves and for those whose care they bear, and to resist the public tyrant. The orders or estates of the realm, to whom this authority has been granted by the laws, may and must oppose themselves to the tyrant in this way, and indeed impose just and deserved penalties if need be, until affairs have been restored to their former state. If they do this, far from being held seditious or traitors, they ought rather to be considered to have properly discharged their duty, since they are bound by their office and oath to both God and country. And although I have already above, by the most evident

units.la: dentissimis Regnorum & Imperiorum, tam veterum quam recentium, exemplis, harum rerum praxim comprobauerimus, ne tamen quisquam obiiciat, legibus potius, quam exem-plis, iudicandum: Addam, ad maiorem fenten-tiae nostrae confirmationem, quam plurimas & alias rationes. Dico enim primum, duas esse propositiones, quas aequitas ipsa iusve illud naturae (a quo vno pendet totius humanae societatis conseruatio) in dubium vocari non patitur: Quarum prior est, in omnibus pactis, & conuentionibus, qua mutuo ac solo consensu inter partes contrahuntur, eos ipsos per quos obligatio contracta est, eandem soluere & dimittere posse, quoties id ratio postulat: Itaque quibus est potestas Regis creandi, iisdem quoque eius abdicandi ius erit. Altera vero, Siqua est iusta soluenda conuentionis aut pacti occasio, qua obli-gatio ipsa per se euanescat, & pro nulla habeatur, hanc vnam esse, si essentiales conditiones, propter quas proprie obligatio contracta est, manifeste vio-lentur. Ostendant igitur qui eo vsq; Regum ac supremorum Magistratuum authorita-tem euehunt, vt dicere audeant, illos non aliū quam Deum solum iudicem habere, cuius factorum suorum rationem reddere tenentur: vllam gen-tem vsquam fuisse, quae scienter, & absque metu, aut vi aliqua, sese arbitrio supremi ali-cuius Magistratus submiserit, non addita ex-presse,
units.tr: Although I have already demonstrated the practice of these things by the most evident examples of kingdoms and empires, both ancient and recent, yet lest anyone object that judgment must be made by laws rather than by examples, I shall add, to confirm my opinion further, several other arguments. I say first that there are two propositions which equity itself, and that law of nature on which alone the preservation of all human society depends, does not allow to be called into doubt. The first is this: in all pacts and agreements which are entered into between parties by mutual and sole consent, those same persons by whom the obligation was contracted are able to loose and dismiss it, whenever reason requires. Therefore those who have the power of creating a king will also have the right of removing him. The second is this: if there is any just occasion for dissolving an agreement or pact, by which the obligation itself vanishes and is held to be void, it is this one alone: that the essential conditions, on account of which the obligation was properly contracted, are manifestly violated. Let those, then, who exalt the authority of kings and supreme magistrates to such a height that they dare to say that they have no judge but God alone, to whom they are bound to render an account of their deeds, show that there has ever been any nation which knowingly and without fear or any force has submitted itself to the will of some supreme magistrate, without this condition being expressly added or tacitly understood: that he rule and govern them justly and equitably.

units.la: presse, aut tacite subintelleƈta, hac conditione, vt ab eo iuste, & ex æquo regatur & gubernetur. Quod si quis exemplum aliquod proferat populorum, qui bello superati, sese iis omnino conditionibus iurati submiserunt, quas victores proponerent: non satis mihi fuerit cum Iurisconsultis respondere, ea qua vi, iniustove metu extorta sunt, pro legitimis non esse habenda (Fateor enim Theologiam, qua conscientiarum est Regula, non facile permittere, vt eiusmodi iuramenta temere violentur) Sed addam præterea, etiamsi populus quispiam scienter & sponte rei per se euidenter irreligiosæ, luriqué naturali contraria, assensum præbuerit, nullam esse eiusmodi obligationem: tantum abest vt dubitari iure possit, An ea valida ac rata sit existimanda, quæ per vim ac metum, aut aperta fraude & malitiis artibus contracta fuerit. Hæc enim generalis iuris & æqui regula communibus naturæ principiis subnixa (quæ adhuc post lapsum in homine, quantumuis corrupto resident) tam certa firmaq; est, vt nihil, quod illis aperte aduersetur & repugnet pro iusto & rato inter homines sit habendum. Hoc porro de rebus penitus iniustis, atque manifeste irreligiosis, intelligendum est, quas nemo non videt (nisi sensu communi prorsus destitutus) non posse bona conscientia à quoquam vel exigi vel præsta-
units.tr: But if someone should produce some example of peoples who, overcome in war, submitted themselves under oath to whatever conditions the victors proposed, it will not be enough for me to answer, with the jurists, that those things which have been extorted by force or unjust fear are not to be regarded as lawful. (For I grant that Theology, which is the rule of consciences, does not easily permit such oaths to be violated rashly.) But I will add moreover that even if some people has knowingly and willingly given its assent to a thing that is plainly irreligious and contrary to natural law, there is no such obligation. Far from it being able to be rightly doubted whether that is to be considered valid and binding which has been contracted by force and fear, or by open fraud and wicked arts. For this general rule of law and equity, supported by the common principles of nature (which still remain in man after the Fall, however corrupted he be), is so certain and firm that nothing which openly opposes and conflicts with them is to be held as just and binding among men. Moreover, this must be understood of things utterly unjust and manifestly irreligious, which no one sees (unless he be wholly destitute of common sense) cannot with a good conscience be either demanded or performed by anyone.

units.la: Nulli vn- qua Regis admissi, nisi aut expressa aut tacite subintelleƈta conditione, siue sanƈtæq; populus reserint. Nota.
units.tr: No one has ever submitted to a king except on an expressed or tacitly understood condition, or the people has sacredly reserved this. Note.

units.la: Conditiones aperte irreligiosæ, & contra conscientiam, nullius esse momenti. præstari. Tale fuit pactum, quod primis tem- poribus inter Minoen Cretensis Insulæ Regem, & Athenienses intercessisse fe- runt: Nempe, vt quotannis illi septem ado- lescentes, septemque puellas adducerent, vt vel à Minotauro devorarentur (sicut fabulæ tradunt) vel (quod magis est credibile) vt illius libidi- ni atque Tyrannidi inseruirent. Eiusmodi et iam fuit conditio ab Ammonitis, habita- toribus Iabes proposita, fore scilicet, vt illi parcerent atque illos in suam tutelam reciperent, si modo singuli alterum sibi oculum eruerent. Mi- nusque adhuc tolerabilis fuit conditio ci- uibus Hierosolymitanis ab Antiocho ex- ecrando Tyranno proposita, & à plerisque eorum promissa, vt scilicet conseruanda vita sua gratia, veram Religionem abiurarent. Sive- ro conditio à victore proposita, & à victis promissa, difficilis est duntaxat atque dura, vi- taque huius tantum incommoda continens, con- cedo, eo casu iurisiurandi potius rationem habendam, quam vllorum commodorum, vel incommodorum. Quà ob causam Deus acriter Sedechiam, vltimum è familia Da- uidis Regem, increpauit & puniuit, Ezech. 17.16. quod contra iuratam fidem à Chaldæo- rum Rege defecisset. Gabaonitæ certe et si in durissimam seruitutem à Iosuaadda&i, nusquam de eo conqueruntur. Iosu. 9. 25. Præci-
units.tr: Conditions openly irreligious and contrary to conscience are of no validity. Such was the pact which they say was made in early times between Minos, king of the island of Crete, and the Athenians: namely, that every year they should bring to him seven young men and seven maidens, to be devoured by the Minotaur (as the fables relate), or (what is more credible) to be given over to his lust and tyranny. Of a similar kind was the condition proposed by the Ammonites to the inhabitants of Jabesh: that they would spare them and receive them into their protection, provided only that each of them should gouge out one of his own eyes. Still less tolerable was the condition proposed by that accursed tyrant Antiochus to the citizens of Jerusalem, and promised by most of them: that, to preserve their lives, they should renounce the true religion. But when the condition proposed by the victor and promised by the vanquished is merely difficult and hard, and contains only inconvenience to life, I concede that in that case the reason of the oath must be considered rather than any advantages or disadvantages. For this reason God sharply rebuked and punished Zedekiah, the last king of the house of David, Ezek. 17.16, because he had revolted from the king of the Chaldeans against his sworn faith. The Gibeonites, indeed, though they were reduced to the hardest servitude by Joshua, never complained about it, Josh. 9.25.

units.la: Præcipue vero cum de Religione agitur, summopere cauendum est, ne quis temere ab iis, qua Deo iuratus promisit, deficiendi licentiam captet: Qua in re tamen modus quoque eiusmodi seruandus erit, vt quemadmodum nihil facile in Religione quisquam immutare debet: sic (quoniam non nisi cum maximo dispensatione in ea decipi possumus) nemo pertinaciter ea tueatur, qua impie & illicite Deo promissa, obtentu Religionis, fuisse constiterit. Quod quia non satis caute hactenus animaduersum fuit, multæ graues ac periculosæ in mundo conuersiones acciderunt.
units.tr: Especially when religion is at stake, great care must be taken lest anyone rashly seek a license to desert what he has promised to God under oath. Yet in this matter a measure must also be observed, so that, just as one ought not to change anything in religion lightly, so (since we can be deceived in it only with the greatest caution) no one should stubbornly defend those things which have been shown to have been promised to God impiously and unlawfully under the pretext of religion. Because this has not been noticed with sufficient caution hitherto, many grave and dangerous upheavals have occurred in the world.

units.la: Verum demus, fuisse gentem aliquam, quæ aut imprudentia, aut blandimentis, aut denique, quia bonum Principem semel ex quapiam familia nacta, nimia facilitate prompserit, tales quoque semper futuros omnes illius posteros: sese omnino, nulla exposita conditione, cuipiam submiserit: An propterea dicemus, Principi illi omnia licere, qua libuerint? An ne potius ea quæ natura sua, sancta sunt & legitima, tanquam expressa habenda erunt? Quorsum enim alioquin euadet? aut qualis demum vita hominum futura est? Si Princeps huiusmodi eousque licentiæ proruperit, vt subditorum parentes truculentus occidat, vxoresac filias constupret, domos ac possessiones expilet, denique fingusingulos pro arbitrio iugulet: quia scilicet populus, ipsius probitate confisus, hunc ab initio sibi Principem, sine vllis conditionibus assumpserit?
units.tr: But let us grant that there was some nation which, either through imprudence, or by flattery, or finally because, having once obtained a good prince from some family, it was too easily persuaded that all his descendants would be likewise, submitted itself wholly to someone without any condition being stated. Shall we then say that that prince may do whatever he pleases? Or rather, shall those things which by their nature are holy and lawful be held as though they had been expressly stated? For where else would this lead? Or what kind of life would men then have? If such a prince should break out into such license that he cruelly kill the parents of his subjects, defile their wives and daughters, plunder their homes and possessions, and finally slaughter each one at his pleasure, merely because the people, trusting in his uprightness, had at the beginning taken him as its prince without any conditions?

units.la: Adhæc iniquissimum sane fuerit, vniuersi sæ alicui genti ac populo id denegare, quod æquitas ipsa priuatis personis (quales sunt mulieres, mentecapti, & qui vltra dimidium iusti pretii se fraudatos conqueruntur) vltro concedit, maximè si de mala eorum fide constiterit, quibus se eiusmodi personæ ob-strinxerunt. An vero quisquam magis improbæ fidei repetiri potest eo tyranno, qui sit vsque adeo imprudens, vt persuasum esse velit, sibi omnia licere per fas nefasque, quia scilicet aut ita cum populo pepigerit, aut à maioribus suis talem potestatem acceperit? Fateor equidem interea (sicuti abunde supra demonstratum est) authoritatem ordinum siue statuum tunc implorandam, & interponendam: ne priuatis hominibus quicquam ex seipsis aggredi aut moliri in statu publicum liceat, neve inferiores Magistratus vocationis suæ cancellos transcendant.
units.tr: Moreover, it would surely be most unjust to deny to a whole nation and people what equity itself willingly grants to private persons (such as women, the mentally incapable, and those who complain that they have been defrauded of more than half of a just price), especially if the bad faith of those to whom such persons have bound themselves is established. Indeed, can anyone be called more faithless than that tyrant who is so imprudent as to wish it to be believed that everything is permitted to him, right or wrong, because he has either made such an agreement with the people or received such power from his ancestors? I grant, meanwhile (as has been amply shown above), that the authority of the orders or estates must then be invoked and interposed, so that private men may not presume to undertake or attempt anything on their own authority against the public state, nor inferior magistrates overstep the bounds of their calling.

units.la: Sed quæro præterea, An maior sit subditorum erga Regem obligatio, quam liberorum erga parentem, Mancipiorum erga Dominum, aut libertorum erga Patronum, qui eos manumisit? Audiamus vero in primis, quid Cicero æquitate habent. quitate & ratione ductus, scribat, de officio filiifamilias, cuius pater potestate sua patria abuti, & vi dominium vsurpare conten- dat. Si Pater, inquit, Dominationem manifesta vi occupare, aut patriam prodere tentet, an filius tacebit? Minime, sed patrem supplex rogabit, ne id faciat: si autem precibus nihil profecerit, accusabit illum, atque minus terrebit: quod si eo iam res processerit, vt periculum sit, ne tandem patria obruatur, vita patris salutem patriae prafe-ret. En qualis fuerit eius viri sententia, non solum rationi consentanea, sed etiam maximae authoritatis. Quod vero ad seruos seu mancipia attinet: iure Romanorum cautum est, vt seruus, cui Dominus aegrotanti opem non tulerit, liber habeatur. Et quod etiam magis ius est, seruo, ex iuris scripti dispositione, Dominum laesa Maiestatis reum, accusare licet. Quis vero hoc crimine magis tenetur quam Tyrannus omnia iuta tam diuina quam humana manifeste peruertens? Sed apud quem, inquies, accusabitur? Respondeo: Vel apud eos, quantum eius creandi potestatem habuerint, habent etiam iudicandi ipsum authoritatem: Vel apud eos, qui praecipui sunt supremae potestatis defensores, & a quibus nulla est prouocatio. Sic quamuis Liberti, omnem Patronis suis obseruantiam debeant, adeo vt, iure ordinario, non nisi ciuiliter
units.tr: But I ask further: is the obligation of subjects toward a king greater than that of children toward a father, of slaves toward a master, or of freedmen toward the patron who manumitted them? Let us first hear what Cicero, guided by equity and reason, writes in his work on the duty of a son in the family, whose father would abuse his paternal power and strive to seize dominion by force. If the father, he says, should attempt to seize mastery by open force, or betray his country, will the son keep silent? Not at all; he will beg his father, as a suppliant, not to do it; but if he has accomplished nothing by entreaties, he will accuse him and frighten him less; but if matters have already gone so far that there is danger the country may finally be overwhelmed, he will place the safety of his country before his father's life. Behold what the opinion of that man was, which is not only consonant with reason but also of the greatest authority. As for slaves or servants, the law of the Romans provides that a slave whose master did not bring help to him when he was sick shall be considered free. And what is even more to the point, by the provision of written law a slave is permitted to accuse his master of treason. Yet who is more bound by this charge than a tyrant who plainly overturns all laws, both divine and human? But before whom, you will say, will he be accused? I answer: either before those who had the power of creating him also have the authority of judging him; or before those who are the chief defenders of supreme power, and from whom there is no appeal. Thus, although freedmen owe all deference to their patrons, so that under ordinary law they may deal with them only in a civil manner, nevertheless for certain causes (for example, if they have been subjected by their patron to some atrocious injury, or have caught him in adultery with their wife) they may bring a capital accusation against them under civil law.

units.la: ant, adeo vt, iure ordinario, non nisi ciui-liter. liter cum eis agere possint: certis tamen de causis, (vtpote, si atroci aliqua iniuria, a patrono fuerint affecti, eumve in adulterio cum vxore deprehenderint) possunt capitalem accusationem aduersus eos, ex iure ciuili instituere. His argumentis ago, non vt conscientiam legibus ciuilibus, aut Philosophorum dictis tanquam Regulis certissimis, astringam: sed duntaxat, vt euidentissime ostendam; quam iniqua sit eorum opinio, qui nullam prorsus hominibus viam relinquunt, qua cursum imminentis vel aperte grassantis tyrannidis abrumpere valeant, quantumuis crudelis & iniqua illa fuerit.
units.tr: ...so that under ordinary law they may bring suit against them only in a civil manner. Yet for certain reasons (for instance, if they have been subjected to some atrocious injury by their patron, or have caught him in adultery with their wife), they may bring a capital accusation against them under civil law. I make these arguments not to bind conscience with civil laws, or with the sayings of philosophers as if they were most certain rules, but only to show most plainly how unjust is the opinion of those who leave people no way at all to cut short the course of an impending or openly raging tyranny, however cruel and unjust it may be.

units.la: Certe quod excipere solent, Regem legibus non astringi, in genere nec potest nec debet accipi, vt Regum assentatores, Regnorumque euersores, occinunt. Nam vt taceam tot, omnium fere nationum, exempla, quae supra allata sunt, quorsum tot graues veterum Iurisconsultorum sententiae, ex iure naturae excerptae? Cuiusmodi sunt, Eos, qui leges ferunt, legibus quoque obtemperare: Et, Quod quisque iuris in alium statuerit, ipse vt eodem iure vtatur: Et, Nihil Imperio magis conducere, quam vt ex Legibus viuatur: Dignam denique vocem esse, Principem legibus sese subditum profiteri? Itaque quod alibi a Iurisconsultis dici videtur, Principem esse supra leges, aut Principem legibus esse solutum, non nisi de legibus ciuilibus, deque particulari & priuatorum iure, est intelligendum: Verbi gratia, de testamentis, de detractione Trebelliana, aut Falcidiana: non autem de iure publico, & ad statum, vt dici solet, pertinente: multoque minus de iure naturali, aut diuino: Cui cum omnes & singuli homines subiiciantur, quatenus homines nati sunt: omnino efficitur, aut Reges homines non esse, aut illos hoc iure teneri.
units.tr: Certainly, the exception that they usually make, that the king is not bound by the laws, can be understood neither in general nor as the flatterers of kings and the subverters of kingdoms sing it. For, to say nothing of so many examples from nearly all nations, which have been cited above, what do the weighty opinions of the ancient jurists, drawn from the law of nature, aim at? Such are these: that those who make laws are bound to obey them too; that whatever right a man lays down for another, he should use under that same right; that nothing is more useful to an empire than that people live under the laws; and, finally, that it is a worthy thing for a prince to profess himself subject to the laws. Therefore, what is said elsewhere by the jurists, that the prince is above the laws, or that the prince is released from the laws, must be understood only of civil laws and of the private and particular law of individuals: for example, concerning wills, concerning the Trebellian or Falcidian deduction. It must not be understood of public law, which, as is commonly said, pertains to the state, and much less of natural or divine law. Since all and each of men are subject to this law, insofar as they are born men, it follows necessarily that either kings are not men, or they are bound by this law.

units.la: Si quis rursus obiiciat, ius illud publicum, & ad statum populi, aut gentis pertinens (de ejusmodi enim loquimur) longe esse diuersum a iure naturae, ac gentibus omnibus communi: Verum id quidem esse quibusdam in rebus fatebor, sed ita vt omne illud discrimen in circumstantiis haereat, quae efficere nequeunt, quin generalis illa aequitas, & ἐπιείκεια firma constansque eousque maneat, vt omnis politia, quae illi aduersetur (veluti, exempli causa, si manifesta impietates, latrocinia, eiusque generis facinora; tum aduersus Deum, tum aduersus ius gentium, ac bonos mores, probarentur) prorsus fit & damnanda, & abiicienda.
units.tr: If someone again objects that that public law, which pertains to the state or people of a nation (for it is of such law that we are speaking), is very different from the law of nature and common to all nations, I will indeed admit that this is so in some matters, but in such a way that all this difference lies in circumstances, which cannot prevent that general equity and [ἐπιείκεια] from remaining so firm and constant that every polity which opposes it (for example, if manifest impieties, robberies and crimes of that kind are shown to be committed, both against God and against the law of nations and good morals) is wholly to be condemned and rejected.

units.la: Posset & illud excipi, supremum Magistratum reum quidem esse, si aliter quam dictum fit, dominetur. At non habere alium iudicem, quam Deum ipsum: quod Dauidis quispiam exemplo proplo probauerit, qui cum effet adulter, & homi-cida nefarius, à nemine tamen mortalium iudica-tus fuit. Sed respondeo primum: Ex supra-dictis satis perspici, Gentes ipsas, populique or-dines, ius sibi plerunque retinuisse franandorum Principum, cui nulla vel vetustas, vel temporis prae-scriptio, obesse possit. Deinde, multum interesse inter eum qui crimen aliquod semel, aut etiam re-petitis vicibus, commiserit, & eum qui ex profes-so omni scelerum genere fit addictus: Item, Inter Principem vita flagitiosa, & eum qui iustam o-mnem gubernandi rationem in Regno suo euertat. Neque enim supremum Magistratuum cen-furerim pro priuatis delictis (& quae proprie personalia sunt) eodem modo, quo Subditos, coercendum, sed tamen posse vsque adeo perditum fieri, vt merito poenis ac suppliciis in eu animaduerti & possit & debeat. Quanto igitur aequius fuerit, cum de publico sta-tu agitur, vt his quibus hoc officii incum-bit, liceat prouidere & omnino satagere, ne-quid Respublica detrimenti patiatur? quod ni fecerint, perfidi & in Deum, & in patriam (quib. fe iuramento obstrinxerunt) habean-tur. His distinctionibus probe expelis, & ad Dauidis mores in genere (necnon ad publicam illam satisfactionem, qua de admissis publi-ce egit poenitentiam) comparatis: nemo mi-rabitur, non fuisse quicquam grauius ad-
units.tr: This too might be objected: that the supreme magistrate is indeed liable if he rules otherwise than has been said, but that he has no judge other than God himself. Someone may prove this by the example of David, who, though he was an adulterer and a wicked murderer, was judged by no mortal. But I answer first: from what has been said above it is sufficiently clear that the nations themselves and the orders of the people have for the most part retained for themselves the right of checking princes, a right that neither antiquity nor the lapse of time can prejudice. Next, there is a great difference between one who has committed some crime once, or even repeatedly, and one who has openly given himself over to every kind of wickedness; likewise, between a prince of scandalous life and one who overturns every just method of governing his kingdom. For I would not judge that the supreme magistrates are to be punished for private offences (those which are properly personal) in the same way as subjects; yet a man may become so depraved that he can and ought rightly to be visited with penalties and punishments. How much more just, therefore, will it be, when the public state is at issue, that those to whom this duty belongs be permitted to take thought and to bestir themselves in every way, "lest the commonwealth suffer any harm"? If they do not do so, they will be held faithless both toward God and toward their country, to which they have bound themselves by oath. Having thoroughly set out these distinctions, and having compared them with the conduct of David in general (and also with that public satisfaction by which he publicly performed repentance for the sins he had committed), no one will wonder that nothing more severe was decreed or attempted against him.

units.la: F uersus eum statutum, vel tentatum. Præterea falsa est in vniuersum eius argumenti conclusio, ex qua infertur, Non debuisse pœnas de delicto aliquo sumi, quia scilicet sumpta non sint.
units.tr: Moreover, the conclusion of that argument, from which it is inferred that no punishment ought to have been taken for some offence because, forsooth, none was taken, is altogether false.

units.la: Sed nec deerunt etiam fortasse, qui Turcarum Imperatoris in suos Subditos authoritatem prætexant. Quibus vno verbo resposum velim, eiusmodi Imperium neque Regium neque humanum dici mereri, sed prorsus barbarum, Tyrannicum, brutum atque execrandum: eo maxime, quod cum cæteræ Monarchiæ, & Imperia (quantumuis multis vitiis obnoxia) instrumenta tamen fuerint ad humanam societatem conseruandam idonea: Contra, Turcicam hanc tyrannidem appareat horrendum esse Dei flagellum, quo Deus mundo huic extremam ruinam, & euersionem iusto suo iudicio minitetur. Itaque clara voce & sonora profiteor, si qui hodie reperiantur, qui Regibus suasores sint, vt inde gubernationis suæ exemplar, & typum effingant, eos tanquam publicos humani generis hostes habendos, & exterminio profligandos.
units.tr: But perhaps there will not be lacking those who put forward the authority of the Emperor of the Turks over his subjects. To these I would answer in one word that such an empire deserves to be called neither royal nor human, but utterly barbarous, tyrannical, brutish and execrable; and especially because, while other monarchies and empires (however much they are liable to many faults) have nonetheless been instruments suited to preserving human society, this Turkish tyranny appears to be a dreadful scourge of God, by which God, in his just judgment, threatens this world with final ruin and overthrow. Therefore I profess with a clear and resounding voice that if there are any today who advise kings to fashion their government after this pattern and model, such men are to be regarded as public enemies of the human race, and to be wiped out.

units.la: Cæterum, vt comparationes supra institutas de iure priuatorum in priuatos, persequar, an vlla strictior iuris obligatio inter homines dabitur quam Matrimonii? (in quo Deus ipse tanquam huius contractus praecipuus author intercedit, & per quod qui duo erant, una caro fiant.) At in matrimonio etiam ipso, si pars una alteram deserat, eam quae deserta est, Apostolus 1. Corinth. 7. verf. 15. ab omni obligatione liberam pronuntiat: quia deserens, praecipuam matrimonii conditionem violat. Fingamus vero, quempiam profiteri, se velle uxorem apud se retinere, idque conatus si tamen innotuerit, ideo uxorem hunc appetere, ut illi mortem inferat, vel eam alia via de medio tollat, an non pro desertore manifesto habendus erit? At certe huic diuersa non est tyrannorum mens, quum non alia ratione Subditos in potestate habere contendant, quam ut miseris suis cupiditatibus indulgentes, eos ad interfectionem usque persequantur & opprimant: Quid ni igitur idem de utrisque statuant, qui iudicandi authoritatem obtinent? Quod si ne Ecclesiastici quidem canones, uxorem, qua tuto apud maritum degere non potest, cogendam esse statuunt, ut cum illo habitet; cur inferiori Magistratui, sibi suisque prouidere non concedetur, & aduersus manifestum Tyrannum ad ordines recurrere?
units.tr: But, to pursue the comparisons made above concerning the right of private persons against private persons: is there any stricter bond of law between men than that of marriage? (in which God himself intervenes as the chief author of this contract, and through which two who were two become one flesh). Yet even in marriage itself, if one party deserts the other, the Apostle, in 1 Cor. 7.15, pronounces the one who has been deserted free from every obligation, because the deserter violates the chief condition of marriage. Now let us suppose that someone professes that he wishes to keep his wife with him, and yet, if it becomes known, that he seeks her for this very purpose, that he may inflict death upon her or otherwise remove her from the world: will he not be regarded as a manifest deserter? Certainly the mind of tyrants is not different from this, since they seek to hold their subjects in power by no other means than by indulging their wretched desires, pursuing and oppressing them even to slaughter. Why then should those who hold the authority of judging not determine the same about both? And if even the ecclesiastical canons decree that a wife who cannot live safely with her husband is not to be compelled to live with him, why will it not be permitted to the inferior magistrate to provide for himself and his own, and to have recourse against a manifest tyrant to the orders of the realm?

units.la: Adhaec, cum & Regna, & Imperia ipsa, in feudis censeatur (quae supremae potestati dominia, siue vt alii vocant, homagia, & fidelitatem seu subiectionem, & seruitutem etiam debeant) videamus quale fit ius Feudorum. Ex libro i-gitur 2. titul.26.§. Domino. & titul.47. apparet, Dominum non minus in Vasallum (siue clientem) crimen perfidiæ committere posse, quam Vasallum in Dominum: quo casu feudum quidem domini ad Vasallum non deuoluitur, sed redit ad directum feudi Dominum, a quo primario illud dependet, vel ad Domini agnatos. Hoc tamen certum firmumq; manet, Dominum perfidiæ conuictum, omne suum ius amittere quod in Vasallum habet. Cuius rei ratio ex eo pendet, quod Dominus in omnibus vicem fideli suo reddere debet, alioqui merito maleficus censetur, vt habetur in titul.6. de forma fidelitatis ad finem. Dico igitur in propositaquæstione, Regem, vel etiam Imperatorem, cuius dominatio a suprema pendet potestate, si in crimen illud perfidiæ erga Vasallos suos, hoc est, Subditos, inciderit, (quod vtinam nunquam accidat) amittere feudum suum, non vt Vasallis adiudicetur; sed vt de eo disponant ii, qui supremam illam potestatem referunt. Vt vero huius argumenti firmitas cognoscatur, notandum est: Eiusmodi indirectos (seu vt vulgo vocant subalternos) Dominos, nullum præstare iusiurandum Vasallis, cum eos inuestiunt, adeo vt quod diximus obseruari aduersus eos qui crimen
units.tr: Besides, since kingdoms and empires themselves are reckoned as fiefs (which owe to the supreme power dominions, or, as others call them, homages, and fealty or subjection, and even servitude), let us see what kind of law feudal law is. From the Book of Fiefs, 2. tit. 26. §. Domino, and tit. 47, it appears that a lord can commit the crime of perfidy against his vassal (or client) no less than a vassal against his lord; in which case the fief does not indeed pass to the vassal, but returns to the lord of the direct fief, from whom it primarily depends, or to the lord's agnates. Yet this remains certain and firm: a lord convicted of perfidy loses every right that he has over his vassal. The reason for this depends on the fact that a lord ought to render to his faithful man a return in all things; otherwise he is rightly regarded as a wrongdoer, as is held in tit. 6, on the form of fealty to the end. I say therefore, in the question proposed, that a king, or even an emperor, whose lordship depends on the supreme power, if he falls into that crime of perfidy toward his vassals, that is, his subjects (which would that it never happen!), loses his fief, not so that it is adjudged to the vassals, but so that those who hold that supreme power may dispose of it. But so that the firmness of this argument may be recognised, it must be noted: lords of this indirect kind (or, as they are commonly called, subordinate lords) give no oath to their vassals when they invest them, so that what we have said is observed against those who commit the crime of perfidy, and rests on no other ground than that natural equity which, even if it is not expressed, always comes to be understood of its own accord. What, then, vassals have of right against their lords of a fief (so that the comparison may be made from the lesser to the greater) must be determined...

units.la: Quid Vasalli, in dominos feudi, iuris habeant. crimen perfidiæ admittunt, non alia quam naturalis illius æquitatis ratione nitatur, quæ etsi expressa non fuerit, per se tamen semper subintelligenda veniat. Quid igitur (vt à minori, ad maius fiat comparatio) statuendum erit de eo, qui in crimen illud lapsus est erga subditos, quibus se expresso iureiurando devinxit? Præterea, etsi demus, Dominum in crimen illud perfidiæ nunquam posse ita incurrere aduersus Vasallum, vt ius feudi amittat: At nemo dubitat, Vasallum, huius criminis reum aduersus Dominum suum, feudo merito priuari. Cum ergo Imperator ipse, vt supra annotatum est, subiectionem (seu hominium, vt vulgus appellat) Imperio debeat, vtpote cuius ipse fit primus, & supremus Cliens: (qua conditione etiam Reges in regnis suis esse multo maiori, aut saltem pari ratione, æstimandum est) Quis dubitet, quin Imperatores, aut Reges a feudis suis decidant, si eo vsque perfidiæ prorupe-rint, vt in manifestos, & deploratos Tyrannos degenerent: quandoquidem id experimento vbique comprobatum fuisse, ostendimus.
units.tr: What rights do vassals have against the lords of a fief? They commit the crime of treachery, and this rests on the principle of natural equity, which, even if it is not stated, is always to be understood. What, then, should be decided about one who has fallen into that crime against his subjects, to whom he has bound himself by an express oath? (To argue from the lesser to the greater.) Moreover, even if we grant that a lord can never incur that crime of treachery against his vassal so as to lose his right to the fief: no one doubts that a vassal guilty of this crime against his lord is rightly deprived of his fief. Since the Emperor himself, as noted above, owes subjection (or homage, as the common people call it) to the Empire, since he is its first member and its chief client (and kings in their kingdoms must be judged to stand in the same condition, or at least by the same reasoning), who could doubt that emperors or kings fall from their fiefs if they break out into such treachery that they degenerate into manifest and notorious tyrants? We have shown that this has been confirmed by experience everywhere.

units.la: Denique cum apud saniores omnes, eorum etiam, qui se Catholicos Romanos vocant, tum certis rationibus, tum infinitis exemplis iampridem constitutum sit & persuasum: concilium Oecumenicum seu generale, esse {a}supra Papam, eumque deponendi, saltem propter crimen haeresewos potestatem habere: consequens est profecto; aut Reges maioris authoritatis quam Pontifices, crimenque haeresewos minus quam Tyrannidis, crimen esse: aut populos tantundem saltem potestatis habere in Reges, Tyrannos factos, quantum habet concilium in Pontificem haereticum. Haec est igitur nostra, de hac quaestione, sententia, qua quaeritur, Quid iuris habeant Subditi (cuiuscunque status fuerint) in supremum Magistratum, qui tyrannus evidens sit effectus.
units.tr: Finally, since among all the more sensible people, including those who call themselves Roman Catholics, it has long been established and believed, on sound grounds and by countless examples, that an ecumenical or general council is above the Pope and has the power to depose him, at least on account of the crime of heresy, it necessarily follows: either kings have greater authority than the Popes, and the crime of heresy is less than that of tyranny; or peoples have at least as much power over kings made tyrants as a council has over a heretical Pope. This, then, is our opinion on this question, namely, what rights subjects (of whatever rank they may be) have against the supreme magistrate, when he has become a manifest tyrant.

units.la: QVÆSTIO VII. Quid tum agendum, cum Ordines cogi contra tyrannum non possunt.
units.tr: QUESTION VII. What is to be done when the Estates cannot be compelled to act against a tyrant?

units.la: SVperest tamen adhuc, in hac disputatione, non exigua difficultas. Quaeritur enim, Quid tum fieri debeat, cum tyrannus eousque potentia excreuit, vt Ordinum conuentus (quod legitimum remedium aduersus eam esse diximus) prorsus vel conniuentia, vel metu, vel malitia valentioris multitudinis, ita impeditur, vt cogi nullo modo possit? Respondeo: Priuatos quidem homines, nisi vel ab inferiori Magistratu, vel a sanioře Statuum parte (de qua mox fusius) authoritatem habeant: nihil hic remedii iusti habere, quam Resipiscentiam, cum patientia & precibus coniunctam, qu as
units.tr: There still remains, however, in this discussion, no small difficulty. For it is asked: What ought to be done when a tyrant has grown so powerful that the assembly of the Estates (which we have said is the lawful remedy against him) is so completely hindered, whether by connivance, by fear, or by the malice of a stronger multitude, that it cannot be convened in any way? I answer: private persons, unless they have authority from an inferior magistrate or from the wiser part of the Estates (of which more shortly, at greater length), have no just remedy here other than repentance, joined with patience and prayers, which God will surely not reject, and without which all other remedies, however lawful, fall under God's curse.

units.la: {a} Priuatorum remedia legitima & necessaria. quas Deus vtique non est alpernaturus, & sine quibus reliqua omnia remedia, quantumuis legitima, Dei maledictioni subcerunt. Nihil tamen impedit, quin priuatae conditionis Subditi ad intermedios Magistratus confugiant, eosque de officio suo interpellent: Qui si vel omnes, vel sanioripsorum pars, priuatorum eiusmodi opera vti voluerint, satis supra ostendi, quid hi & Deo & patriae debeat. Sane inferiorum Magistratuum partes sunt, concordibus animis simul statuum conuentum vrgere: sesque interea, quantum & possunt & licet, aduersus manifestam tyrannidem tueri, & conseruare. Denique singulis quoque Ordinibus hoc officii incumbit, vt legitimum ac generalem omnium Ordinum conuentum ferio procuret; ne improbi, bonos; tardi, diligentes; multitudo, potiorem sanioremque partem, aut impediant aut remorentur. Quin etiam priuati quique, in eiusmodi necessitate, magistratibus suis subalternis sese adiungere tenentur, & officium Subditorum praestare: & si res postulet, licebit etiam saniori parti oppressae, auxilia aliunde conquirere; praesertim apud Regni cofoederatos & amicos. Ad cuius sententiae confirmationem citabo probatissima aliquot exempla. Ecce duae integrae Tribus, Ruben & Gad, & dimidia TriTribus Manassis, cum in idololatriam incideffe existimarentur, à reliquis omnibus tribubus armis impetuntur, Ios. 22. 12. Verum tamen nulla tribus, in aliam ius potestatem que habebat, cum omnes duodecim nō nisi vnum vniuersitatis corpus constituerent.
units.tr: {a} Lawful and necessary remedies for private persons. Nothing prevents subjects of private rank from fleeing to the intermediate magistrates and calling upon them to perform their duty. If all of them, or the wiser part of them, are willing to make use of the labour of such private persons, we have shown above enough of what these owe both to God and to their country. Indeed, it is the task of the inferior magistrates to press together, with united minds, for an assembly of the Estates, and meanwhile to defend and preserve themselves, as far as they are able and permitted, against manifest tyranny. Finally, it is also the duty of each of the Estates to take care that a lawful and general assembly of all the Estates is promptly procured, so that the wicked do not hinder or delay the good, the sluggish the diligent, or the multitude the better and wiser part. Indeed, every private person in such a necessity is also bound to join himself to his subordinate magistrates and to perform the duty of a subject; and if the matter requires it, it will be permissible for the oppressed wiser part to seek help elsewhere, especially among the allies and friends of the kingdom. To confirm this opinion I will cite some very well-attested examples. Behold, two whole tribes, Reuben and Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh, when they were thought to have fallen into idolatry, were attacked with arms by all the other tribes (Josh. 22. 12). Yet no tribe had any power over another, since all twelve constituted only one body of the whole community.

units.la: Hinc igitur apparet, potiorem partem posse alteram in Ordinem cogere, non expectato omnium communi consensu, si simul omnes conuenire non possint.
units.tr: From this it therefore appears that the greater part can compel the other to order itself, without waiting for the common consent of all, if all cannot assemble together.

units.la: Idem etiam in bello, iustissime abvnde cim tribubus aduersus tribu Beniamin suscepto, videre est, Iud. 20. cum hi horrendum facinus, in Gibea patratum, defenderent.
units.tr: The same may be seen in war, undertaken most justly against the tribe of Benjamin by the other tribes, Judg. 20, when they defended that horrible crime committed at Gibeah.

units.la: Quid ergo, si aut duæ illæ tribus cum dimidia Manassis, aut tribus ipsa Beniamin, in fratres & consanguineos suos tyrannidem affectassent?
units.tr: What then, if either those two tribes with half of Manasseh, or the tribe of Benjamin itself, had aspired to tyranny over their brothers and kinsmen?

units.la: Sic & Romani, Constantini opem aduersus Maxentium implorarunt, cum Occidentis Imperium obtinens, crudelissimum tyrannum aperte ageret. Quod bellum non solum Deo propitio, & votis ipsorum saeuente, gestum est, sed habet etiam ab omnibus historiographis approbationis testimonium. At Constantinus supremum Imperium in Maxentium non habuit, cum hic non minus summum Principatum in Occidente, quam ille in Oriente obtineret.
units.tr: So too the Romans implored the help of Constantine against Maxentius, when, holding the Western empire, he openly acted as a most cruel tyrant. That war was waged not only with God favouring it and their prayers attending it, but it also has the testimony of approval from all the historians. Yet Constantine did not hold supreme power over Maxentius, since the latter held the chief principate in the West no less than the former did in the East.

units.la: Quo iure vero, aut quo titulo, Occidentis Imperium adeptus est Carolus Magnus? Nisi quod à potiore Italiæ parte, ac nominatim à Patriciis Romanis (qui tunc nondum, ac ne multis quidem post annis, in potestatem Pontificum venerant) adversus Longobardorum tyrannidem euocatus est, propter Orientalium Imperatorum ignauiam, qui in Græcia delitescebant?
units.tr: But by what right, or under what title, did Charlemagne obtain the empire of the West? Was it not that he was summoned by the greater part of Italy, and particularly by the Roman patricians (who at that time had not yet, nor even for many years afterwards, come under the power of the Popes), against the tyranny of the Lombards, because of the cowardice of the Eastern emperors, who lay hidden in Greece?

units.la: Existimo igitur, sententiam meam hactenus abunde confirmatam probatamque; esse, modo hæc tria axiomata constanter in omnibus hisce definitionibus, retineantur; nempe, 1. Tyrannidem manifestam notamque esse oportere. 2. Nec prius ad arma progrediendum esse, quam cætera remedia omnia tentata sint. 3. Ac denique, quam probe exploratum fuerit, non solum quid liceat, sed etiam quid expediat, ne remedia ipso morbo periculosiora existant.
units.tr: I think, therefore, that my opinion has been sufficiently confirmed and proved so far; it holds provided these three axioms are consistently retained in all these definitions: (1) a tyranny must be manifest and notorious. (2) One must not proceed to arms before all other remedies have been tried. (3) And finally, it must be carefully examined not only what is permitted but also what is expedient, lest the remedies prove more dangerous than the disease itself.

units.la: Reliquum est, opinor, vt, pro huius tratationis catastrophe, argumentis præcipuis respondeamus, quæ in contrariam sententiam adduci solent, præter ea, quæ incidenter iam & per occasionem attigimus.
units.tr: It remains, I think, that, for the conclusion of this treatise, we should answer the principal arguments which are usually brought against the contrary opinion, apart from those things which we have already touched on incidentally and in passing.

units.la: Iastari vero illud in primis solet: Magistratuum esse, maxime iupremorum, præcipere, & Imperium exercere. Assentior & ipse, sed ad-do; hanc potestatem legibus, tum diuinis, tum humanis, esse definitam. Addunt præ-
units.tr: This objection is especially commonly raised: it belongs to magistrates, and above all to the supreme ones, to command and to exercise authority. I too agree, but I add that this power is defined by laws, both divine and human. They add furthermore:

units.la: tercea: terea: si Reges in tyrannos degenerent, neminem quidem iniquorum mandatorum ministrum esse aut fieri debere: sed Subditorum esse, pati, ac supremi Magistratus mores patienter ferre, non sese illis vlla vi opponere. Istud ego, nisi adhibitis superioribus distinctionibus non facile concederim: Quarum summa est, Priuatas qui-dem personas (nisi, authoritate legitimi alicuius Magistratus inferioris, vel Ordinum gentis illius, tueri se possint) aut omnino secedere, vsq; dum melior illis aura affulgeat, aut colla iugo subdere debere; à Deo patientiam assiduis precibus poscendo, & interim sub ipsius correctionibus proficienda.
units.tr: if kings degenerate into tyrants, no one of the subjects ought to be, or to become, a minister of their unjust commands, but it is the duty of subjects to suffer, and to bear patiently the conduct of the supreme magistrate, and not to oppose themselves to him by any force. I would not readily grant this, unless the distinctions above were applied. The sum of these is this: private persons (unless they can defend themselves by the authority of some lawful inferior magistrate, or of the Estates of that nation) ought either to withdraw altogether until a better air shines upon them, or to submit their necks to the yoke, asking patience of God by constant prayers, and meanwhile making progress under his corrections.

units.la: Magistratuum autem inferiorum partes esse, bonas leges, quarum defensionem ipsi iurauerint, strenue aduersus omnes tueri, pro ea quam quisque in statu publico statione sortitus est: Et huc, in genere, omnes incumbere, ne leges ac conditiones quibus status publicus nititur, vlla vi, vel externa, vel interna, labefactentur. Denique Imperatores, Reges, aliosve supremos Magistratus, summa potestate ita potiri, vt, si quidem interea conspicuum fit, eos, quam regendam prouinciam susceperint, potius depopulari, iurique ac rationi versute & impotenter aduersari, & quod iurati promiserint, protertransgredi, possint ac debeat ad officium, etiam armata manu (si aliter fieri nequit) reduci, compelli, adigique, ab iis, qui eos ad hanc dignitatem certis conditionibus, promouerunt.
units.tr: It is the duty of the inferior magistrates, however, to defend vigorously against all the good laws which they have sworn to defend, in the station which each has received in the commonwealth. And in general all are bound to this, that the laws and conditions on which the commonwealth rests may not be weakened by any force, external or internal. Finally, if emperors, kings, or other supreme magistrates have obtained supreme power in such a way that, while meanwhile it becomes plain that they are plundering the province they have undertaken to govern, and are craftily and violently opposing justice and reason, and are breaking through what they promised on oath, they can and ought to be brought back to their duty, compelled and forced, even by armed hand (if this cannot be done otherwise), by those who promoted them to this dignity on certain conditions.

units.la: Adhæc communiunt sese exemplo Dauidis, cui, etsi iam Regni successio promissa esset, & Ducis præcipui officio in bello fungeretur, dum tamen tyrannice impetitur à Saule, tantæ apud se authoritatis vnctum Domini fuisse ostendit, 1.Sam.24.v.7.& 1.Sam.26.v.4. vt deprehensum neq; ipse laedere, neq; ab aliis laedi, voluerit: sed exemplo illum mortis supplicio affici iusserit, 2.Sam.1.16. qui de eo ab se occiso gloriaretur: Illum denique, quantumuis iniquissimum tyrannum, viuû & mortuû honore maximo sit prosecutus. Cuncta hæc ego non inuitus agnosco, & fateor etiam, Fidem, patientiam, ac bonitatem Dauidis, dotes fuisse incomparabiles & commendatissimas, quas deceat omnes Christianos quam maxime imitari, & in exemplar sibi proponere: Adodo etiam, omnibus promissue, siue superioribus, siue æqualibus, siue inferioris conditionis, bona pro malis rependenda esse. At nego interim, Patientiam, & mansuetudinem, qua in Christianis requiritur, impedire, quominus quis legitimis remediis vti possit, ad propulsandam iniuriam qua illi infertur. Licitum est sane, rem suam in iudicio ab iniusto possessore vindicare, & apud summum Magistratum de iniuria inferioris conqueri : Quidni igitur eadem ratione,apud Ordines,aduersus Tyrannum ius experiri licebit? Quod fi,prę tyrannide, nulla ad iustitiam via pateat, tantum abest, vt Dauidis exemplum, iis quæ à nobis dicta sunt,aduersetur,vt manifeste etiam pro nobis faciat. Dauid enim Saulis furori ita cessit, vt interim militum copias non paruas secum aggregarit:quibus (haud dubie) liberius,ad suam suorumque vitam afferendam, vsus fuisset, si eo necessitatis à Deo adactus foret,vt non,nisi conferta manu,vim sibi illatam valuisset propellere. Quod vero tyranni vitæ,cum in manus suas incidisset,pepercit; id certe merito, & pro officio fecit: Saul enim solium adhuc Regium obtinebat: neque vel Dauidi, vel cuiquam alteri ius fuit, Regnum illi aut vitam adimere; sed solius Dei,aut Ordinum,vt supra ostensum est. Cætera longe aliud est, aduersus tyrannum, vel in iudicio, vel oppositis armis, sese tueri, Aliud, ex professo aliquid, aut in tyranni vitam, aut in eius ditionem, moliri.
units.tr: Furthermore, they take refuge in the example of David. Although the succession to the kingdom had already been promised to him, and although he discharged the office of chief commander in war, he was nonetheless attacked tyrannically by Saul. Yet he showed that he regarded the anointed of the Lord as having such great authority that, when he had Saul in his power, he willed neither to harm him himself nor to let him be harmed by others. 1 Sam. 24:7 and 1 Sam. 26:4. Instead he ordered the man who boasted that he had killed Saul to be put to death. 2 Sam. 1:16. Finally, he showed the greatest honour to Saul, however unjust a tyrant he was, both living and dead. I acknowledge all these things willingly, and I also confess that David's faith, patience and goodness were incomparable and most commendable gifts, which all Christians ought above all to imitate and set before themselves as an example. I add too that good must be returned for evil to all men alike, whether superiors, equals or those of lower condition. But I deny that the patience and gentleness required in Christians prevent anyone from using lawful remedies to repel the injury done to him. It is certainly lawful to vindicate one's property in court against an unjust possessor, and to complain before the highest magistrate of an injury done by an inferior. Why, then, by the same reasoning, should it not be lawful to seek justice against a tyrant before the Estates? But if, because of the tyranny, no way to justice lies open, then the example of David is so far from opposing what we have said that it even clearly supports us. For David yielded to the fury of Saul in such a way that in the meantime he gathered together no small number of soldiers with him. He would doubtless have used them more freely to defend his own life and that of his men, had he been driven by God's necessity to repel the violence done to him only by force of arms. As for the fact that, when he had fallen into his hands, he spared the life of the tyrant, he certainly did this rightly and as a matter of duty. For Saul still held the royal throne, and neither David nor anyone else had the right to take away from him his kingdom or his life; that belongs to God alone, or to the Estates, as has been shown above. It is quite another thing to defend oneself against a tyrant, either in court or by armed resistance, and another thing to plot openly against the tyrant's life or against his rule.

units.la: IV. Obiect. Sedechiam non debuisse à Rege Chaldæorum deficere.
units.tr: IV. Objection: Zedekiah ought not to have revolted from the king of the Chaldeans.

units.la: Aiunt postmodum, Sedechiam Regem Iuda grauiter fuisse reprehensum atq; multatum, quod contra iusiurandum à Chaldæorum Rege defecisset, 2. Par. 36.v.13. qui tamen legitimus Iudæ Dominus non erat, sed apertissimus alienæ ditionis vsurpator, Ezech.17. v.12. & 13.verf.14. Quomodo igitur plus licebit Subditis, aduersus legitimum Regem, qui Tyrannus euaserit? Respondeo, Sedechiam expresso Dei mandato, ac etiam præstito in ramento, sese cum suis, Regi Chaldæorum subiecisse: qui nullam non soluendi tributi occasionem præbuisset: Quæ circumstantiæ conuincunt omnino Sedechiā, & eius populares, tanquam reos tum defectionis, tum periurii. Deinde concedo etiam, non licere Subditis a iuramento suo discedere: neq; probo, quod dici solet trito prouerbio, Frangenti fidem, fides frangatur eidem: contra enim censeo, non licere vnquam fidem iuste datam fallere. Sed nego, fidem a Subditis falli, aut violari erga tyrannum, quoties singuli ipsorum intra metas vocationis suæ sese continentes, cum tyrannidi impedire conantur. Est enim Regula generalis; Pactum sub conditione vel expressa, vel tacite subintellecta, contractum, ab eo solui, qui conditionem violarit; non autem ab eo, qui, cum sub conditione tantum obligatus effet, ab obligatione liber fit: non per se (esse enim perfidus) sed per eum ipsum, qui prior rupit vinculum obligationis, nempe conditionem appositam. Supremo igitur Magistratu Tyranno facto, ipse, suo periurio populum a iuramento liberasse, censendus est, non contra: cum popupopulus merito in eum suo iure vtatur.
units.tr: They say afterwards that Zedekiah, king of Judah, was severely rebuked and punished because he revolted, contrary to his oath, from the king of the Chaldeans. 2 Chr. 36:13. Yet that king was not the lawful lord of Judah, but a plainly manifest usurper of another's dominion. Ezek. 17:12 and 13, verse 14. How, then, can subjects be allowed more against a lawful king who has turned out to be a tyrant? I answer: Zedekiah, by the express command of God, and also after giving his oath, had submitted himself and his people to the king of the Chaldeans, who had given him no occasion at all to refuse the tribute. These circumstances wholly convict Zedekiah and his fellow countrymen as guilty both of revolt and of perjury. Next, I also concede that subjects may not depart from their oath; nor do I approve of the worn-out proverb, "Let faith be broken with him who breaks faith." On the contrary, I hold that a faith rightly given may never be deceived. But I deny that subjects deceive or violate faith towards a tyrant whenever individuals, keeping within the limits of their calling, try to hinder the tyranny. For there is a general rule: a pact, made under a condition either expressed or tacitly understood, is dissolved by the one who has violated the condition, and not by the one who, having been bound only under a condition, is freed from the obligation. He is freed not by his own act (for that would be perfidy), but by the very one who first broke the bond of obligation, namely the condition attached. Therefore, when the supreme magistrate has become a tyrant, he is to be judged to have released the people from their oath by his own perjury, and not the reverse, since the people rightly exercise their own right against him.

units.la: Praetexunt adhaec mandatum Dei, Ierem. 29.verf.7. qui iubeat nominatim Israelitas, preces pro pace, & felici statu Nebuchadnezaris, crudelissimi tyranni, fundere: nedum vt Iudaeis ab illius obedientia & Imperio sese subducere licuerit. Concedo id quoque: At primum respondeo: Iudaeos non solum Subditos, priuata que conditionis, sed etiam plerosque serues fuisse sub Chaldaeorum Imperio. Iam verò supra a nobis positum est, Priuata conditionis hominibus non licere in suos Magistratus insurgere, vel sese illis aperta vi opponere: multo minus seruis in Dominos, quantumuis duros iniquos ve: quandoquidem hi & corpora ipsorum & bona in sua potestate habeant: Hoc praeceptum ergo iis, quae supra a nobis sunt posita, nihil derogat. Praeterea repeto rursus; Iudaeos (quod in tota hac historia maxime est observandum) in potestatem Chaldaeorum expressa Dei voluntate venisse, quae illis per Prophetas saepe fuit praedicta: Tam abest igitur, vt Sedechiae & reliquae multitudini cuerit, tempore captiuitatis, tyrannidi Chaldaeorum resistere; vt ne antea quidem bona conscientia potuerint sese illis opponere, aut urbem Ierusalem aduersus illorum oppugnationem protegere: quandoquidem praeceperat Deus nominatim per Ieremiam, Ier.
units.tr: They also put forward the command of God in Jeremiah 29:7, which bids the Israelites by name to pour out prayers for the peace and prosperous state of Nebuchadnezzar, a most cruel tyrant, much less to escape from obedience to him and his rule. I concede this too. But first I answer: the Jews were not only subjects of private condition, but most of them were also slaves under the rule of the Chaldeans. Now, as we have already laid down above, men of private condition may not rise against their magistrates or oppose them by open force, much less slaves against their masters, however harsh or unjust, since the masters hold their bodies and goods in their power. This command therefore takes nothing away from what has been set down above by us. Besides, I repeat again: the Jews (which must be most carefully observed throughout this whole history) came into the power of the Chaldeans by the express will of God, which had often been foretold to them through the prophets. So far, then, was it from being lawful for Zedekiah and the rest of the multitude, in the time of captivity, to resist the tyranny of the Chaldeans, that they could not even before that, with a good conscience, oppose them or defend the city of Jerusalem against their siege, since God had expressly commanded through Jeremiah, Jer.

units.la: V. Obiect. Iudaos ser-vos Babylo-niorum su-isse, nedum Subditos. 38.v.17. vt vrbem in manus Chaldaeorum dederent, seseque illis vltro subiicerent.
units.tr: V. Objection: The Jews were slaves of the Babylonians, let alone subjects. 38:17: that they should surrender the city into the hands of the Chaldeans and voluntarily submit themselves to them.

units.la: Hic etiam frustra regerunt quidam, Hanc eandemDei voluntatem in omni tyrannide locum habere, cum nulla vel sine, vel praeter Dei voluntatem, obtingat. Possem enim hoc idem argumentum in tyrannos retorquere: Quoniam nomi-nus a Dei voluntate pendet, quod tyranni a suis Subditis & populariter expelluntur (ut plerisque accidit) quam quod populos tyranni sepe numero opprimant. Sed verior hęc erit responsio, si dicamus, Dei voluntatem eatenus nobis spectandam, quatenus ipse nobis eam patefacere dignatus est: A. Nam lioquin nullum erit tam atrox facinus, quod diuinę voluntati imputari non possit: Cū ne ea quidem, quae maxime fortuita censentur, casu vel fortuito contingant. Hinc fit, vt qui latronibus publicis occurrit (a quibus nemo truci-datur, nisi id diuina voluntate permittente) iustam illis ac inculpatam tutelam ex legum authoritate opponere valeat: nempe, quia speciale a Deo mandatum nemo habet, vt sese a latronibus vltro iugulari patiatur. Idem est omnino iudicium, de ordinaria illa, de qua loquimur, a duersus tyrannos defensione. Quae tamen tum demum locum habere definit, cum de Dei contraria voluntate apparet, sicut euenit in eo Sedechia facto, de quo prorsus dximus, 2.Par.11.v.4. Et prius etiam in RoboaRoboami ipsius antecessoris causa: quiiure a-lioquin decem alias tribus à se deficientes fuisset insectatus, nisi Deus id fieri expresse vetasset. At contra Mathathias ipsiusque liberi summa laude digni celebrantur, 1. Mach. 1.2. quod sese crudelissimo Tyranno Antiocho tám cordate opposuerunt, nullo id vetante Dei mandato, etsi absque illius iusto iudi-cio populum Dei non inuasisset Antiochus, & plerisque etiam probaretur gratusque es-set.
units.tr: Here too some people argue to no purpose that this same will of God holds in every tyranny, since nothing happens either without or against the will of God. For I could turn this same argument against tyrants: since the fact that tyrants are expelled by their own subjects, and by the people, as happens in most cases, depends on the will of God, no less than the fact that tyrants often oppress peoples. But the truer answer will be this: we must regard the will of God only so far as he has deigned to make it known to us. For otherwise there will be no atrocious deed which cannot be imputed to the divine will, since not even those things which are thought to be most accidental happen by chance or fortune. Hence it follows that a man who meets public robbers (by whom no one is slain unless God permits it) may lawfully set against them a just and blameless defence by the authority of the laws; namely, because no one has a special command from God to allow himself to be slaughtered by robbers. The judgement is wholly the same concerning that ordinary defence, of which we are speaking, against tyrants. Yet this defence ceases to have a place only when the contrary will of God becomes apparent, as happened in the case of Zedekiah, of which we have spoken in full, 2 Chr. 11:4. And earlier also in the case of Rehoboam, the predecessor himself, who otherwise would have pursued with right the ten tribes that revolted from him, had not God expressly forbidden this to be done. On the contrary, Mattathias and his sons are celebrated as worthy of the highest praise, 1 Macc. 1:2, because they so boldly set themselves against the most cruel tyrant Antiochus, no command of God forbidding it, although Antiochus had not invaded the people of God without God's just judgement, and it would have been approved by most people and been welcome to them.

units.la: Obiiciunt hoc quoque, Israelitarum defectionem illam à Roboamo, 1. Reg. 12. v. 18. 20. quamquam iniquo exactore, maxime improbari. Respondeo & ipse, duplicitér in eo peccasse Israelitas. Primum, quod non conuocatis Israelitici populi ordinibus (quo Roboamum siue volentem, siue nolentem ad officium cogerent) Nouum Regem eligendo, Regnum illud, quod vnicum esse Deus voluit, in duo discerpserint. Deinde, quod à Dauidis familia (quam non ignorabant ad Regnum à Deo ipso fuisse selectam) discesserint: At hæc aduersus nos minime militant. Nec quicquam etiá iuuerit, Ieroboami vocationem ab Ahia Propheta ipsi patefactam, 1. Reg. 11. v. 30, prætexere: quandoquidem tota historia satis testatur, non eo respexisse populū cum à domo Dauidis rebellaret, & Aburamum Q[?]aliorem occideret: sed viam qua suntin-gressi manifestam fuisse defectionem: cum potius legitimo iustoque armorum vsu tyrannidi occurrere, & potuerint & debuerint. Ita fit sæpe aliquid iniuste, quod tamen per se iustum esse, nihil prohibet.
units.tr: They also object that the revolt of the Israelites from Rehoboam, 1 Kgs 12:18, 20, is greatly condemned, although he was an unjust exactor. I answer in turn that the Israelites sinned in that revolt in two ways. First, because, without summoning the orders of the Israelite people (by whom they might have forced Rehoboam, whether willing or unwilling, to do his duty), they chose a new king and tore apart into two that kingdom which God willed to be one. Second, because they withdrew from the house of David, which they knew had been chosen for the kingdom by God himself. But these points do not bear at all against us. Nor will it help in the least to plead the calling of Jeroboam, revealed to him by the prophet Ahijah, 1 Kgs 11:30, since the whole history sufficiently testifies that the people, when they rebelled from the house of David and stoned Adoram the tax-collector, did not look to that, but to the manifest way in which they had seceded; whereas they could and ought rather to have met the tyranny with the lawful and just use of arms. So it often happens that something is done unjustly which in itself nothing prevents from being just.

units.la: Contendut insuper & illud pro se facere, Quod diui Petrus, 1. Pet. 2. 17. & Paulus, 1. Tim. 2. 2. iubent aperte, preces pro Regib. ac aliis Magistratibus fieri, qui tamen ipsorum tempore non solum Ethnici, sed immanissimi adeo tyranni erant. Fateor sane: Sed præterquam quod ad priuatas personas adhortationes illæ diriguntur (quibus nullum aliud remedium quam preces & patientiam reliquû esse semper diximus) meminisse hic quoque oportet, cum diximus, Magistratus inferiores, aut Regni alicuius Ordines, posse, imo & debere tyrannidi obsistere; Id neq; officio priuatorû Christi fidelium quicquam detrahere, quo vetantur malum malo rependere, sed in bono vincere malum, & pro inimicis etiam orare: neque Magistratuum eiusmodi defensionem, prohibere, quin pro conuersione etiam ipsius tyranni, cui resistunt, apud Deum sint supplices: Illique resistendo, quantam fieri potest reuerentiam ex animo & vere exhibeant. Quanquam & illud notandum fuerit, Posse tyrannum eo vsq; impietatis prouolui, & tam exe-crancrandas inDeū inimicitias exercere, vt nominatim aduersus eum publicas preces & execrationes concipere non solum liceat, sed fit etiam aliquando operae pretium: Quod exemplo suo olim vetus ac primitiua Ecclesia palam testata est, cum Iuliano Caesari, cognomine Apostatae, non solum publice imprecata, sed etiam exaudita est.
units.tr: They further argue that this supports their case, because the divine Peter (1 Pet. 2:17) and Paul (1 Tim. 2:2) plainly command that prayers be made for kings and other magistrates, who in their time were not only heathen but also most savage tyrants. I grant it. But apart from the fact that those exhortations are addressed to private persons (for which, as we have always said, prayer and patience are the only remedy left), we must also remember what we said here: that lower magistrates or the orders of some kingdom can, and indeed ought, to resist tyranny.
