This does not take anything away from the duty of private Christians, who are forbidden to repay evil with evil, but are to overcome evil with good and to pray even for their enemies. Nor does it prevent such magistrates from defending themselves, provided they still make supplication to God for the conversion of the very tyrant they resist, and while resisting him show him all the reverence they can, from the heart and sincerely. It should also be noted, however, that a tyrant may sink into such impiety and carry on such execrable hostility against God that it is not only permitted to make public prayers and curses against him by name, but sometimes it is also worthwhile. The ancient and primitive Church openly bore witness to this by its own example, when it publicly invoked curses against the Emperor Julian, surnamed the Apostate, and was indeed heard.

units.la: Citant deniq; Christi ipsius exemplum, qui tributum Tyberio Caesari quamuis iniusto Iudaea vsurpatori, monstroque potius quam homini, pependit, cum constet ex aduerso, quotquot Romanis Imperatoribus per seditionem restiterunt (quales imprimis memorantur Iudas ille Golonites, Theudas, aliique factiosi, ac tandem Iudaeorum natio, ne falsam Ethnicorum Religionē amplectiti cogeretur) mi-fere periisse. Quibus respondeo: Magnum esse discrimen inter Ius Regium, & Tyrannidem: Itaque quamuis Iesus Christus coeli terraeque Dominus esset: ad quem etiam, tanquam ex Dauide prognatum, Regnum Iudaeorum potius quam ad Romanos, vel ad Herodem, iure pertineret: Quia tamen non ideo in mundum venerat, vt humano more dominaretur, sed vt quasi priuatus hac in parte, & praerogatiuae Dauidicae familiae renuntians, vitam hic degeret: Ideo suo illo exemplo confirmare voluit, iuste Regibus ac Principibus Tributa ac reliqua subsidia, & deberi, & perfol-ui. Quanquam enim Romani Imperatores iniuste ab initio Regnum Iudaeorum inuaserunt, eius tamen legitimi tandem Domini euaserunt, partim iusto Dei Iudicio, partim consensu, & approbatione, si non omnium at certe valentioris multitudinis Iudaeorum, quod satis aperte significarunt, cum omnes fere acclamarent: Non habemus Regem nisi Caesarem, Ioan. 19. vers. 15.
units.tr: Finally, they cite the example of Christ himself, who paid tribute to Tiberius Caesar, though he was an unjust usurper of Judaea, more a monster than a man. Yet on the other side it is clear that all who resisted the Roman emperors by sedition (above all that Judas the Gaulonite, Theudas and other factious men, and finally the Jewish nation itself, which was forced to embrace the false religion of the heathen) almost always perished. To this I reply: there is a great difference between lawful kingship and tyranny. Although Jesus Christ was the Lord of heaven and earth, and the kingdom of the Jews belonged to him by right rather than to the Romans or to Herod, since he was descended from David, yet he had not come into the world to rule in the manner of men. Rather, in this respect he lived here as a private person, renouncing the privileges of the house of David. Therefore by that example he wished to confirm that tributes and other aids are rightly owed and paid to kings and princes. For although the Roman emperors at the beginning unjustly invaded the kingdom of the Jews, they nevertheless became its lawful lords in the end, partly by the just judgment of God, and partly by the consent and approval of the Jews, if not of all, at least of the stronger part of the multitude, which they made quite plain when almost all of them cried out: We have no king but Caesar, Ioan. 19. vers. 15.

units.la: QVÆSTIO VIII. Quid liceat aduersus iniustos exactores?
units.tr: QUESTION VIII. What is permitted against unjust tax-collectors?

units.la: Vid si vero, dicet quispiam, Princeps populum nimis iniustisque tributis opri-mat? Tunc vbi decenter admonitus fuerit, possunt certe ac etiam debent, ii, qui prima ac summa valent authoritate ex Regni legibus publica vtilitati consulere. Sed & hic notandum est? Principem qui eiusmodi in rebus modum excedit (quia aut prodigus, aut auarus, aut aliis est vitiis deditus) non statim pro Tyranno esse habendum: Tyrannidis enim index ac veluti indiui-duus comes est, obfirmata malignitas, quae ad statum publicum, legesque (quibus Regnum ceu fundamentis cohaeret) euertendas totis viribus enititur. Addo & illud: Quamuis iusta occasio opponendi se manifesto tyranidi quandoque offeratur, meditanda tamen subinde, atque atque si fieri potest, sequendam, eximiam il- lam ab homine ethnico prolatâ γνῶμλω: O- multa prius experiri consilio sapientem, quam ar-mis decet. Itaque cum Imaginem Cæsaris in templum inferre conaretur Petronius, iu-stam quidem videbantur habere Iudæi ad arma capessenda occasionem (vt suadebat Mathathiæ zelus) potius quam vt templum Dei idolo violari paterentur: At multo pru-dentius consilium inierunt, cui etiam Deus benedixit, cum Petronio libere indicarent, Nolle se equidem aduersus ipsum pugnare: Verum nunquam passuros, quandiu essent superstites, Idolum illud in templo collocari. Cæterum etsi Albini & Flori exactiones æquissimam illis denuo querimoniarum causam praebererent, & tum quoque de rebus ad Religionem pertinentibus quadantenus ageretur: Omnia tamen Iudæorum acta satis ostenderunt, nō aliud eos, quam meram defectionem, ac rebellionem affectasse, quæ cum legitimis, de quibus diximus, remediis nihil haberent commune.
units.tr: But if, someone will say, the prince oppresses the people with excessive and unjust taxes? Then, when he has been properly admonished, those who hold the first and highest authority under the laws of the realm can certainly, and indeed ought to, look to the public good. But here too it must be noted: a prince who exceeds the proper measure in such matters (because he is either a spendthrift, or greedy, or given over to other vices) is not to be regarded at once as a tyrant. For the mark and, as it were, the inseparable companion of tyranny is a hardened malice that strives with all its strength to overthrow the public state and the laws, to which the kingdom clings as to its foundations. I add this too: although a just occasion of openly opposing a tyrant is sometimes offered, it should nevertheless be considered again and again, and, if possible, followed, that famous maxim uttered by a heathen man [γνώμην]: it is fitting for a wise man to try many things by counsel before arms. Thus when Petronius tried to bring the image of Caesar into the temple, the Jews seemed to have a just occasion to take up arms (as the zeal of Mattathias urged), rather than suffer the temple of God to be violated by an idol. But they adopted a much more prudent plan, and God blessed it too: they freely told Petronius that they were not indeed willing to fight against him, but that, as long as they were alive, they would never allow that idol to be placed in the temple. Moreover, although the exactions of Albinus and Florus gave them a most just cause of complaint once more, and although matters pertaining to religion were then also to some extent at issue, yet all the actions of the Jews showed well enough that they aimed at nothing but mere defection and rebellion, which had nothing in common with the lawful remedies of which we have spoken.

units.la: QVÆSTIO IX. An Subditi cum Principibus possint pacisci.
units.tr: QUESTION IX. Whether subjects can make pacts with princes.

units.la: REspondendum est porro nunc illis quoque, qui existimant, non decere subditos ditos cum superioribus pacisci. Quero igitur primum, quibus nitatur fundamentis? Si enim rationibus agendum est, quales quaeso illas satis firmas praetexent? Subditorum est, inquiunt, a Principum suorum authoritate & mandatu pendere, no contra. Unde consequens est, posse quidem Subditos modeste ac reuerenter Principibus suas exponere querimonias, atque illis libere suum consilium impertiri, si rogentur: ac minime vlterius progredi. Respondeo: Non licere omnino Subditis Magistratus suos, siue inferiores siue supremos, nisi cum summa reuerentia accedere: idque non solum propter metum indignationis eorum, sed etiam propter conscientiam, vt docet Apostolus, Rom. 13. verf. 5. cum haec potestas a Deo sit constituta. At nego ex hoc fundamento talem posse necessarium consequutionem: Oportere ergo Subditos, quoties de rebus politicis & adstatum, vt dicitur, Regni pertinentibus agitur, vbi quod iustum & aequum, legibusque (sub quibus Princeps ille electus & constitutus fuit) consentaneum ipsis videtur, modeste ac reuerenter illi exposuerint, deinceps necessario se illius arbitrio totos subiicere, idque omnino absque vlla exceptione sequi, quod illi fuerit collibitum. Quinimo contra libere affero: Nullam ipsi iniuriam fieri, si ad officium compellatur: &c, vbi nullus amplius rationi locus superest, vlterius etiam aduersus cum eum fiat progressus. Siquidem cum non, nisi certis conditionibus, administratio illi sit commissa: minime censendum est, nouas pactiones cum ipso iniri, quoties interpel-latur, ut vel priores conditiones ratas habeat, easque deinceps obseruet: vel alteri locum cedat, qui de illarum obseruatione magis fit futurus sollicitus. Quod si exemplis probandum est, arbitror satis multa supra a me allata esse, quibus constet aperte, nulla ratione nullo-que visu aut bene constitutae Monarchiae vlla experientia niti, aut defendi eorum propositionem posse, qui audent affirmare, Sufficere cunctis debere Subditis nudam Regis jui voluntatem.
units.tr: I must now also answer those who think that subjects should not make pacts with their superiors. I ask first, on what foundations do they rest? For if we are to argue by reasons, what reasons, I ask, will they put forward that are firm enough? It is the duty of subjects, they say, to depend upon the authority and command of their princes, not against them. From this it follows that subjects may indeed set out their complaints to their princes modestly and respectfully, and offer their counsel freely if asked, but must go no further. I reply: subjects may by no means approach their magistrates, whether inferior or supreme, except with the greatest reverence. This is required not only from fear of their anger but also from conscience, as the Apostle teaches, Rom. 13. vers. 5, since this power has been ordained by God. But I deny that such a necessary consequence can follow from this foundation: Therefore subjects ought, whenever matters pertaining to politics and to the state of the kingdom, as it is called, are under discussion, and when they have modestly and respectfully set out to that prince what seems to them just and fair and consistent with the laws under which that prince was chosen and appointed, then necessarily to surrender themselves wholly to his judgement, and to follow without any exception whatever has pleased him. On the contrary, I affirm freely: No injury is done to him if he is compelled to his duty, etc. Where no room is left for reason, further progress is made against him as well. For since administration has been committed to him only on certain conditions, it is by no means to be thought that new pacts are to be entered into with him whenever he is challenged, either so that he may hold the earlier conditions valid and observe them henceforth, or so that he gives place to another who will be more anxious about their observance. If this must be proved by examples, I think that many have been adduced above by me, which plainly show that no reason and no experience of a well-constituted monarchy supports, or can defend, the proposition of those who dare to affirm that the bare will of the king ought to suffice for all subjects.

units.la: QVÆSTIO X.
units.tr: QUESTION X.

units.la: An, qui propter religionem persecutionem patiuntur, aduersus tyrannos sese tuerì salua conscientia possint.
units.tr: Whether those who suffer persecution on account of religion may defend themselves against tyrants with a clear conscience.

units.la: REliquum est tandem vt maximi momenti quæstionem soluam, qua quæritur, an Tyrannidi, veram religionem impetenti, atque etiam quoad potest opprimenti, liceat, iuxta superius positas conditiones distinctionesque, armata manu obsistere, & persecutioni obuiam ire? Dubitandi hæ præcipue causæ esse possunt.
units.tr: It remains at last to resolve the question of greatest importance: whether it is lawful, under the conditions and distinctions laid down above, to resist with armed hand a tyranny that attacks the true religion and oppresses it as far as it can, and to meet persecution head on. There are chiefly these grounds for doubt.

units.la: Primum, Cum Religio ad conscientias pertineat, quibus nullo modo vis inferri potest, non vide-turtur illa vllu armis stabilienda aut defendenda: Quam ideo prædicatione verbi Dei, precibus, ac patientia hastenus potius propagatam conspi-cimus. Extant præterea, loci permulti inscri-pturæ, quibus ostenditur, quanta sit inter Regna huius mundi, & Regnum Christi spiritua-le, differentia. His denique subiiciuntur ex-empla sanctorum Prophetarum, ac ipsius demum Domini nostri Iesu Christi, penes quem etsi omnis foret authoritas, potentia, & virtus, nunquam tamen ipse hanc defensionis rationem est aggref-sus: quemadmodum nec ipsi Apostoli, nec subsequentes vlli Martyres: vsque adeo vt ne integra quidem Christi fidelium legiones, armis instructissima, mortem oppetere recusarint, potius quam exerto gladio aduersus hostes veritatis ipsos infestantes, sese defenderent. Respon-deo primum: Absurdam esse, imo etiam falsam eorum opinionem, qui putant, Media illa, quibus proprie res ac negotia huius mundi defenduntur (qualia sunt tum Iudicia tum arma) non modo differre à mediis, quibus spiri-tualia defendi possunt, sed cum illi velut ex dia-metro pugnare, adeoque iis aduersari, vt nullum possint aut debeant illa, in Religionis negotio la-cum habere. At ego contra, Præcipuum opti-mi piiqué Magistratus munus esse dico, vt quic-quid mediorum authoritatis, & potentia, illi aDeo concessum est, huc totum omnino conferat, vt inter sibi. sibi Subditos Deus ipse vere agnoscatur, agnitusque tanquam summus regum omnium rex, colatur, & adoretur. Itaque qui talis erit, non solum omnes Iurisdictionis suae vires, legumque authoritatem, aduersus veras Religionis contemptores, perturbatoresve (qui censuris, admonitionibusque Ecclesiasticis nullum locum relinquunt) exeret, sed armata etiam manu in eos animaduertet, qui aliter ab impietate cohiberi nequeunt. Ad cuius sententiae confirmationem scriptura ipsa, & rationes, & exempla innumera nobis suppeditat. Rationes quidem sunt huiusmodi. Cū finis omnium bene constitutarum Politiarum non sit simpliciter huius vitae tranquillitas (vt quidam Ethnicorum Philosophorum sunt arbitrati) sed Dei gloria, ad quam tota haec hominū vita dirigenda est: Inde consequitur: Eos qui populis praesunt, omnia sua studia omnesque facultates a Deo acceptas, huc referre debere, vt purus Dei cultus, a quo ipsius gloria pendet maxime, apud eos quos in potestate habent conseruetur, promoueaturque. Deinde, vt demus, vltimum politiarum finem esse huius vitae quietam conseruationem: fatendum tamen fuerit, eius & obtinendae & conseruandae vnicam hanc esse rationem, si Deus vitae nostrae tum author, tum moderator pie, recteque colatur. Testimonia autem seu exem-pla plafunt prope infinita in scripturis. Patet enim imprimis Patriarchas illos veteres, fummos fuisse simul, & sacerdotes, & Magistratus apud suos: Quod de Melchifedecho & Heli nominatim traditur;Gen. 14. 18. 1. Sam. 4. 18. Et quamuis distincta postea duo hæc munera fuerint à Domino, hoc ideo non accidit, quod illa inter fe pugnarent: sed quod vnus vir, vtrique exercendo vix sufficeret. Præ- terea cum Rex iubetur volumen legis apud fe habere,Deut. 17. 18. vt dies & noctes in illius le lectione exerceat, non tanquam à priuato homine istud exigitur, sed tanquam à Rege & publico Magistratu. Porro inter leges, quarum executio Deut. 13. demandatur Magiftratib. illæ præcipuæ habentur, quæ veræ Religionis contemptores morti adiudicant. Quarum obseruatione in Dauide cernimus, 1. Paral. 28. qui totum Dei cultum certis legibus sanxit: Item in Salomone, qui mandata patris in transgressores impleuit. Item in ea dictis regum Asæ, Iosaphat, Ezechiæ, Iosiæ, 2. Paral. 15. & 20. v. 21. & 31.2. & 34.31. Imo etiam Nebuchadnezaris, & Darii, cum à Daniele Propheta ad Deum adorandum persuaderentur, Dan. 3 99. & 6.26. Postremo cū Apostol. affirmat, 1. Tim. 2. 2. Reges & Principes à Deo in hoc esse constitutos, non vt honeste tantum, sed etiam vt pie vitam transfigamus, (hoc est, vt
units.tr: First, since religion pertains to consciences, upon which no force can be brought to bear in any way, it does not seem that it is to be established or defended by any arms; and therefore we see that it has hitherto been propagated rather by the preaching of God's Word, by prayers and by patience. Moreover, there are very many passages of Scripture which show how great is the difference between the kingdoms of this world and the spiritual Kingdom of Christ. Finally, these are followed by the examples of the holy prophets, and of our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who, although all authority, power and might were his, never once resorted to this method of defence; nor did the Apostles themselves, nor any of the martyrs who followed; so much so that not even whole legions of Christ's faithful, most fully armed, refused to meet death rather than defend themselves by drawing the sword against the enemies who attacked the truth. I reply first: the opinion of those who think that those means by which the affairs and concerns of this world are properly defended (such as judgements and arms) not only differ from the means by which spiritual things can be defended, but fight against them as if diametrically opposed, so that they can have, or ought to have, no dealings with them in matters of religion, is absurd, indeed even false. But I, on the contrary, say that the chief duty of the best and most pious magistrate is to devote entirely to this whatever means of authority and power God has granted him: that God himself be truly acknowledged among his subjects, and, being acknowledged as the highest King of all kings, be worshipped and adored. And so whoever is such a magistrate will not only put forth all the powers of his jurisdiction and the authority of the laws against the true despisers or disturbers of religion (who leave no room for ecclesiastical censures and admonitions), but will also punish with armed hand those who cannot otherwise be restrained from impiety. For the confirmation of this view Scripture itself supplies us with reasons and countless examples. The reasons are of this kind. Since the end of all well-constituted commonwealths is not simply the tranquillity of this life (as some of the heathen philosophers have thought) but the glory of God, to which this whole human life must be directed, it follows that those who preside over peoples ought to refer all their zeal and all their faculties, received from God, to this: that the pure worship of God, on which his glory chiefly depends, be preserved and promoted among those whom they have in their power. Next, granting that the ultimate end of commonwealths is the quiet preservation of this life, it must nevertheless be admitted that the only way to attain and preserve it is if God, the author and governor of our life, is piously and rightly worshipped. The testimonies or examples are almost infinite in Scripture. For it is clear above all that those ancient patriarchs were at once chief priests and magistrates among their people; this is recorded by name of Melchizedek and Eli (Gen. 14. 18; 1 Sam. 4. 18). And although these two offices were afterwards distinguished by the Lord, this did not happen because they fought against each other, but because one man would scarcely suffice to exercise both. Moreover, when the king is commanded to keep the book of the law by him (Deut. 17. 18), so that he may exercise himself in reading it day and night, this is demanded not of him as a private man but as king and public magistrate. Further, among the laws whose execution is entrusted to magistrates (Deut. 13), those are regarded as chief which condemn to death the despisers of the true religion. We see their observance in David, who (1 Chron. 28) established the whole worship of God by fixed laws; likewise in Solomon, who carried out his father's commands against transgressors; likewise in the deeds of the kings Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah and Josiah (2 Chron. 15 and 20:21 and 31:2 and 34:31). Indeed also of Nebuchadnezzar and Darius, when they were persuaded by the prophet Daniel to worship God (Dan. 3. 99 and 6. 26). Lastly, when the Apostle affirms that kings and princes have been appointed by God in order that we may pass our lives not only honourably but also piously (1 Tim. 2. 2) (that is,

units.la: non solum sicut probos & honestos homines decet, cõuerfari in hac vita, sed etiam vt religiosos & fecundũ pietate in Deum viuere possimus, non est dubium quin tota hanc quæstionem paucissimis verbis definierit. Hinc videmus, prisca Consilia aduersus hæreticos, non authoritate Romanorum Pontificũ (qui nondum tales deprehensi fuerât, quales lõgo post tempore innotuerunt) sed Imperatorũ mandato fuisse coacta, quoties opus esse hoc remedio, expiorum Episcoporum fuafionibus cognoscerent. Extant quoque innumeræ Cõftitutiones, & Ecclesiasticì Canones, tam ab Imperatore Iustiniano, quam ab eius successoribus, atq; etiã à Carolo Magno, aliifq; editi, qui idem comprobãt. Quorsum vero hodie etiã Monarchæ à Romana illa meretrice tã furiose incitantur, ad eos, quos ipsi hæreticos vocant, igni ferreq; persequendos, & eliminandos, nisi quod hoc ipsorum muneris esse, contedit? Quain re optimo quidé & certissimo nititur fundamento, sed quo non minus, quã innumeris aliis veritatis testimoniis, abutitur, ad suas scilicet impietates & blasphemias vel stabiliendas, vel tuedas. Sed quorsum inquies, tã prolixa digressio? Neq; enim quæritur; An Reges aut magistratus pietatem tueri, & promouere debeant: Sed, an Subditi aduersus persecutores sese armis tueri possint? Respondeo ergo ad id, quod priore loco supra fuit pro-positum: Aliud efle, religionem nunc primum in aliqua regione introducere: Aliud, ea iam alicubi receptam conferuare, seu collapsam, hominumque aut conniuentia, aut inscitia, aut malitia, sepulta, velle restituere. Nam plantandam quidem ac propagandam abinitio sola fpiritusDei vir-tute confiteor, idq; verbo Dei ad docendû, arguendû, hortandumq; idoneo. Hoc enim proprium S. Sanđi opus est, instrumentis fpiritualib.vtentis. Itaq; pii Principis, q. suos ab Idololatria & falsis fuperftitionib ad vera religionem pellicere cupit, partes erunt, cu-rare primum, vt illi veris firmifq; argumentis, in pietate instituantur: Sicut è diuerso Subdito-rum partes sunt, veritati rationiq; assentiri, at facile cedere. Tandem vero Princeps piis fan-ctifque edictis, veram Religionem stabilire fata-get, aduersus eos, qui mera pertinacia illam impu-gnabunt eiue resistent. Quemadmodum no-ftris temporibus in Anglia, Dania, Suecia, Scotia, & maxima Germaniæ atque Helue-tiæ parte factum cernimus, aduersus Pon-tificios, Anabaptistas, aliosque hæreticos. Quorum exemplum si reliquæ nationes sequi mallent, quam Romanæ illi, tam fan-guinariæ Meretrici fidei, & obsequi: Næ maior in toto orbe tranquillitas, tamin sta-tu Religionis, quam Politiæ conspicere-tur, tur! Quid igitur Subditis erit agendum, si contra ad Idola colenda à suo Magistratu compellantur? Certe non patitur quidem ratio, vt principem ad mutationem omnino statim fui astringant, quin imo aut persecutionem patienter ferre (dum interea Deum pure colant) aut omnino solum vertere, nouasque sedes quaerere necesse habebunt. At si, Edictis legitime rogatis, & publica authoritate constitutis confirmatisque, semel pura Religionis liberum exercitium fuerit concessum: Tum primum dico ad eorum obseruationem tanto magis obligari, quanto negotium religionis, maioris est prae ceteris omnibus rebus momenti: adeo vt illi fas non sit, ea profuso arbitrio, & sine causa cognitione abrogare, sed eadem authoritate duntaxat intercedente, qua ab initio fuerunt sancita. Si secus fecerit, manifestam tyrannidem ipsum exercere affirmo: Cui sese opponere (adhibitis tamen supradictis obseruationibus) eo etiam liberius licebit, quo animarum salutem, conscientiaque libertatem demus plusquam res vllas, quantumuis optabiles, chariorem, pretiosioremque habere. Neminii igitur, Christi tur iam mirum fuerit, quod Dominus noster Iesus, Apostolus Christus, Prophetas item ac Apostoli, reliquiue martyres, cum priuati essent homines, sese intra metas vocationis sua continuerint. Et quod vel ad illos spectat, qui publicum gerebant munus:
units.tr: not only as honest and upright men ought to conduct themselves in this life, but that we may also live religious lives and devoted to God in piety, there is no doubt that he has defined the whole question in very few words. Hence we see that the ancient councils against heretics were compelled not by the authority of the Roman Pontiffs (who had not yet been discovered to be such as they were later well known to be) but by the command of the emperors, whenever they recognised from the advice of the holy bishops that this remedy was needed. Countless constitutions and ecclesiastical canons also survive, issued both by the emperor Justinian and his successors, and by Charlemagne and others, which confirm the same. But why today too are monarchs so furiously incited by that Roman harlot to pursue and eliminate with fire and sword those whom they call heretics, unless because they contend that this is their duty? This rests indeed on a very good and most certain foundation, but it is abused no less than countless other testimonies of truth, namely to establish or defend their own impieties and blasphemies. But you will ask, why such a long digression? For the question is not whether kings or magistrates ought to defend and promote piety, but whether subjects can defend themselves by arms against persecutors. I reply therefore to what was proposed earlier: it is one thing to introduce religion for the first time in some region; another to preserve it where it is already received, or, when it has fallen and been buried by men's connivance, ignorance or malice, to want to restore it. For I confess that to plant and propagate it from the beginning is the work of the Spirit of God alone, by his power, and that by the Word of God, suited to teaching, convicting and exhorting. For this is the proper work of the Holy Spirit, who uses spiritual instruments. Therefore it will be the part of a pious prince, who wishes to draw his subjects from idolatry and false superstitions to the true religion, first to take care that they are instructed in piety by true and firm arguments; just as, conversely, it is the part of subjects to assent to truth and reason and to yield readily. At last indeed the prince ought to establish the true religion by pious and holy edicts, against those who will attack it or resist it out of sheer obstinacy. As we see has been done in our times in England, Denmark, Sweden, Scotland, and the greatest part of Germany and Helvetia, against the Papists, the Anabaptists and other heretics. If the other nations preferred to follow this example rather than that of those Romans, who are faithful and obedient to that bloody harlot, there would be seen greater tranquillity throughout the whole world, both in the state of religion and in the commonwealth! What, then, are subjects to do if, on the contrary, they are compelled by their magistrate to worship idols? Certainly reason does not permit them to bind the prince to an immediate change of mind; rather they will necessarily have either to bear persecution patiently (meanwhile worshipping God purely) or altogether to leave their homeland and seek new dwellings. But if, once edicts have been lawfully requested and established and confirmed by public authority, free exercise of the pure religion has been granted: then I say that they are bound to observe these all the more, inasmuch as the matter of religion is of greater importance than all other things; so that it is not lawful for him to abrogate them at his arbitrary pleasure and without examining the cause, but only by the same authority by which they were originally enacted. If he acts otherwise, I affirm he is exercising manifest tyranny. Against this it will be all the more lawful to resist (with the above observations still adhered to), inasmuch as we hold the salvation of souls and freedom of conscience more precious and valuable than any things, however desirable. It should therefore be no wonder that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Apostles, the Prophets likewise, and the other martyrs, although they were private men, kept themselves within the bounds of their calling. And as to what concerns those who held public office:

units.la: Quare Pro- (marginal note, left) nus : Vel ad legiones illas, qua cum Ducibus suis Martyrium in media acie sunt perpessi, nulla oppe- sita defensione, etiam si qui illas initiabantur edicta in fauorem Christianorum prius fa- cta violassent (ut sub Diocletiano & Iuliano Imperatoribus praesertim accidit.) Duplex est, inquam, de illa responsio. Nam primo, etsi quidam Imperatores ante Diocletianum, persecutiones aliquatenus leniissent (ut fecisse Adrianum, Antoninum, & Alexandrum constat) publicum tamen religionis Christianae exercitium nunquam quisquam eorum concesserat. Deinde repeto hic quoque illud, Non quicquid licet, idque semper expedire. Neque enim dixerim semper necesse esse, Religionem publicis Edictis concessam, armis aduersus manifestam tyrannidem tueri & retinere: sed istud tamen fas esse, & licere, praesertim illis quibus hoc onus incumbit, & quibus Deus opportunitatem dederit; ut Lobnenses exemplum aduersus Ioramum, & Hierosolymitanorum, aduersus Amasiam, bellumque Constantini aduersus Maxentium, rogatu civium Romanorum suscepturn (de quibus supra) abunde euincunt. Hinc conficio, inter martyres censendos esse non solum eos, qui tyrannidem hostium veritatis, nulla alia defensione, quam patientia peruicerunt: Verum etiam illos, qui legum, aut eorum quibus ius est legis tueri, authoritate, ut par est, suffulti, manus suas Deo adduad defensionem vera Religionis confecrarunt.
units.tr: Wherefore, as for those legions which, together with their commanders, suffered martyrdom in the midst of battle without offering any defence, even though some of them had violated edicts previously issued in favour of the Christians (as happened especially under the emperors Diocletian and Julian): I say that the answer to this is twofold. First, although some emperors before Diocletian had somewhat relaxed the persecutions (as Hadrian, Antoninus and Alexander are known to have done), none of them had ever granted the public exercise of the Christian religion. Second, I repeat here also that principle: not everything that is lawful is always expedient. For I would not say that it is always necessary to defend and maintain with arms a religion conceded by public edicts against manifest tyranny; but nevertheless it is right and lawful, especially for those upon whom this burden lies and to whom God has given the opportunity. The examples of the people of Libnah against Jehoram, of the Jerusalemites against Amaziah, and of Constantine's war against Maxentius, undertaken at the request of Roman citizens (of which I spoke above), abundantly prove this. Hence I conclude that not only those who have overcome the tyranny of the enemies of the truth by no other defence than patience are to be counted among the martyrs, but also those who, supported by the authority of the laws, or of those who have the right to defend the laws, as is fitting, have dedicated their hands to God for the defence of the true religion.

units.la: Atque hęc quidem hactenus ad hanc pro- stremam obiectionem respondere placuit, in eorum gratiam qui eam in medium proponunt, vt conscientiæ suæ consulant, quia verentur nempe, ne contra Deum peccent, si quid eiusmodi tentauerint.
units.tr: And so far it has seemed good to answer this last objection, for the sake of those who put it forward, so that they may consult their conscience, since they fear, namely, lest they sin against God if they attempt anything of this kind.

units.la: Ad genus vero illud hominum quod attinet, qui aliud mundo emolumentum non præstant, quam quod innocuo sanguine omnia complent: principum authoritate abutentes, vt ex eorum ruinis, sua commoda venentur, & augeant; quique interim tanta sunt impudentia, vt his obiectionibus eos im-petere, & oppugnare audeant, qui non vltro sese illis iugulandos præbent, suam scilicet crudelitatem & effrenem licentiam, prætextu Religionis & zeli, fallo palliantes. Hoc inquam genus hominum non alia responsione dignarer, quam ea, quæ prædonibus merito fieret, qui mercatores, aliosve Viatores in ius vocarent, quod non nisi gladio accincti ad sui defensionem, itineri sese committerent, illis hoc non licere contendentes, etsi ipsi quoduis genus armorum ad illos iugulandos sufurparent. Quin mihi isti exemplum illum Fimbriam Romanum (cuiusmodi sicarios, ære conductos, multos hominum vidi et est) in memoria redūcunt: Cuius
units.tr: As for that class of men who bring the world no advantage other than that they fill everything with innocent blood, abusing the authority of princes so that they may hunt for and increase their own gains from the ruin of others; who are meanwhile so shameless that they dare to assail and attack with these objections those who do not of their own accord offer themselves to be slaughtered, thinly veiling their cruelty and unbridled license under the pretext of religion and zeal: this class of men, I say, I would not deign to answer otherwise than as one would rightly answer robbers who summon merchants or other travellers to court, contending that they may not commit themselves to a journey girded with swords except in their own defence, while the robbers themselves seize every kind of weapon to slaughter them. Indeed, these men call to my mind that Roman Fimbria (I have seen many men of that kind, hired assassins for money, and there are still many)

units.la: tam insolens fuit audacia, aut potius impudens proteruia, vt cum tempore Syllanæ proscriptionis Scæuolam, (virum inter Romanos ciues eximia tum virtute, tum probitate clarum) vulnere sauciandum curasset, nec, vt optabat, illo interemptus esset: Conqueri, illiqueminari audebat; futurum, vt in Iudicium absfe, quasi maxima iniuria affecto, vocaretur, quod sicam ad praecordia vsque non vltro admisisset. Cum eiusmodi vero hominibus, quia superflua, & inutilis foret omnis disputatio: omnes non tam ad propriam ipsorum conscientiam (qua plerique iam prorsus destituitur) quam ad illius Tribunal mihi sunt relegandi, cuius summum Imperium iudiciumque, ipsos vitare nequiuisse, & tempus & res ipsa tandem certo experimento comprobabunt.
units.tr: whose audacity was so insolent, or rather whose shameless arrogance was so great, that when, in the time of Sulla's proscription, he had arranged for Scaevola (a man among Roman citizens distinguished at that time both by outstanding virtue and by integrity) to be wounded, and he was not killed by the blow as he wished, he dared to complain and to threaten that he would be summoned to judgment, as if he had been most grievously wronged, because he had not of his own accord allowed the dagger to reach his vitals. But with men of this kind, since all disputation would be superfluous and useless, I must refer them all not so much to their own conscience (which most of them have now utterly lost) as to the tribunal of him whose supreme power and judgment they could not escape; time and the thing itself will at last prove this by certain experience.
